title: TimeSeries ML
text:
This site is organised around one concrete problem. The problem is household energy: given hourly meter readings, forecast consumption, detect anomalies, and work out which appliances are running from the total draw alone. Phisaver Project states that brief.
The site is a curriculum that follows the field’s topic map (plan: Knowledge #28). Each section covers one family of methods, from free baselines to pretrained foundation models. The original library walkthroughs (Darts, Nixtla) stay as API references under Libraries.

title: TimeSeries ML
text:
How the site works
Three choices make the pages comparable:

One dataset. Every single-series notebook uses the same public household meter data (UCI, one house, 2006 to 2010, with three sub-meters). Every many-series notebook uses M4 Hourly (414 series). Datasets loads both.
One backtest. Every forecasting notebook is scored by the same rolling-origin backtest against a seasonal naive forecast (Backtesting).
One scoreboard. Every forecasting notebook adds a row to a shared results table, so the gain of each method is a number on the same scale (Scoreboard).

The notebooks run on a small machine (4 CPU cores, 8 GB RAM, 12 GB GPU). Pages that run on CPU in a few minutes execute in CI on every push; GPU pages store their outputs.

Three lessons recur across the sections. How a model is fitted and fed matters more than its architecture (Holt-Winters goes from -13% to +12% by fitting for the right horizon). Pretrained models now beat everything built for one series, unless they have seen the test data, which one of them appears to have. And most of an hour in a household is unpredictable: the best model removes about a quarter of the simplest model’s error.

title: TimeSeries ML
text:
Start Here



Page
Covers




Phisaver Project
The brief. What is being predicted (solar, total consumption, aircon) and from which inputs, the three resolutions the meter data arrives at (hourly energy, five-minute power, one-minute sensor readings), and a taxonomy of the model families worth trying: auto-forecast, exponential smoothing, benchmarks, intermittent-demand, multiple-seasonality, and Theta

title: TimeSeries ML
text:
01 Foundations
What a series is made of, and how to get it into shape before any model sees it.



Page
Covers




Datasets
The household and M4 Hourly datasets, the download cache, resampling minutes to energy per period, gap filling, and the chart helpers every page uses


Decomposition and Stationarity
MSTL with daily and weekly seasons and their strength, the periodogram and its harmonics, ACF and PACF (lag 168 beats lag 24), and ADF against KPSS


Data Preparation
Peak versus mean power, why the timestamps are local clock time and must stay naive, a measured comparison of gap-filling methods, robust outlier flags, and scaling and log transforms


Feature Engineering
Lags, calendar and holidays, Fourier terms, rolling statistics and sub-meters added one group at a time on the backtest (the calendar gives the largest gain), and catch22 features of whole days


FFT Analysis
Building a synthetic multi-frequency signal, then using wavelets and FFT features to feed a random forest regressor

title: TimeSeries ML
text:
02 Evaluation
How every model on the site is scored, and the ways a score can lie. Read Backtesting before any model page.



Page
Covers




Backtesting and Leakage
The rolling-origin protocol (30 day-ahead windows over the last 150 days), the backtest, score and record functions, and five leakage bugs measured side by side: shuffled CV, short lags, unshifted rolling means, whole-series statistics and tuning on the test set


Forecast Metrics
MAE, RMSE, MAPE, sMAPE, WAPE, MASE and skill on three series from the same house; why MAPE is infinite and sMAPE flatters on sparse series; why the site reports MASE and skill


Benchmarks
M4, Monash, ETT, GIFT-Eval and fev-bench; five questions for reading a leaderboard; the ETTh1 long-horizon protocol (a ridge layer beats both baselines) and the M4 Hourly protocol run by hand


Scoreboard
Every model on the site in one table per dataset, best MASE first

title: TimeSeries ML
text:
03 Classical Statistical Forecasting
From free baselines to state space models, each scored on the household backtest. The best classical model, SARIMA, is level with gradient boosting.



Page
Covers




Baselines
Naive, mean, drift, seasonal naive and four-week seasonal windows; the window mean or median (+4%) is the free forecast to beat


Exponential Smoothing (ETS)
Holt-Winters equations; the default one-step fit loses to seasonal naive, smoothing chosen for 24 steps gives +12%; ETS on daily totals


ARIMA
Identification from ACF and PACF, order by AIC, Ljung-Box residual checks, SARIMA (+17%), and weekly Fourier terms that cost skill on three weeks of data


Theta and Intermittent Demand
Theta as SES with drift; Croston, SBA, TSB and ADIDA on the sparse kitchen circuit, and why MAE rewards the zero forecast


State Space and the Kalman Filter
A Kalman filter in twelve lines, the proof that SES is its steady state, gaps handled by the smoother, and a structural model on the backtest


VAR and Granger Causality
Every circuit Granger-causes every other through a common cause; a VAR on the circuits does not beat an AR on the total


GARCH
Volatility clustering in daily consumption, highest in winter; GARCH intervals closer to 90% coverage and 13% narrower than constant-variance ones


Prophet
The original hourly-energy tutorial, plus Prophet on this site’s backtest, where it ties the four-week seasonal window

title: TimeSeries ML
text:
04 Machine Learning Forecasting
Forecasting rewritten as regression. Gradient boosting with one model per output hour is the best model on the household scoreboard so far (+18%).



Page
Covers




Forecasting as Regression
Building the supervised table without leaks; ridge from a two-week window to 24 hours (+12%), and gradient boosting on the same table (+18%); why ridge weights on correlated lags cannot be read


Multi-step Strategies
Recursive, direct, MIMO and lags-of-24-hours compared hour by hour: recursive errors compound, and direct only wins in the first hours


Global vs Local Models
One LightGBM for 414 M4 series against one per series: global wins once the series are differenced and scaled, and the metric decides the transform


XGBoost
The algorithm itself, worked through from first principles


XGBoost: Forecast Energy Consumption
The original PJM energy tutorial, plus XGBoost on this site’s backtest with the shared features (+17.5%)

title: TimeSeries ML
text:
05 Deep Learning Forecasting
Neural forecasters trained on the GPU (these pages store their outputs and do not run in CI). The best model on the site lives here: N-BEATS written from scratch, at +24% skill.



Page
Covers




The Deep Learning Data Pipeline
Windows at every hour, normalisation (no measurable effect on this series) and lookback length (one week is best) with a small PyTorch MLP; seed spread and seed ensembles


RNN, LSTM and DeepAR
Recurrence and gating, DeepAR’s probabilistic autoregression; both near +20%, and why the field moved on anyway


The MLP Family
N-BEATS, N-HiTS, TiDE and DLinear; DLinear reaches +15% with 8,112 parameters


Transformers
PatchTST, iTransformer and TFT; TFT best at +20%, and the DLinear test (a linear layer is 7% behind on this task, and why)


N-BEATS from Scratch
Doubly residual stacking in sixty lines of PyTorch, each block’s contribution plotted, and a result that beats the library version

title: TimeSeries ML
text:
06 Foundation Models
Pretrained forecasters used zero-shot, with no training on this house (GPU pages with stored outputs). Three of them beat every classical and gradient-boosting model built for it.



Page
Covers




Chronos-2 Zero-Shot
What a foundation model is; Chronos-2 univariate (+22%), with calendar covariates and with the sub-meters (no gain)


Foundation Model Comparison
The GIFT-Eval standings on 14 Nov 2026 and licences; Chronos-2, Chronos-Bolt, TiRex (+24%) and TimesFM 2.5 on the backtest, and a spike test suggesting TimesFM 2.5 has seen this dataset


Fine-Tuning Chronos-2
Full and LoRA fine-tuning on the pre-test history: about one point of gain for 1.5 to 5 minutes of GPU time


Small Models on CPU
Chronos-Bolt tiny (9 M parameters, 15 ms per forecast on one thread, +20%), Chronos-2 and TiRex without a GPU

title: TimeSeries ML
text:
07 Probabilistic Forecasting
Forecasting ranges instead of numbers, and checking that a “90%” interval really covers 90%.



Page
Covers




Probabilistic Forecasting
Quantiles, pinball loss, CRPS, coverage and width; empirical quantiles from four weeks cover only half of a “90%” band, quantile LightGBM covers 86%


Conformal Prediction
Split conformal, CQR and adaptive conformal inference on a drifting series; ACI reaches 88%, CQR is 13% narrower than split conformal, and why 30 days cannot settle a coverage claim

title: TimeSeries ML
text:
08 Other Tasks
Time series problems that are not forecasting, each tested on labelled events.



Page
Covers




Anomaly Detection
24 injected meter faults (spikes, dropouts, stuck readings); generic detectors miss most of them, two structural rules plus a spike score find 23 of 24 at 0.1 false flags a week


Change-Point Detection
PELT and binary segmentation find the real regimes (heating, the August 2008 absence); a negative result on injected +40% shifts, which are ordinary in this house


The Matrix Profile
Motifs and discords with STUMPY; the exact motif is the loader’s own gap filling; shape versus size


Classification with MiniRocket
Random convolution kernels against catch22: 96.5% against 84.3% on ItalyPowerDemand, and weekday or weekend in this house

title: TimeSeries ML
text:
09 Many Series



Page
Covers




Hierarchical Reconciliation
The house total and its four circuits made to add up: bottom-up, top-down, OLS, WLS and MinT in numpy; bottom-up is best for the total

title: TimeSeries ML
text:
10 Production
What happens after the backtest: explaining a forecast, keeping a model current, and shipping it.



Page
Covers




Explainability
SHAP values from LightGBM itself and grouped permutation importance; why correlated time series features make importance rankings disagree


Drift and Retraining
Five retraining schedules (refitting adds a point, forgetting old data costs six) and PSI drift that is mostly the calendar


ONNX Export
A PyTorch forecaster exported to ONNX, verified to a millionth of a kWh, and 2.4 times faster in ONNX Runtime

API walkthroughs, mostly following each project’s own tutorials and data. The topic pages above link here instead of repeating them.



Page
Covers




Darts
The long tour: training and predicting, inspecting seasonality, hyper-parameter search with Theta, backtesting against history, global models trained across many series, N-BEATS for the deep learning case, covariates and encoders for external data, and probabilistic forecasts with their distributions


Darts Hyper-parameter Optimization
Tuning a deep model for electricity load with confidence intervals: a linear baseline, then TCN, then Optuna over its parameters, then picking the winner

Training many statistical models over many series at once, evaluating them, and selecting the best per series


Nixtla MLForecast
The machine learning arm, including distributed training via Spark and LightGBM

Fitting LSTM and NHITS on AirPassengers, then plotting the predictions

Training and forecasting with external inputs, both historical and known-future

Persisting a trained neural forecaster and reading it back


Nixtla Neural Advanced
The multi-series version: train several neural models, evaluate, and select per series


Nixtla All Methods
Statistical, machine learning, and neural forecasts over the M5 dataset, cross-validated and evaluated per series and per window

title: TimeSeries ML
text:
Not Covered Yet
Stated plainly, so the gaps are not mistaken for oversights:

Appliance disaggregation: recovering per-appliance draw from the total signal. The household dataset’s sub-meters make it possible, but no page attempts it.
Phisaver’s own data: it is private, so no page here uses it. It would also be the clean test for foundation models, which may have seen this public dataset.
Newer foundation models: TimesFM-3, Toto-2.0 and TiRex-2 lead GIFT-Eval but are not tested here; Moirai and IBM’s TTM cannot be installed in this environment without downgrades.
Weather and other covariates: no page uses temperature, which drives heating load; every covariate tried (calendar, sub-meters) added nothing over the target’s own history.
Probabilistic scoring of the deep and foundation models: DeepAR, Chronos-2 and TiRex produce quantiles, but only quantile LightGBM and the conformal methods are scored on coverage and CRPS.
Change points on forecast residuals, and TFT attention explanations, both proposed on their pages and not run.
A winter test period: the backtest covers late June to late November 2010, so every score here is a summer-into-autumn score.

WarningPrerequesites





This Guide assumes basic familiarity with NeuralForecast. For a minimal example visit the Quick Start
Follow this article for a step to step guide on building a production-ready forecasting pipeline for multiple time series.
During this guide you will gain familiary with the core NueralForecastclass and some relevant methods like NeuralForecast.fit, NeuralForecast.predict, and StatsForecast.cross_validation.
We will use a classical benchmarking dataset from the M4 competition. The dataset includes time series from different domains like finance, economy and sales. In this example, we will use a subset of the Hourly dataset.
We will model each time series globally Therefore, you will train a set of models for the whole dataset, and then select the best model for each individual time series. NeuralForecast focuses on speed, simplicity, and scalability, which makes it ideal for this task.

title: Nixtla - Neural Advanced Forecast
text:
1. Install libraries
We assume you have NeuralForecast already installed. Check this guide for instructions on how to install NeuralForecast.
Additionally, we will install s3fs to read from the S3 Filesystem of AWS, statsforecast for plotting, and datasetsforecast for common error metrics like MAE or MASE.
Install the necessary packages using pip install statsforecast s3fs datasetsforecast ``

%%capture ! pip install statsforecast s3fs datasetsforecast
%%capture ! pip install git+https://github.com/Nixtla/neuralforecast.git@main

title: Nixtla - Neural Advanced Forecast
text:
2. Read the data
We will use pandas to read the M4 Hourly data set stored in a parquet file for efficiency. You can use ordinary pandas operations to read your data in other formats likes .csv.
The input to NeuralForecast is always a data frame in long format with three columns: unique_id, ds and y:

The unique_id (string, int or category) represents an identifier for the series.
The ds (datestamp or int) column should be either an integer indexing time or a datestampe ideally like YYYY-MM-DD for a date or YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS for a timestamp.
The y (numeric) represents the measurement we wish to forecast. We will rename the

This data set already satisfies the requirement.
Depending on your internet connection, this step should take around 10 seconds.


import pandas as pd

Y_df = pd.read_parquet('https://datasets-nixtla.s3.amazonaws.com/m4-hourly.parquet')

title: Nixtla - Neural Advanced Forecast
section: 4. Train multiple models for many series
text:
4. Train multiple models for many series
NeuralForecast can train many models on many time series globally and efficiently.


from ray import tune

from neuralforecast import NeuralForecast
from neuralforecast.auto import AutoNHITS, AutoLSTM
from neuralforecast.losses.pytorch import MQLoss

Each Auto model contains a default search space that was extensively tested on multiple large-scale datasets. Additionally, users can define specific search spaces tailored for particular datasets and tasks.
First, we create a custom search space for the AutoNHITS and AutoLSTM models. Search spaces are specified with dictionaries, where keys corresponds to the model’s hyperparameter and the value is a Tune function to specify how the hyperparameter will be sampled. For example, use randint to sample integers uniformly, and choice to sample values of a list.

config_nhits = {
    "input_size": tune.choice([48, 48*2, 48*3]),              # Length of input window
    "start_padding_enabled": True,
    "n_blocks": 5*[1],                                              # Length of input window
    "mlp_units": 5 * [[64, 64]],                                  # Length of input window
    "n_pool_kernel_size": tune.choice([5*[1], 5*[2], 5*[4],         
                                      [8, 4, 2, 1, 1]]),            # MaxPooling Kernel size
    "n_freq_downsample": tune.choice([[8, 4, 2, 1, 1],
                                      [1, 1, 1, 1, 1]]),            # Interpolation expressivity ratios
    "learning_rate": tune.loguniform(1e-4, 1e-2),                   # Initial Learning rate
    "scaler_type": tune.choice([None]),                             # Scaler type
    "max_steps": tune.choice([1000]),                               # Max number of training iterations
    "batch_size": tune.choice([1, 4, 10]),                          # Number of series in batch
    "windows_batch_size": tune.choice([128, 256, 512]),             # Number of windows in batch
    "random_seed": tune.randint(1, 20),                             # Random seed
}

config_lstm = {
    "input_size": tune.choice([48, 48*2, 48*3]),              # Length of input window
    "encoder_hidden_size": tune.choice([64, 128]),            # Hidden size of LSTM cells
    "encoder_n_layers": tune.choice([2,4]),                   # Number of layers in LSTM
    "learning_rate": tune.loguniform(1e-4, 1e-2),             # Initial Learning rate
    "scaler_type": tune.choice(['robust']),                   # Scaler type
    "max_steps": tune.choice([500, 1000]),                    # Max number of training iterations
    "batch_size": tune.choice([1, 4]),                        # Number of series in batch
    "random_seed": tune.randint(1, 20),                       # Random seed
}

To instantiate an Auto model you need to define:

h: forecasting horizon.
loss: training and validation loss from neuralforecast.losses.pytorch.
config: hyperparameter search space. If None, the Auto class will use a pre-defined suggested hyperparameter space.
search_alg: search algorithm (from tune.search), default is random search. Refer to https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/tune/api_docs/suggestion.html for more information on the different search algorithm options.
num_samples: number of configurations explored.

In this example we set horizon h as 48, use the MQLoss distribution loss for training and validation, and use the default search algorithm.

nf = NeuralForecast(
    models=[
        AutoNHITS(h=48, config=config_nhits, loss=MQLoss(), num_samples=5),
        AutoLSTM(h=48, config=config_lstm, loss=MQLoss(), num_samples=2),
    ],
    freq='H'
)







Tip



The number of samples, num_samples, is a crucial parameter! Larger values will usually produce better results as we explore more configurations in the search space, but it will increase training times. Larger search spaces will usually require more samples. As a general rule, we recommend setting num_samples higher than 20.


Next, we use the Neuralforecast class to train the Auto model. In this step, Auto models will automatically perform hyperparameter tuning training multiple models with different hyperparameters, producing the forecasts on the validation set, and evaluating them. The best configuration is selected based on the error on a validation set. Only the best model is stored and used during inference.

%%capture
nf.fit(df=Y_df)

title: Nixtla - Neural Advanced Forecast
text:
5. Evaluate the model’s performance
In previous steps, we’ve taken our historical data to predict the future. However, to asses its accuracy we would also like to know how the model would have performed in the past. To assess the accuracy and robustness of your models on your data perform Cross-Validation.
With time series data, Cross Validation is done by defining a sliding window across the historical data and predicting the period following it. This form of cross-validation allows us to arrive at a better estimation of our model’s predictive abilities across a wider range of temporal instances while also keeping the data in the training set contiguous as is required by our models.
The following graph depicts such a Cross Validation Strategy:








Tip



Setting n_windows=1 mirrors a traditional train-test split with our historical data serving as the training set and the last 48 hours serving as the testing set.


The cross_validation method from the NeuralForecast class takes the following arguments.

df: training data frame
step_size (int): step size between each window. In other words: how often do you want to run the forecasting processes.
n_windows (int): number of windows used for cross validation. In other words: what number of forecasting processes in the past do you want to evaluate.


from neuralforecast.auto import AutoNHITS, AutoLSTM
config_nhits = {
    "input_size": tune.choice([48, 48*2, 48*3]),              # Length of input window
    "start_padding_enabled": True,
    "n_blocks": 5*[1],                                              # Length of input window
    "mlp_units": 5 * [[64, 64]],                                  # Length of input window
    "n_pool_kernel_size": tune.choice([5*[1], 5*[2], 5*[4],         
                                      [8, 4, 2, 1, 1]]),            # MaxPooling Kernel size
    "n_freq_downsample": tune.choice([[8, 4, 2, 1, 1],
                                      [1, 1, 1, 1, 1]]),            # Interpolation expressivity ratios
    "learning_rate": tune.loguniform(1e-4, 1e-2),                   # Initial Learning rate
    "scaler_type": tune.choice([None]),                             # Scaler type
    "max_steps": tune.choice([1000]),                               # Max number of training iterations
    "batch_size": tune.choice([1, 4, 10]),                          # Number of series in batch
    "windows_batch_size": tune.choice([128, 256, 512]),             # Number of windows in batch
    "random_seed": tune.randint(1, 20),                             # Random seed
}

config_lstm = {
    "input_size": tune.choice([48, 48*2, 48*3]),              # Length of input window
    "encoder_hidden_size": tune.choice([64, 128]),            # Hidden size of LSTM cells
    "encoder_n_layers": tune.choice([2,4]),                   # Number of layers in LSTM
    "learning_rate": tune.loguniform(1e-4, 1e-2),             # Initial Learning rate
    "scaler_type": tune.choice(['robust']),                   # Scaler type
    "max_steps": tune.choice([500, 1000]),                    # Max number of training iterations
    "batch_size": tune.choice([1, 4]),                        # Number of series in batch
    "random_seed": tune.randint(1, 20),                       # Random seed
}
nf = NeuralForecast(
    models=[
        AutoNHITS(h=48, config=config_nhits, loss=MQLoss(), num_samples=5),
        AutoLSTM(h=48, config=config_lstm, loss=MQLoss(), num_samples=2), 
    ],
    freq='H'
)

section: 6. Select the best model for every unique series
text:
6. Select the best model for every unique series
Define a utility function that takes your forecast’s data frame with the predictions and the evaluation data frame and returns a data frame with the best possible forecast for every unique_id.

def get_best_model_forecast(forecasts_df, evaluation_df, metric):
    df = forecasts_df.set_index('ds', append=True).stack().to_frame().reset_index(level=2) # Wide to long 
    df.columns = ['model', 'best_model_forecast'] 
    df = df.join(evaluation_df.query('metric == @metric').set_index('unique_id')[['best_model']])
    df = df.query('model.str.replace("-lo-90|-hi-90", "", regex=True) == best_model').copy()
    df.loc[:, 'model'] = [model.replace(bm, 'best_model') for model, bm in zip(df['model'], df['best_model'])]
    df = df.drop(columns='best_model').set_index('model', append=True).unstack()
    df.columns = df.columns.droplevel()
    df = df.reset_index(level=1)
    return df

title: Exogenous Variables
text:
Exogenous variables can provide additional information to greatly improve forecasting accuracy. Some examples include price or future promotions variables for demand forecasting, and weather data for electricity load forecast. In this notebook we show an example on how to add different types of exogenous variables to NeuralForecast models for making day-ahead hourly electricity price forecasts (EPF) for France and Belgium markets.
All NeuralForecast models are capable of incorporating exogenous variables to model the following conditional predictive distribution: \[\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{y}_{t+1:t+H} \;|\; \mathbf{y}_{[:t]},\; \mathbf{x}^{(h)}_{[:t]},\; \mathbf{x}^{(f)}_{[:t+H]},\; \mathbf{x}^{(s)} )\]
where the regressors are static exogenous \(\mathbf{x}^{(s)}\), historic exogenous \(\mathbf{x}^{(h)}_{[:t]}\), exogenous available at the time of the prediction \(\mathbf{x}^{(f)}_{[:t+H]}\) and autorregresive features \(\mathbf{y}_{[:t]}\). Depending on the train loss, the model outputs can be point forecasts (location estimators) or uncertainty intervals (quantiles).
We will show you how to include exogenous variables in the data, specify variables to a model, and produce forecasts using future exogenous variables.
You can run these experiments using GPU with Google Colab.

title: Exogenous Variables
text:
3. Training with exogenous variables
We distinguish the exogenous variables by whether they reflect static or time-dependent aspects of the modeled data.

Static exogenous variables: The static exogenous variables carry time-invariant information for each time series. When the model is built with global parameters to forecast multiple time series, these variables allow sharing information within groups of time series with similar static variable levels. Examples of static variables include designators such as identifiers of regions, groups of products, etc.
Historic exogenous variables: This time-dependent exogenous variable is restricted to past observed values. Its predictive power depends on Granger-causality, as its past values can provide significant information about future values of the target variable \(\mathbf{y}\).
Future exogenous variables: In contrast with historic exogenous variables, future values are available at the time of the prediction. Examples include calendar variables, weather forecasts, and known events that can cause large spikes and dips such as scheduled promotions.

To add exogenous variables to the model, first specify the name of each variable from the previous dataframes to the corresponding model hyperparameter during initialization: futr_exog_list, hist_exog_list, and stat_exog_list. We also set horizon as 24 to produce the next day hourly forecasts, and set input_size to use the last 5 days of data as input.

from neuralforecast.auto import NHITS
from neuralforecast.core import NeuralForecast

import logging
logging.getLogger("pytorch_lightning").setLevel(logging.WARNING)


horizon = 24 # day-ahead daily forecast
models = [NHITS(h = horizon,
                input_size = 5*horizon,
                max_steps=10,
                futr_exog_list = ['gen_forecast', 'week_day'], # <- Future exogenous variables
                hist_exog_list = ['system_load'], # <- Historical exogenous variables
                stat_exog_list = ['market_0', 'market_1'], # <- Static exogenous variables
                scaler_type = 'robust')]

Global seed set to 1








Tip



When including exogenous variables always use a scaler by setting the scaler_type hyperparameter. The scaler will scale all the temporal features: the target variable y, historic and future variables.








Important



Make sure future and historic variables are correctly placed. Defining historic variables as future variables will lead to data leakage.


Next, pass the datasets to the df and static_df inputs of the fit method.

nf = NeuralForecast(models=models, freq='H')
nf.fit(df=df,
       static_df=static_df,
      )

title: Darts - Hyper-parameters Optimization for Electricity Load Forecasting
text:
We will work with this dataset (readily available in darts.datasets), which contains measurements of the electricity consumption for 370 clients of a Portuguese energy company, obtained with a 15 minutes frequency. We will attempt to forecast over a horizon of 2 weeks. At this frequency, this means we attempt to forecast 2,688 time steps in the future. This is a quite demanding requirements, and we will try to find a good model to do this.
We will use the open-source Optuna library for the hyperparameter optimization, and Darts’ TCN Model (see here for an introductory article to this model). This model employs dilated convolutions, which work great when capturing such high frequency series (15 minutes) over long periods (multiple weeks), while keeping a small overall model size.
It is recommended to have a GPU to run this notebook, although all of the concepts apply irrespective of whether the models run on CPU or GPU.

text:
Data Preparation
The following cell can take a few minutes to execute. It’ll download about 250 MB of data from the Internet. We specify multivariate=False, so we get a list of 370 univariate TimeSeries. We could also have specified multivariate=True to obtain one multivariate TimeSeries containing 370 components.

We keep the last 80 days for each series, and cast all of them to float32:
We have 370 univariate TimeSeries, each with a frequency of 15 minutes. In what follows, we will be training a single global model on all of them.
First, we create our training set. We set aside the last 14 days as test set, and the 14 days before that as validation set (which will be used for hyperparameter optimization).
Note that the val and test sets below only contain the 14-days “forecast evaluation” parts of the series. Throughout the notebook, we’ll evaluate how accurate some 14-days forecasts are over val (or test). However, to produce these 14-days forecasts, our models will consume a certain lookback window in_len worth of time stamps. For this reason, below we will also create validation sets that include these extra in_len points (as in_len is a hyper-parameter itself, we create these longer validation sets dynamically); it will be mainly useful for early-stopping.

# Split in train/val/test
val_len = 14 * DAY_DURATION  # 14 days

train = [s[: -(2 * val_len)] for s in all_series_fp32]
val = [s[-(2 * val_len) : -val_len] for s in all_series_fp32]
test = [s[-val_len:] for s in all_series_fp32]

# Scale so that the largest value is 1.
# This way of scaling perserves the sMAPE
scaler = Scaler(scaler=MaxAbsScaler())
train = scaler.fit_transform(train)
val = scaler.transform(val)
test = scaler.transform(test)

for i in [10, 50, 100, 150, 250, 350]:

We start off without any hyperparameter optimization, and try a simple linear regression model first. It will serve as a baseline. In this model, we use a lookback window of 1 week.
Note: doing significantly better than linear regression is often not trivial! We recommend to always consider at least one such reasonably simple baseline first, before jumping to more complex models.

text:
Build a Simple TCN Model
We now build a TCN model with some simple choice of hyperparameters, but without any hyperparameter optimization.


""" We write a function to build and fit a TCN Model, which we will re-use later.
"""

#|eval: false

def build_fit_tcn_model(
    in_len,
    out_len,
    kernel_size,
    num_filters,
    weight_norm,
    dilation_base,
    dropout,
    lr,
    include_dayofweek,
    likelihood=None,
    callbacks=None,
):

    # reproducibility
    torch.manual_seed(42)

    # some fixed parameters that will be the same for all models
    BATCH_SIZE = 512
    MAX_N_EPOCHS = 4
    NR_EPOCHS_VAL_PERIOD = 1
    MAX_SAMPLES_PER_TS = 100

    # throughout training we'll monitor the validation loss for early stopping
    early_stopper = EarlyStopping("val_loss", min_delta=0.001, patience=3, verbose=True)
    if callbacks is None:
        callbacks = [early_stopper]
    else:
        callbacks = [early_stopper] + callbacks

    # detect if a GPU is available
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        pl_trainer_kwargs = {
            "accelerator": "gpu",
            "callbacks": callbacks,
        }
        num_workers = 4
    else:
        pl_trainer_kwargs = {"callbacks": callbacks}
        num_workers = 0

    # optionally also add the day of the week (cyclically encoded) as a past covariate
    encoders = {"cyclic": {"past": ["dayofweek"]}} if include_dayofweek else None

    # build the TCN model
    model = TCNModel(
        input_chunk_length=in_len,
        output_chunk_length=out_len,
        batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,
        n_epochs=MAX_N_EPOCHS,
        nr_epochs_val_period=NR_EPOCHS_VAL_PERIOD,
        kernel_size=kernel_size,
        num_filters=num_filters,
        weight_norm=weight_norm,
        dilation_base=dilation_base,
        dropout=dropout,
        optimizer_kwargs={"lr": lr},
        add_encoders=encoders,
        likelihood=likelihood,
        pl_trainer_kwargs=pl_trainer_kwargs,
        model_name="tcn_model",
        force_reset=True,
        save_checkpoints=True,
    )

    # when validating during training, we can use a slightly longer validation
    # set which also contains the first input_chunk_length time steps
    model_val_set = scaler.transform(
        [s[-((2 * val_len) + in_len) : -val_len] for s in all_series_fp32]
    )

    # train the model
    model.fit(
        series=train,
        val_series=model_val_set,
        max_samples_per_ts=MAX_SAMPLES_PER_TS,
        num_loader_workers=num_workers,
    )

    # reload best model over course of training
    model = TCNModel.load_from_checkpoint("tcn_model")

    return model


model = build_fit_tcn_model(
    in_len=7 * DAY_DURATION,
    out_len=6 * DAY_DURATION,

    num_filters=5,
    weight_norm=False,
    dilation_base=2,
    dropout=0.2,
    lr=1e-3,
    include_dayofweek=True,
)

Above, we built a first TCN model without any hyper-parameter search, and got an sMAPE of about 17%. Although this model looks like a good start (performing quite well on some of the series), it’s not as good as the simple linear regression.
We can certainly do better, because there are many parameters that we have fixed but could have a large impact on performance, such as:

The architecture of the network (number of filters, dilation size, kernel size, etc…)
The learning rate
Whether to use weight normalization and/or the dropout rate
The length of the lookback and lookforward windows
Whether to add calendar covariates, such as day-of-the-week
…


One Option: using gridsearch()
One way to try and optimize these hyper-parameters is to try all combinations (assuming we have discretized our parameters). Darts offers a gridsearch() method to do just that. The advantage is that it is very simple to use. However, it also has severe drawbacks:

It takes exponential time in the number of hyper-parameters: grid-searching over any non-trivial number of hyperparameters thus quickly becomes intractable.
Gridsearch is naive: it does not attempt to pay attention to regions of the hyperparameter space that are more promising than others. It is limited points in the pre-defined grid.
Finally, for simplicity reasons the Darts gridsearch() method is (at least at the time of writing) limited to working on one time series only.

For all these reasons, for any serious hyperparameter search, we need better techniques than grid-search. Fortunately, there are some great tools out there to help us.

title: Darts - Hyper-parameters Optimization for Electricity Load Forecasting
text:
Using Optuna
Optuna is a very nice open-source library for hyperparameter optimization. It’s based on ideas such as Bayesian optimization, which balance exploration (of the hyperparameter space) with exploitation (namely, exploring more the parts of the space that look more promising). It can also use pruning in order to stop unpromising experiments early.
It’s very easy to make it work: Optuna will take care of suggesting (sampling) hyper-parameters for us, and more or less all we need to do is to compute the objective value for a set of hyperparameters. In our case it consists in using these hyperparameters to build a model, train it, and report the obtained validation accuracy. We also setup a PyTorch Lightning pruning callback in order to early-stop unpromising experiments. All of this is done in the objective() function below.


def objective(trial):
    callback = [PyTorchLightningPruningCallback(trial, monitor="val_loss")]

    # set input_chunk_length, between 5 and 14 days
    days_in = trial.suggest_int("days_in", 5, 14)
    in_len = days_in * DAY_DURATION

    # set out_len, between 1 and 13 days (it has to be strictly shorter than in_len).
    days_out = trial.suggest_int("days_out", 1, days_in - 1)
    out_len = days_out * DAY_DURATION

    # Other hyperparameters
    kernel_size = trial.suggest_int("kernel_size", 5, 25)
    num_filters = trial.suggest_int("num_filters", 5, 25)
    weight_norm = trial.suggest_categorical("weight_norm", [False, True])
    dilation_base = trial.suggest_int("dilation_base", 2, 4)
    dropout = trial.suggest_float("dropout", 0.0, 0.4)
    lr = trial.suggest_float("lr", 5e-5, 1e-3, log=True)
    include_dayofweek = trial.suggest_categorical("dayofweek", [False, True])

    # build and train the TCN model with these hyper-parameters:
    model = build_fit_tcn_model(
        in_len=in_len,
        out_len=out_len,
        kernel_size=kernel_size,
        num_filters=num_filters,
        weight_norm=weight_norm,
        dilation_base=dilation_base,
        dropout=dropout,
        lr=lr,
        include_dayofweek=include_dayofweek,
        callbacks=callback,
    )

    # Evaluate how good it is on the validation set
    preds = model.predict(series=train, n=val_len)
    smapes = smape(val, preds, n_jobs=-1, verbose=True)
    smape_val = np.mean(smapes)

    return smape_val if smape_val != np.nan else float("inf")

Now that we have specified our objective, all we need to do is create an Optuna study, and run the optimization. We can either ask Optuna to run for a specified period of time (as we do here), or a certain number of trials. Let’s run the optimization for a couple of hours:

def print_callback(study, trial):
    print(f"Current value: {trial.value}, Current params: {trial.params}")
    print(f"Best value: {study.best_value}, Best params: {study.best_trial.params}")


study = optuna.create_study(direction="minimize")

study.optimize(objective, n_trials=2, callbacks=[print_callback])

# We could also have used a command as follows to limit the number of trials instead:
# study.optimize(objective, n_trials=100, callbacks=[print_callback])

# Finally, print the best value and best hyperparameters:
print(f"Best value: {study.best_value}, Best params: {study.best_trial.params}")

title: Darts - Hyper-parameters Optimization for Electricity Load Forecasting
text:
Conclusions
We have seen in this notebook that Optuna can be seamlessly used to optimize the hyper-parameters of Darts’ models. In fact, there’s nothing really particular to Darts when it comes to hyperparameter optimization: Optuna and other libraries can be used as they would with other frameworks. The only thing to be aware of are the PyTorch Ligthning integrations, which are available through Darts.

Side conclusion: shall we go with linear regression or TCN to forecast electricty consumption?
Both approaches have pros and cons.
Pros of linear regression:

Simplicity
Does not require scaling
Speed
Does not require a GPU
Often provides good performance out-of-the-box, without requiring tuning

Cons of linear regression:

Can require a significant amount of memory (when used as a global model as here), although there are ways around that (e.g., SGD-based).
In our setting, it’s impractical to train a stochastic version of the LinearRegression model, as this would incur too large a computational complexity.

TCN, pros:

Potentially more tuneable and powerful
Typically lower memory requirements thanks to SGD
Very rich support to capture stochasticity in different ways, without requiring significantly more computation
Very fast bulk inference over many time series once the model is trained - especially if using a GPU

TCN, cons:

More hyperparameters, which can take longer to tune and offer more risks of overfitting. It also means that the model is harder to industrialize and maintain
Will often require a GPU

title: ONNX Export
text:
A model trained in a notebook usually runs somewhere else: a web service, a gateway beside the meter, a job written in another language. ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) is a file format for the computation graph and its weights; ONNX Runtime executes it on CPU or GPU from Python, C++, C#, Java or JavaScript, without PyTorch installed. The deployment then depends on one small runtime instead of the training stack.
Exporting is a translation, and translations can be wrong: an operator with a different default, a shape that was fixed when it should be dynamic. So the rule is to verify before deploying: run the same inputs through both and check the outputs agree to floating-point precision.
The model is the calendar-aware MLP from The Deep Learning Data Pipeline (one-week lookback), retrained here on the CPU in a few seconds. PyTorch’s exporter (torch.onnx.export with dynamo=True) needs the onnx and onnxscript packages.
This page carries skip_exec and stored outputs for a packaging reason, not a GPU one: the shared environment uses onnxruntime-gpu, and listing onnxruntime in this site’s CI dependencies would install a second, conflicting copy of the same module. The exported file goes to a temporary folder and is not committed.


import contextlib
import io
import os
import tempfile
import time
import warnings

import numpy as np
import onnxruntime as ort
import pandas as pd
import torch
from torch import nn

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, origins, score
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, load_household, show

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # exporter deprecation warnings print local install paths
torch.manual_seed(0)
torch.set_num_threads(4)


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
L, H = 168, 24
O = origins(y.index)
train = torch.tensor(y.iloc[:O[0]].to_numpy(np.float32))
idx = y.index[:O[0]]
x = train[:-H].unfold(0, L, 1)
t = train[L:].unfold(0, H, 1)
n = min(len(x), len(t))
first = idx[L:L + n]
cal = torch.tensor(np.column_stack([np.eye(24)[first.hour], np.eye(7)[first.dayofweek]]), dtype=torch.float32)
x, t = x[:n], t[:n]


class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden: int = 256):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(L + 31, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, H))

    def forward(self, window, calendar):
        mu = window.mean(1, keepdim=True)
        sd = window.std(1, keepdim=True) + 1e-3
        return self.net(torch.cat([(window - mu) / sd, calendar], 1)) * sd + mu


model = MLP()
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(10):
    for b in torch.randperm(n).split(512):
        loss = (model(x[b], cal[b]) - t[b]).abs().mean()
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
model.eval()
print(f"trained on CPU in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s; {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()):,} parameters")

trained on CPU in 3 s; 123,160 parameters

title: ONNX Export
text:
A model trained in a notebook usually runs somewhere else: a web service, a gateway beside the meter, a job written in another language. ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) is a file format for the computation graph and its weights; ONNX Runtime executes it on CPU or GPU from Python, C++, C#, Java or JavaScript, without PyTorch installed. The deployment then depends on one small runtime instead of the training stack.
Exporting is a translation, and translations can be wrong: an operator with a different default, a shape that was fixed when it should be dynamic. So the rule is to verify before deploying: run the same inputs through both and check the outputs agree to floating-point precision.
The model is the calendar-aware MLP from The Deep Learning Data Pipeline (one-week lookback), retrained here on the CPU in a few seconds. PyTorch’s exporter (torch.onnx.export with dynamo=True) needs the onnx and onnxscript packages.
This page carries skip_exec and stored outputs for a packaging reason, not a GPU one: the shared environment uses onnxruntime-gpu, and listing onnxruntime in this site’s CI dependencies would install a second, conflicting copy of the same module. The exported file goes to a temporary folder and is not committed.


import contextlib
import io
import os
import tempfile
import time
import warnings

import numpy as np
import onnxruntime as ort
import pandas as pd
import torch
from torch import nn

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, origins, score
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, load_household, show

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")  # exporter deprecation warnings print local install paths
torch.manual_seed(0)
torch.set_num_threads(4)


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
L, H = 168, 24
O = origins(y.index)
train = torch.tensor(y.iloc[:O[0]].to_numpy(np.float32))
idx = y.index[:O[0]]
x = train[:-H].unfold(0, L, 1)
t = train[L:].unfold(0, H, 1)
n = min(len(x), len(t))
first = idx[L:L + n]
cal = torch.tensor(np.column_stack([np.eye(24)[first.hour], np.eye(7)[first.dayofweek]]), dtype=torch.float32)
x, t = x[:n], t[:n]


class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden: int = 256):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(L + 31, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, H))

    def forward(self, window, calendar):
        mu = window.mean(1, keepdim=True)
        sd = window.std(1, keepdim=True) + 1e-3
        return self.net(torch.cat([(window - mu) / sd, calendar], 1)) * sd + mu


model = MLP()
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(10):
    for b in torch.randperm(n).split(512):
        loss = (model(x[b], cal[b]) - t[b]).abs().mean()
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
model.eval()
print(f"trained on CPU in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s; {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()):,} parameters")

trained on CPU in 3 s; 123,160 parameters

title: ONNX Export
text:
1. Export
The batch dimension is declared dynamic, so the same file serves one forecast or a thousand.


workdir = tempfile.mkdtemp()
path = os.path.join(workdir, "mlp_forecaster.onnx")
example = (x[:2], cal[:2])
batch = torch.export.Dim("batch")
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):  # the exporter narrates its passes
    torch.onnx.export(model, example, path, dynamo=True, input_names=["window", "calendar"], output_names=["forecast"],
                      dynamic_shapes=({0: batch}, {0: batch}))
files = {f: os.path.getsize(os.path.join(workdir, f)) for f in sorted(os.listdir(workdir))}
print("exported:", ", ".join(f"{f} ({b / 1e6:.2f} MB)" for f, b in files.items()))

exported: mlp_forecaster.onnx (0.02 MB), mlp_forecaster.onnx.data (0.49 MB)



opts = ort.SessionOptions()
opts.intra_op_num_threads = 4  # explicit, so ONNX Runtime does not try to pin threads (refused inside this LXC container)
session = ort.InferenceSession(path, sess_options=opts, providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"])
print([(i.name, i.shape) for i in session.get_inputs()], "->", [(o.name, o.shape) for o in session.get_outputs()])

[('window', ['batch', 168]), ('calendar', ['batch', 31])] -> [('forecast', ['batch', 24])]

title: ONNX Export
text:
2. Verify
All 30 test windows through both, as one batch: the largest absolute difference between the PyTorch and ONNX Runtime forecasts.


def inputs(origin):
    hist = y.iloc[:origin]
    nxt = hist.index[-1] + pd.Timedelta(hours=1)
    w = hist.to_numpy(np.float32)[-L:]
    c = np.concatenate([np.eye(24)[nxt.hour], np.eye(7)[nxt.dayofweek]]).astype(np.float32)
    return w, c


W = np.stack([inputs(o)[0] for o in O])
C = np.stack([inputs(o)[1] for o in O])
with torch.no_grad():
    torch_out = model(torch.tensor(W), torch.tensor(C)).numpy()
onnx_out = session.run(None, {"window": W, "calendar": C})[0]
max_diff = float(np.abs(torch_out - onnx_out).max())
print(f"largest difference over {torch_out.size} forecast values: {max_diff:.2e} kWh")

largest difference over 720 forecast values: 9.54e-07 kWh


The exported model is the same model. It also forecasts the same: both score identically on the backtest, because they produce the same numbers.


def onnx_forecaster(history, horizon):
    nxt = history.index[-1] + pd.Timedelta(hours=1)
    w = history.to_numpy(np.float32)[-L:][None]
    c = np.concatenate([np.eye(24)[nxt.hour], np.eye(7)[nxt.dayofweek]]).astype(np.float32)[None]
    return session.run(None, {"window": w, "calendar": c})[0][0, :horizon]


onnx_score = score(backtest(y, onnx_forecaster), y, exclude=FILLED)
print(f"ONNX Runtime forecaster on the backtest: skill {onnx_score['skill']:+.1%}, MASE {onnx_score['mase']:.3f}")

ONNX Runtime forecaster on the backtest: skill +20.1%, MASE 0.643

title: ONNX Export
text:
3. Speed
One forecast at a time, the way a service answers requests, timed over 2,000 calls after a warm-up:


w1, c1 = W[:1], C[:1]
tw, tc = torch.tensor(w1), torch.tensor(C[:1])
timings = {}
for name, call in (("PyTorch (eager)", lambda: model(tw, tc)), ("ONNX Runtime", lambda: session.run(None, {"window": w1, "calendar": c1}))):
    with torch.no_grad():
        for _ in range(100):
            call()
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        for _ in range(2000):
            call()
    timings[name] = 1e6 * (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 2000
speed = pd.Series(timings, name="microseconds per forecast")
show(bar_chart(speed.index, {"microseconds per forecast": speed}, height="260px"))
speed.round(1)

PyTorch (eager)    37.2
ONNX Runtime       15.2
Name: microseconds per forecast, dtype: float64


The export checks out on every count:

Identical forecasts: the largest disagreement over 720 forecast values is about a millionth of a kWh, the rounding of 32-bit floats taken in a different order. The backtest score is the same model’s score.
A small artefact: half a megabyte of weights plus a tiny graph file (PyTorch stores the weights beside the graph). Nothing else is needed to run it.
Faster: ONNX Runtime answers a single forecast more than twice as fast as eager PyTorch on the same CPU threads, because it runs a fixed, optimised graph with no Python in the loop.

For a forecaster serving many meters, the deployed process can then be a small service holding one ONNX file, with PyTorch and the training environment left behind. The verification step is the part not to skip: an export that silently fixed the batch size, or changed a normalisation, would still produce plausible numbers.

title: Explainability
text:
Explainability for a forecaster splits into two questions:

Global: which inputs does the model rely on overall? Answered here by permutation importance: shuffle one input across the test rows, re-score, and see how much worse the forecast gets.
Local: why this forecast? Answered by SHAP values (Lundberg and Lee, 2017): each feature’s contribution to one prediction, measured against the average prediction, with the contributions adding up exactly to the forecast. For tree ensembles they are exact and fast (Tree SHAP), and LightGBM computes them itself with predict(X, pred_contrib=True), so no extra library is needed.

The model is LightGBM with the shared features (seasonal lags, calendar, Fourier terms, rolling statistics), trained before the first test origin.


import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import mae, origins
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, load_household, show
from ML_Timeseries.features import make_features

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page OpenMP pools would oversubscribe the 4 cores.
_ = threadpool_limits(1)


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
O = origins(y.index)
X = make_features(y)
model = lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=31, verbose=-1, n_jobs=1, random_state=0)
model.fit(X.iloc[700:O[0]], y.iloc[700:O[0]])
test_idx = np.concatenate([np.arange(o, o + 24) for o in O])
test_idx = test_idx[~FILLED.to_numpy()[test_idx]]
X_test, y_test = X.iloc[test_idx], y.iloc[test_idx]
base_mae = mae(y_test, model.predict(X_test))
print(f"{X.shape[1]} features; test MAE {base_mae:.3f} kWh over {len(test_idx)} scored hours")

26 features; test MAE 0.436 kWh over 671 scored hours

title: Explainability
section: 1. Global: permutation importance by feature group
text:
1. Global: permutation importance by feature group
Shuffling one feature at a time understates correlated features: shuffle sin24_1 and the model still has cos24_1, hour and the lags carrying the same information. Shuffling whole groups together measures what each kind of information is worth.


GROUPS = {
    "seasonal lags": [c for c in X if c.startswith("lag")],
    "calendar": ["hour", "dow", "month", "holiday"],
    "Fourier terms": [c for c in X if c.startswith(("sin", "cos"))],
    "rolling statistics": ["mean_24h", "std_24h", "mean_168h", "same_hour_4w"],
}
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
importance = {}
for name, cols in GROUPS.items():
    worse = []
    for _ in range(5):
        Xp = X_test.copy()
        perm = rng.permutation(len(Xp))
        Xp[cols] = Xp[cols].to_numpy()[perm]  # shuffle the group's rows together, keeping its columns aligned
        worse.append(mae(y_test, model.predict(Xp)) / base_mae - 1)
    importance[name] = np.mean(worse)
imp = pd.Series(importance).sort_values()
show(bar_chart(imp.index, {"MAE increase when shuffled": imp}, horizontal=True, height="260px"))
imp.map("{:+.1%}".format)

calendar               +3.7%
seasonal lags          +7.0%
rolling statistics    +10.0%
Fourier terms         +19.0%
dtype: str

title: Explainability
section: 2. Local: SHAP values for one forecast
text:
2. Local: SHAP values for one forecast
SHAP values for the 19:00 forecast in the last test window. The bars are each feature’s push away from the model’s average prediction; together with that average they add up to the forecast exactly.


row = O[-1] + 19
contrib = model.predict(X.iloc[[row]], pred_contrib=True)[0]
shap = pd.Series(contrib[:-1], index=X.columns)
expected = contrib[-1]
pred = model.predict(X.iloc[[row]])[0]
print(f"{y.index[row]:%a %d %b %H:00}: average prediction {expected:.3f} + sum of SHAP values {shap.sum():+.3f} "
      f"= forecast {pred:.3f} kWh (actual {y.iloc[row]:.3f})")
top = shap.reindex(shap.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index[:8])[::-1]
show(bar_chart(top.index, {"SHAP value (kWh)": top}, horizontal=True, height="320px"))

Thu 25 Nov 19:00: average prediction 1.095 + sum of SHAP values +1.289 = forecast 2.384 kWh (actual 2.330)

title: Explainability
text:
3. Global SHAP: mean absolute contribution
Averaging the absolute SHAP values over all test hours gives a second global ranking, per feature:


all_shap = pd.DataFrame(model.predict(X_test, pred_contrib=True)[:, :-1], columns=X.columns)
mean_abs = all_shap.abs().mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
group_of = {c: g for g, cols in GROUPS.items() for c in cols}
by_group = mean_abs.groupby(group_of).sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
pd.DataFrame({"top features": mean_abs.head(6).round(3).to_dict()}).T








same_hour_4w
sin24_2
hour
cos8766_1
lag24
lag48




top features
0.22
0.094
0.08
0.075
0.054
0.045







The local explanation reads naturally. For 19:00 on a Thursday in late November, the biggest push above the average comes from same_hour_4w (the last four weeks at this hour were high), then a daily Fourier term (evening shape) and the slow annual term (it is nearly winter). The contributions add up to the forecast exactly, which makes them easy to show to someone who asks “why 2.4?”.
The global rankings disagree with each other, and with the Feature Engineering ablation. There, adding the calendar gave the largest gain; here, shuffling the calendar costs the least. Both are correct, because they answer different questions. The daily Fourier terms also encode the hour of day, so once they are in the model, the calendar is largely redundant: shuffle it and the Fourier terms still say it is 19:00. The ablation added the calendar before the Fourier terms, so the calendar got the credit for information both groups carry.
That is the general caution for time series features, which are correlated by construction (lags of the same series, several encodings of the same clock):

importance measures what a feature adds given the others, so redundant groups split or lose the credit;
shuffle correlated features together, as groups, or the numbers mostly measure redundancy;
an explanation describes the model, not the household. The model uses same_hour_4w heavily because it is a good summary of the routine, not because the household consults it.

title: Time Series Classification with MiniRocket
text:
Classification assigns a label to a whole series: this day’s load profile is a winter day or a summer day; this vibration trace is a healthy or a failing bearing; this meter belongs to a house or a shop. The inputs are many short series of equal length; the output is one label each.
ROCKET (Dempster, Petitjean and Webb, 2020) made this fast and accurate with a deliberately simple idea: apply thousands of random convolution kernels to each series, record two numbers per kernel (the maximum response and the proportion of positive values), and train a linear classifier on the result. No kernel is learned. MiniRocket (2021) makes the kernels almost deterministic and is about 75 times faster, with the same accuracy. On the 128-dataset UCR archive, these methods matched far more complex deep models.
The comparison here is catch22, the 22 hand-picked shape features from the Feature Engineering page, with a logistic regression on top. Both come from sktime.


import time

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sktime.datasets import load_italy_power_demand
from sktime.transformations.panel.catch22 import Catch22
from sktime.transformations.panel.rocket import MiniRocket
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, line_chart, load_household, show

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page thread pools would oversubscribe the 4 cores.
_ = threadpool_limits(1)

Classification assigns a label to a whole series: this day’s load profile is a winter day or a summer day; this vibration trace is a healthy or a failing bearing; this meter belongs to a house or a shop. The inputs are many short series of equal length; the output is one label each.

No kernel is learned. MiniRocket (2021) makes the kernels almost deterministic and is about 75 times faster, with the same accuracy. On the 128-dataset UCR archive, these methods matched far more complex deep models.
The comparison here is catch22, the 22 hand-picked shape features from the Feature Engineering page, with a logistic regression on top. Both come from sktime.


import time

import pandas as pd

from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

from sktime.transformations.panel.catch22 import Catch22
from sktime.transformations.panel.rocket import MiniRocket
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page thread pools would oversubscribe the 4 cores.

title: Time Series Classification with MiniRocket
text:
1. ItalyPowerDemand
A standard UCR benchmark that ships with sktime: 24-hour electricity demand profiles from Italy in 1997, labelled by season (October to March, or April to September). It has 67 training days and 1,029 test days, so the classifier must generalise from very little.


X_train, y_train = load_italy_power_demand(split="train", return_type="numpy3D")
X_test, y_test = load_italy_power_demand(split="test", return_type="numpy3D")
print(f"train {X_train.shape}, test {X_test.shape}, classes {sorted(str(c) for c in set(y_train))}")
show(line_chart([f"{h:02d}" for h in range(24)],
                {f"class {c}, mean profile": X_train[y_train == c, 0].mean(axis=0) for c in sorted(set(y_train))},
                y_name="normalised demand", height="280px", zoom=False))

train (67, 1, 24), test (1029, 1, 24), classes ['1', '2']





        





def minirocket_accuracy(Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    mr = MiniRocket(random_state=0).fit(Xtr)
    clf = RidgeClassifierCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3, 3, 10)).fit(mr.transform(Xtr), ytr)
    return clf.score(mr.transform(Xte), yte), time.perf_counter() - t0


def catch22_accuracy(Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    c22 = Catch22().fit(Xtr)
    clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000)).fit(c22.transform(Xtr).fillna(0), ytr)
    return clf.score(c22.transform(Xte).fillna(0), yte), time.perf_counter() - t0


italy = {}
for name, fn in (("MiniRocket", minirocket_accuracy), ("catch22 + logistic", catch22_accuracy)):
    acc, secs = fn(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test)
    italy[name] = {"test accuracy": acc, "seconds": secs}
italy = pd.DataFrame(italy).T
italy.style.format({"test accuracy": "{:.1%}", "seconds": "{:.1f}"})

seconds




MiniRocket
96.5%

title: Time Series Classification with MiniRocket
section: 2. Weekday or weekend in this house
text:
2. Weekday or weekend in this house
The same two methods on this site’s data: each of the 1,440 days’ 24-hour profiles, labelled weekday or weekend, scored by 5-fold cross-validation. On the Feature Engineering page catch22 managed 75% against a 71.5% base rate (always guessing “weekday”).


y_h = load_household()["kwh"]
start = y_h.index[y_h.index.hour == 0][0]
days = y_h[start:]
n = len(days) // 24
X_days = days.to_numpy()[:n * 24].reshape(n, 1, 24)
weekend = np.where(days.index[::24][:n].dayofweek >= 5, "weekend", "weekday")
base = (weekend == "weekday").mean()

mr_feats = MiniRocket(random_state=0).fit(X_days).transform(X_days)
acc_mr = cross_val_score(RidgeClassifierCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3, 3, 10)), mr_feats, weekend, cv=5).mean()
c22_feats = Catch22().fit_transform(X_days).fillna(0)
acc_c22 = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000)), c22_feats, weekend, cv=5).mean()
house = pd.Series({"always 'weekday'": base, "catch22 + logistic": acc_c22, "MiniRocket": acc_mr}, name="accuracy")
show(bar_chart(house.index, {"accuracy": house}, height="280px"))
house.map("{:.1%}".format)

always 'weekday'      71.5%
catch22 + logistic    75.0%
MiniRocket            78.9%
Name: accuracy, dtype: str


On ItalyPowerDemand, MiniRocket is right on about 96% of test days after seeing 67 examples, in well under a second, and catch22 trails it by 12 points. Twenty-two summary features of the whole series lose information that thousands of random convolutions keep. Each kernel responds to a local pattern at one of several dilations (time scales), and the proportion of the day where the response is positive records how much of the day has that pattern, so ten thousand of them describe the profile far more finely than 22 global statistics.
On this house the gap is smaller and both stay close to the base rate. Weekend and weekday days in one household overlap far more than winter and summer days across a whole country: a Saturday spent at home and a Wednesday spent at home look alike. MiniRocket still extracts more than catch22, and both confirm what the forecasting pages already showed: this household’s day-to-day variation is mostly noise around a weak weekly pattern.
As a default for a new classification problem on short series, MiniRocket is hard to beat for the effort: no tuning, CPU only, seconds to train.

title: Change-Point Detection
text:
An anomaly is a moment; a change point is the start of a new regime: a household goes on holiday, a heat pump is installed, a tenant moves in. Change-point detection splits a series into segments, each with its own mean (or variance, or distribution), placing the boundaries where the series changes behaviour.
The standard formulation: choose boundaries to minimise the total cost of fitting each segment (for a mean shift, the sum of squared deviations from each segment’s mean) plus a penalty per boundary. Without the penalty, every point would be its own segment. Two search methods from the ruptures library:

PELT (pruned exact linear time; Killick et al., 2012): the exact optimum for a given penalty, fast because it prunes candidates that can never be optimal.
Binary segmentation: find the single best split, then recurse into each half. Approximate, but it can be asked for a fixed number of boundaries.

The series here is daily household energy, on a log scale so that a 40% rise is the same size whether the base is summer or winter.


import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import ruptures as rpt

from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, line_chart, load_household, show


daily = load_household("D")["kwh"]
signal = np.log(daily.clip(lower=0.5))
z = ((signal - signal.mean()) / signal.std()).to_numpy()

title: Change-Point Detection
text:
1. Regimes in the real series
PELT with a moderate penalty on the whole four years:


breaks = rpt.Pelt(model="l2", min_size=7).fit(z).predict(pen=20)
cps = [daily.index[i] for i in breaks[:-1]]
segment = np.zeros(len(daily))
for a, b in zip([0] + breaks[:-1], breaks):
    segment[a:b] = daily.iloc[a:b].mean()
print(f"{len(cps)} change points: " + ", ".join(c.strftime("%Y-%m-%d") for c in cps))
show(line_chart(daily.index.date, {"daily kWh": daily, "segment mean": segment}, y_name="kWh", height="340px"))

12 change points: 2007-02-24, 2007-03-06, 2007-04-05, 2007-11-06, 2008-02-24, 2008-08-02, 2008-09-01, 2009-06-18, 2009-09-11, 2010-02-28, 2010-07-18, 2010-08-27





        




The boundaries fall at the household’s large regime changes: the onset and end of winter heating, and the long August 2008 absence, when consumption drops to a few kWh a day for almost three weeks. These are real and useful: a monthly report that says “consumption has been in a new, higher regime since 14 October” is more actionable than a daily anomaly flag.

title: Change-Point Detection
section: 2. Can it find a change we put there?
text:
2. Can it find a change we put there?
To measure detection, three blocks of +40% lasting three weeks are injected into the daily series (March and October 2009, April 2010), giving six true boundaries. The series is first deseasonalised by removing a weekday effect and a smooth annual cycle (three Fourier pairs), so that winter itself is not mistaken for a change. A boundary counts as found if a detected change point lies within three days of it.


x = daily.copy()
blocks = []
for start in ("2009-03-02", "2009-10-05", "2010-04-12"):
    s = pd.Timestamp(start)
    x[s:s + pd.Timedelta(days=20)] *= 1.4
    blocks += [s, s + pd.Timedelta(days=21)]
xs = x["2008-01-01":]
t = (xs.index - xs.index[0]).days.to_numpy()
design = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(t))] + [f(2 * np.pi * k * t / 365.25) for k in (1, 2, 3) for f in (np.sin, np.cos)]
                         + [(xs.index.dayofweek == d).astype(float) for d in range(1, 7)])
logx = np.log(xs.clip(lower=1)).to_numpy()
coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(design, logx, rcond=None)
resid = logx - design @ coef
r = (resid - resid.mean()) / resid.std()


def recall(found):
    return np.mean([any(abs((c - b).days) <= 3 for c in found) for b in blocks])


rows = {}
for pen in (5, 10, 20):
    found = [xs.index[i] for i in rpt.Pelt(model="l2", min_size=5).fit(r).predict(pen=pen)[:-1]]
    rows[f"PELT, penalty {pen}"] = {"change points": len(found), "recall of the 6 boundaries": recall(found)}
for n in (6, 15):
    found = [xs.index[i] for i in rpt.Binseg(model="l2", min_size=5).fit(r).predict(n_bkps=n)[:-1]]
    rows[f"binary segmentation, {n} boundaries"] = {"change points": len(found), "recall of the 6 boundaries": recall(found)}
cp_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
cp_table.style.format({"change points": "{:.0f}", "recall of the 6 boundaries": "{:.2f}"})

Recall stays low however the penalty is set, and even binary segmentation told there are exactly six boundaries places most of them elsewhere. The detectors are not broken. The question is: how unusual is a three-week +40% shift in this house?


m21 = daily.rolling(21).mean()
ratio = (m21 / m21.shift(21)).dropna()
share_30 = ((ratio >= 1.3) | (ratio <= 1 / 1.3)).mean()
share_40 = (ratio >= 1.4).mean()
print(f"21-day windows whose mean differs from the previous 21 days by 30% or more: {share_30:.0%}")
print(f"21-day windows at least 40% above the previous 21 days: {share_40:.1%}")

21-day windows whose mean differs from the previous 21 days by 30% or more: 20%
21-day windows at least 40% above the previous 21 days: 5.6%


One three-week window in five already differs from the previous three weeks by 30% or more, and one in eighteen is 40% higher. Cold spells, guests, a run of home-working days: this household changes regime constantly. An injected +40% block is therefore not a special event to the detector; it is one more change among dozens of the same size, and with a limited budget of boundaries the detector spends them on the larger real ones.
So this page records a negative result: the goal of finding at least 80% of injected changes is not met, and it is not a tuning problem. Change-point detection answers “where does the behaviour change?”, and in a household the honest answer is “often”. It works when the change of interest is large relative to the series’ natural regime swings: the August 2008 absence, when consumption fell by more than half for three weeks, is found in section 1.
Two ways to make it useful on meter data:

Detect against a model, not the raw series. Run change-point detection on the residuals of a good forecast (the scoreboard models), where weather and routine are already explained, so what is left is the change that is not.
Detect across many meters. A new heat pump changes one house’s load shape the same way it changes others’; comparing a meter with its peers removes the shared swings that hide the change here.

title: Conformal Prediction
text:
Conformal prediction (Vovk and colleagues, from 2005) turns any point forecaster into an interval forecaster with a coverage guarantee. The recipe:

Forecast a calibration set the model did not train on, and record a nonconformity score for each outcome, usually the absolute error \(|y - \hat y|\).
Take the \(\lceil (n+1)(1-\alpha) \rceil / n\) empirical quantile of those scores, \(\hat q\).
The interval for a new forecast is \(\hat y \pm \hat q\).

If the calibration errors and the new error are exchangeable (any order equally likely), the interval covers the outcome with probability at least \(1 - \alpha\), whatever the model and whatever the error distribution. Time series break exchangeability: errors cluster, and the distribution drifts. So the guarantee becomes an approximation, and the test is empirical.
Every method here wraps the quantile LightGBM from Probabilistic Forecasting (its median as the point forecast, its 5% and 95% quantiles where needed). Calibration uses the 30 days before each test origin, so it always reflects the recent past. The target is a 90% interval, with 88% to 92% fixed as the success band before running anything.


import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import future_index, origins
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, line_chart, load_household, show
from ML_Timeseries.features import make_features
from ML_Timeseries.probabilistic import LEVELS, coverage

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page OpenMP pools would oversubscribe the 4 cores.
_ = threadpool_limits(1)


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
O = origins(y.index)
train = y.iloc[:O[0]]
X_train = make_features(train).iloc[700:]
models = {l: lgb.LGBMRegressor(objective="quantile", alpha=l, n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=31,
                               verbose=-1, n_jobs=1, random_state=0).fit(X_train, train.iloc[700:]) for l in (0.05, 0.5, 0.95)}
_cache = {}


def quantiles(origin):
    "5%, 50% and 95% forecasts for the 24 hours after `origin` (cached: calibration windows overlap)."
    if origin not in _cache:
        hist = y.iloc[:origin]
        ext = pd.concat([hist.iloc[-800:], pd.Series(np.nan, index=future_index(hist, 24))])
        X = make_features(ext).iloc[-24:]
        _cache[origin] = np.sort(np.column_stack([models[l].predict(X) for l in (0.05, 0.5, 0.95)]), axis=1)
    return _cache[origin]


def actual(origin):
    return y.iloc[origin:origin + 24].to_numpy()


def observed(origin):
    return ~FILLED.iloc[origin:origin + 24].to_numpy()


CAL_DAYS = 30
ALPHA = 0.1

import lightgbm as lgb

title: Conformal Prediction
section: 1. Four ways to build the interval
text:
1. Four ways to build the interval

Uncalibrated quantiles: the LightGBM 5% and 95% quantiles as they are.
Split conformal: median \(\pm \hat q\), with \(\hat q\) from the absolute errors of the previous 30 days. Same width every hour.
CQR (conformalised quantile regression; Romano et al., 2019): keep the quantile model’s shape and widen or narrow it by a conformal margin. The score is how far the outcome fell outside the quantile band, so the interval stays narrow at night and wide in the evening.
ACI (adaptive conformal inference; Gibbs and Candès, 2021): CQR with a level that adapts. After each day, if the interval missed more than 10% of hours, the next day’s level rises, and if it missed less, it falls: \(\alpha_{t+1} = \alpha_t + \gamma\,(\alpha - \text{miss rate}_t)\), with \(\gamma = 0.05\) fixed in advance. Built for distributions that drift.



def conformal_quantile(scores, alpha):
    n = len(scores)
    return np.quantile(scores, min(1.0, max(0.0, np.ceil((n + 1) * (1 - alpha)) / n)))


def run(method, gamma=0.05):
    alpha, hits, widths = ALPHA, [], []
    for o in O:
        cal = [o - 24 * k for k in range(1, CAL_DAYS + 1)]
        Q = quantiles(o)
        if method == "uncalibrated quantiles":
            lo, hi = Q[:, 0], Q[:, 2]
        elif method == "split conformal":
            q = conformal_quantile(np.concatenate([np.abs(actual(c) - quantiles(c)[:, 1]) for c in cal]), ALPHA)
            lo, hi = Q[:, 1] - q, Q[:, 1] + q
        else:  # CQR, and ACI on top of it
            s = np.concatenate([np.maximum(quantiles(c)[:, 0] - actual(c), actual(c) - quantiles(c)[:, 2]) for c in cal])
            q = conformal_quantile(s, alpha if method == "ACI" else ALPHA)
            lo, hi = Q[:, 0] - q, Q[:, 2] + q
        keep = observed(o)
        hit = ((actual(o) >= lo) & (actual(o) <= hi))[keep]
        hits.append(hit)
        widths.append(np.mean((hi - lo)[keep]) if keep.any() else np.nan)
        if method == "ACI" and keep.any():  # a fully gap-filled day carries no information about coverage
            alpha += gamma * (ALPHA - (1 - hit.mean()))
    daily = np.array([h.mean() for h in hits if len(h)])
    return {"coverage": float(np.mean(np.concatenate(hits))), "mean width": float(np.nanmean(widths)),
            "daily coverage std": float(daily.std(ddof=1)), "days": len(daily)}, daily


results, daily = {}, {}
for m in ("uncalibrated quantiles", "split conformal", "CQR", "ACI"):
    results[m], daily[m] = run(m)
table = pd.DataFrame(results).T
table["coverage 95% CI"] = [f"{c - 1.96 * s / np.sqrt(n):.0%} to {c + 1.96 * s / np.sqrt(n):.0%}"
                            for c, s, n in zip(table.coverage, table["daily coverage std"], table.days)]
table[["coverage", "coverage 95% CI", "mean width"]].style.format({"coverage": "{:.1%}", "mean width": "{:.2f}"})

Three findings:

ACI reaches the target band (88% to 92%), the only method that does. Its level rises after days that missed too often, so it tracks the test months’ higher variability instead of trusting last month’s errors.
CQR is the efficient choice. It matches split conformal’s coverage with intervals about 13% narrower, because it keeps the quantile model’s hour-by-hour shape: tight at night, wide in the evening. Split conformal pays for one width everywhere.
Plain split conformal and CQR did not fix the under-coverage. Their calibration is the previous 30 days, and the test windows were a little more variable than the days before them. Exchangeability, the assumption behind the guarantee, does not hold for a drifting series, which is exactly the gap ACI was designed to close.

And the honest caveat: 30 test days measure coverage to about plus or minus four points. Hours within a day are strongly correlated, so the effective sample is the 30 days, not the 700 hours. Every method’s interval in the table contains 90%. “86% versus 88%” is a real difference in the methods’ behaviour on this data, but it is not one these 30 days can confirm statistically. A coverage claim needs many independent periods, or it is an anecdote with a percentage sign.
