2. Coverage day by day
The total hides how coverage moves. ACI’s daily hit rate against the target, with the uncalibrated quantiles for comparison:


days = [y.index[o].strftime("%d %b") for o in O if observed(o).any()]
show(line_chart(days, {"ACI": daily["ACI"], "uncalibrated quantiles": daily["uncalibrated quantiles"], "target": np.full(len(days), 0.9)},
                y_name="share of hours covered", height="320px", zoom=False))

title: Small Models on CPU
text:
A forecast that runs once an hour per meter does not need a GPU, and most places a forecast is needed (an edge gateway, a small cloud function, a home server) do not have one. The question is how much accuracy survives on a CPU, and how long each forecast takes.
Chronos-Bolt (Amazon, 2024) is built for this: it forecasts all quantiles in one forward pass instead of sampling, and comes in sizes from 9 million parameters (tiny) to 205 million (base). Two other small CPU candidates named in this site’s plan could not be tested: IBM’s TTM (Tiny Time Mixers) would downgrade the shared environment’s PyTorch, and TabPFN-TS does not resolve against it at all.
Everything here runs on the CPU only, with the GPU hidden. The page still carries skip_exec, because it imports the vendor packages that only the root environment has.


import gc
import logging
import os
import time
import warnings

os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = ""  # force CPU for every model on this page

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import tirex
import torch
from chronos import BaseChronosPipeline, Chronos2Pipeline

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, record, score
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, load_household, show

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
logging.disable(logging.WARNING)
print(f"CUDA visible: {torch.cuda.is_available()}; CPU threads available: {os.cpu_count()}")

CUDA visible: False; CPU threads available: 4

y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
NB = "06_Foundation_Models/04_Small_Models_on_CPU"
CTX = 2048


def context(history):
    return torch.tensor(history.to_numpy(dtype=np.float32)[-CTX:])


MODELS = {
    "Chronos-Bolt tiny": (lambda: BaseChronosPipeline.from_pretrained("amazon/chronos-bolt-tiny", device_map="cpu"),
                          lambda m, h, n: m.predict_quantiles(context(h)[None], prediction_length=n, quantile_levels=[0.5])[0][0, :, 0].numpy()),
    "Chronos-Bolt small": (lambda: BaseChronosPipeline.from_pretrained("amazon/chronos-bolt-small", device_map="cpu"),
                           lambda m, h, n: m.predict_quantiles(context(h)[None], prediction_length=n, quantile_levels=[0.5])[0][0, :, 0].numpy()),
    "Chronos-2": (lambda: Chronos2Pipeline.from_pretrained("amazon/chronos-2", device_map="cpu"),
                  lambda m, h, n: m.predict_quantiles([context(h)], prediction_length=n, quantile_levels=[0.5])[0][0][0, :, 0].numpy()),
    "TiRex": (lambda: tirex.load_model("NX-AI/TiRex", device="cpu"),
              lambda m, h, n: m.forecast(context=context(h)[None], prediction_length=n)[0][0, :, 4].numpy()),
}

title: Small Models on CPU
text:
Accuracy and latency
Each model forecasts the 30 backtest windows twice: with four threads (the whole machine) and with one (a fair share on a busy server). Latency is the mean time per 24-hour forecast.


rows = {}
for name, (load, forecast) in MODELS.items():
    model = load()
    params = sum(p.numel() for p in (model.model if hasattr(model, "model") else model).parameters())
    row = {"parameters (M)": params / 1e6}
    for threads in (4, 1):
        torch.set_num_threads(threads)
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        with torch.no_grad():
            bt = backtest(y, lambda h, n: forecast(model, h, n))
        row[f"ms per forecast, {threads} thread{'s' if threads > 1 else ''}"] = 1000 * (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 30
    row |= {k: v for k, v in score(bt, y, exclude=FILLED).items() if k in ("mase", "skill")}
    rows[name] = row
    del model
    gc.collect()
torch.set_num_threads(4)
cpu = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
_ = record("Chronos-Bolt tiny, zero-shot (CPU)", "foundation model",
           {"mase": rows["Chronos-Bolt tiny"]["mase"], "skill": rows["Chronos-Bolt tiny"]["skill"],
            "seconds": rows["Chronos-Bolt tiny"]["ms per forecast, 1 thread"] * 30 / 1000}, notebook=NB, notes="9 M parameters, one CPU thread")

Chronos-Bolt tiny is the headline. Nine million parameters, 15 milliseconds per forecast on a single CPU thread, and a skill within two points of Chronos-2, with no training. That is better than every classical and gradient-boosting model on the scoreboard, from a 30 MB file. At 15 milliseconds, one core produces about 240,000 day-ahead forecasts an hour, enough for a large fleet of meters.
The other rows show how the architectures differ off the GPU:

Chronos-2 is the slowest on one thread (about a quarter of a second) and gains the most from four, because its transformer layers are large matrix products that parallelise well.
TiRex is the most accurate and does not speed up with more threads: its xLSTM reads the context one step at a time, and a sequential loop cannot be split across cores. On a GPU it was the slowest of the three for the same reason.
Chronos-Bolt small buys half a point over tiny for four times the latency.

Pick by the deployment, not the leaderboard: tiny where cost and latency dominate, TiRex where the last points of accuracy matter, and check its licence if the use is commercial.

title: Foundation Model Comparison
text:
Too good to be true
TimesFM 2.5’s score is far above every other model on this site, including models trained on this very house. A forecaster that good on a noisy household series would be remarkable. The first question to ask of such a result is the one from the Benchmarks page: was the test data in the training data?
This household dataset has been public on UCI since 2012 and is a common example in tutorials and benchmarks, so it may well sit in a pretraining corpus. Google does not publish the list of datasets TimesFM 2.5 was trained on, so this cannot be checked directly. It can be tested from the outside.
The spike test. Many of this house’s large hours are appliances switched on at times nothing in the past predicts. A model that forecasts should miss most of them. A model that remembers the series will hit them. Count, for every hour above 2.5 kWh in the test windows, how often each model predicted more than 2 kWh:

check = pd.DataFrame({name: {"spike hours predicted above 2 kWh": (bt.yhat[spike] > 2).mean(),
                             "correlation with actual": np.corrcoef(bt.y, bt.yhat)[0, 1]} for name, bt in bts.items()}).T
print(f"{int(spike.sum())} spike hours in the test windows")
check.style.format({"spike hours predicted above 2 kWh": "{:.0%}", "correlation with actual": "{:.2f}"})

TimesFM 2.5 predicts more than three quarters of the unpredictable spikes; the three other models catch a quarter to a third, which is about what a good honest forecaster manages. Its forecasts also track the actual hours far more closely. Adding noise to its context (tested while preparing this page) barely changes the result, which fits recognising a familiar series rather than reading fragile details.
This is consistent with TimesFM 2.5 having seen this household’s data, or a copy of it, during pretraining. It is not proof: Google does not list the 2.5 training corpus, and the test cannot tell which copy it saw. The result is therefore left off the scoreboard, and the GIFT-Eval numbers above remain the fair measure of TimesFM 2.5 (where it is a strong but ordinary member of the top group).
The general lesson outlasts this case. Any public dataset may be inside a foundation model’s training data. Before trusting a zero-shot result on a public series, run a recall test like this one, or evaluate on data that has never been published, such as a company’s own meters.


clean = [n for n in results if n != "TimesFM 2.5"]
for name in clean[1:]:
    _ = record(f"{name}, zero-shot", "foundation model",
               {k: results[name][k] for k in ("mase", "skill", "mae", "rmse", "wape", "smape")} | {"seconds": results[name]["ms per forecast"] * 30 / 1000},

show(bar_chart(order.index, {"skill vs seasonal naive": order.skill}, horizontal=True, height="260px"))




        




Among the three clean models, TiRex is the most accurate, close to the best model trained on this house, and also the slowest at about a sixth of a second per forecast: it is built on xLSTM, a recurrent architecture that reads the context step by step. Chronos-2 is a little less accurate and five times faster. Chronos-Bolt small, at 9 milliseconds and 0.2 GB, gives up little accuracy for its size; the small models page runs it without a GPU.
The order here differs from GIFT-Eval, where Chronos-2 sits slightly ahead of TiRex. One series is one draw; the leaderboard averages 97 configurations. Both views agree on the main point: three different pretrained models, used with no training, all forecast this house better than any classical or gradient-boosting model built for it.

title: N-BEATS from Scratch
text:
The library models on the previous pages hide their machinery behind fit. N-BEATS (Oreshkin et al., 2020) is small enough to write out in full, and writing it shows the one idea that makes it work: doubly residual stacking.
Each block takes an input window and produces two things:

a forecast of the next 24 hours;
a backcast: its own reconstruction of the input window.

The next block receives the input minus the backcast, the part the first block could not explain. The final forecast is the sum of all blocks’ forecasts. Early blocks pick up the dominant pattern (the daily shape), later blocks refine what is left. It is boosting, built into one differentiable network and trained end to end.

title: N-BEATS from Scratch
N-BEATS from Scratch
text:
2. Training
Mean absolute error, AdamW, 20 passes over the 30,000 windows in batches of 1,024. Three seeds, averaged at forecast time, as on the data pipeline page.


def train_nbeats(seed: int, epochs: int = 20):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = NBeats().to(DEVICE)
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
    sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max=epochs)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        for idx in torch.randperm(n, device=DEVICE).split(1024):
            loss = (model(X[idx]) - T[idx]).abs().mean()
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
        sched.step()
    return model.eval()


t0 = time.perf_counter()
torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
models = [train_nbeats(s) for s in (0, 1, 2)]
train_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
params = sum(p.numel() for p in models[0].parameters())
print(f"3 models trained in {train_s:.0f} s; {params:,} parameters each; peak VRAM {torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9:.2f} GB")

3 models trained in 8 s; 1,739,904 parameters each; peak VRAM 0.13 GB



def forecaster(ms):
    def f(history, horizon):
        x = torch.tensor(history.to_numpy(dtype=np.float32)[-L:])[None].to(DEVICE)
        with torch.no_grad():
            return np.mean([m(x)[0, :horizon].cpu().numpy() for m in ms], axis=0)
    return f


bt = backtest(y, forecaster(models))
ours = score(bt, y, exclude=FILLED) | {"seconds": train_s}
singles = [score(backtest(y, forecaster([m])), y, exclude=FILLED)["skill"] for m in models]
_ = record("N-BEATS from scratch (PyTorch), 3-seed ensemble", "deep learning", ours, notebook=NB)
library = load_results().query("model == 'N-BEATS (neuralforecast)'").iloc[0]
print(f"from scratch: single seeds {', '.join(f'{s:+.1%}' for s in singles)}; ensemble {ours['skill']:+.1%}")
print(f"neuralforecast N-BEATS (one seed, previous page): {library.skill:+.1%}")

from scratch: single seeds +21.2%, +22.6%, +22.3%; ensemble +24.3%
neuralforecast N-BEATS (one seed, previous page): +17.5%

title: N-BEATS from Scratch
text:
3. What the blocks learned
The doubly residual design can be inspected: run one window through the first model and plot each block’s contribution to the forecast. The contributions add up to the final forecast exactly.


model = models[0]
o = origins(y.index)[-1]
x = torch.tensor(y.iloc[o - L:o].to_numpy(dtype=np.float32))[None].to(DEVICE)
with torch.no_grad():
    mu, sd = x.mean(1, keepdim=True), x.std(1, keepdim=True) + 1e-3
    residual, parts = (x - mu) / sd, []
    for block in model.blocks:
        back, fore = block(residual)
        residual = residual - back
        parts.append((fore * sd)[0].cpu().numpy())
labels = y.index[o:o + H].strftime("%a %H:00")
series = {"actual": y.iloc[o:o + H].to_numpy(), "sum of blocks + level": np.sum(parts, axis=0) + mu.item()}
series |= {f"block {i + 1}": p for i, p in enumerate(parts[:3])}
show(line_chart(labels, series, y_name="kWh", height="360px", zoom=False))




        




The plot shows the residual design at work. Block 1 draws most of the daily shape; the later blocks make smaller corrections around it, and their sum (plus the window’s level, added back) is the forecast.
The surprise is the score. Sixty lines of PyTorch beat the library’s N-BEATS by several points, and every single seed beats it, so this is not ensemble luck. I have not isolated the cause. The two models differ in several ways at once, any of which could matter:

block design: six generic blocks here, against the library’s default of identity, trend and seasonality stacks;
normalisation: per-window instance normalisation here, against one robust scaler per series;
training: every hourly window once per epoch with a cosine learning-rate schedule, against random window sampling for a fixed number of steps.

Finding out which one matters is an ablation, the same method as the feature engineering page: change one at a time. The general lesson is already clear, though. Library defaults are tuned for benchmark suites, not for your series, and a model you can read end to end is a model you can tune.
This page closes the deep learning section with the best model on the scoreboard: a network trained in eight seconds on a consumer GPU.

title: The MLP Family: N-BEATS, N-HiTS, TiDE and DLinear
text:
All four map a lookback window straight to the forecast with fully connected layers, with no recurrence and no attention:








Model
Year
Idea




N-BEATS (Oreshkin et al.)
2020
stacks of blocks; each block forecasts part of the series and removes its part of the input (a residual “backcast”), so later blocks model what earlier ones missed. It beat the M4 winner on M4 with no time-series-specific components


N-HiTS (Challu et al.)
2023
N-BEATS with each stack reading a pooled (coarser) input and forecasting at a coarser rate, then interpolating: some stacks handle slow patterns, others fast ones, at a fraction of the compute


TiDE (Das et al., Google)
2023
a dense encoder-decoder with residual connections that also takes future covariates, built for long horizons


DLinear (Zeng et al.)
2023
split the window into a moving-average trend and a remainder; one linear layer each. That is all



DLinear’s paper, Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?, showed that this linear model matched or beat most transformer forecasters of 2021 and 2022 on the standard long-horizon benchmarks. It reset the field: every architecture since is expected to beat a linear baseline first. The Benchmarks page reproduced the effect on ETTh1 with a ridge layer.
Same protocol as the previous page: univariate, one-week lookback, trained once before the first origin. GPU page, so skip_exec with stored outputs.


import gc
import logging
import time
import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
from neuralforecast import NeuralForecast
from neuralforecast.losses.pytorch import MAE
from neuralforecast.models import NBEATS, NHITS, DLinear, TiDE

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, origins, record, score
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, load_household, show, to_long

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
for name in ("pytorch_lightning", "lightning", "lightning.pytorch", "lightning_fabric"):
    logging.getLogger(name).setLevel(logging.ERROR)


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
NB = "05_Deep_Learning/03_MLP_Family"
INPUT, H = 168, 24
train = to_long(y.iloc[:origins(y.index)[0]])
COMMON = dict(h=H, input_size=INPUT, loss=MAE(), max_steps=1000, scaler_type="robust", random_seed=0,
              enable_progress_bar=False, enable_model_summary=False, logger=False,
              accelerator="gpu" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu", devices=1)


def fit_and_score(model):
    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    nf = NeuralForecast(models=[model], freq="h")
    nf.fit(train)
    fit_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
    col = type(model).__name__

    def f(history, horizon):
        return nf.predict(df=to_long(history.iloc[-(INPUT + 48):]))[col].to_numpy()[:horizon]

    sc = score(backtest(y, f), y, exclude=FILLED) | {"seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0, "fit seconds": fit_s,
                                                       "peak VRAM GB": torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9,
                                                       "parameters": sum(p.numel() for p in nf.models[0].parameters())}
    del nf
    gc.collect()
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    return sc


models = {
    "N-BEATS": NBEATS(**COMMON),
    "N-HiTS": NHITS(**COMMON),
    "TiDE": TiDE(**COMMON),
    "DLinear": DLinear(**COMMON),
}
results = {}
for name, model in models.items():
    results[name] = fit_and_score(model)
    _ = record(f"{name} (neuralforecast)", "deep learning",

title: The MLP Family: N-BEATS, N-HiTS, TiDE and DLinear
text:
All four map a lookback window straight to the forecast with fully connected layers, with no recurrence and no attention:








Model
Year
Idea




N-BEATS (Oreshkin et al.)
2020
stacks of blocks; each block forecasts part of the series and removes its part of the input (a residual “backcast”), so later blocks model what earlier ones missed. It beat the M4 winner on M4 with no time-series-specific components


N-HiTS (Challu et al.)
2023
N-BEATS with each stack reading a pooled (coarser) input and forecasting at a coarser rate, then interpolating: some stacks handle slow patterns, others fast ones, at a fraction of the compute


TiDE (Das et al., Google)
2023
a dense encoder-decoder with residual connections that also takes future covariates, built for long horizons


DLinear (Zeng et al.)
2023
split the window into a moving-average trend and a remainder; one linear layer each. That is all



DLinear’s paper, Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?, showed that this linear model matched or beat most transformer forecasters of 2021 and 2022 on the standard long-horizon benchmarks. It reset the field: every architecture since is expected to beat a linear baseline first. The Benchmarks page reproduced the effect on ETTh1 with a ridge layer.
Same protocol as the previous page: univariate, one-week lookback, trained once before the first origin. GPU page, so skip_exec with stored outputs.

title: The Deep Learning Data Pipeline
text:
Deep forecasting papers compare architectures. In practice, three choices made before the architecture often matter more:

Windows: the network sees fixed-length slices of history (the lookback) and predicts a fixed-length slice of future (the horizon). How long should the lookback be?
Normalisation: neural networks train badly on raw values that drift. Normalise globally, or per window?
Sampling: which windows go into each training batch.

This page fixes one small network, a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) from the 336 inputs (or other lookbacks) to the 24 outputs, and changes only these choices. Everything runs on the GPU in seconds.
This page trains on the GPU, so it does not run in CI: it carries skip_exec and stores its outputs from a run on the site’s machine (RTX 3060, 12 GB).

title: The Deep Learning Data Pipeline
text:
1. Windows
Every hour of the training data can end a lookback, so a series of 29,000 hours gives about 29,000 overlapping training windows. Unlike the regression page, which used one row per midnight, the network trains on windows starting at every hour: more examples of the same patterns, at every phase of the day. The calendar is given as the hour of day and weekday of the first forecast hour.
torch.Tensor.unfold builds all windows as a view, without copying the series 29,000 times.


def make_windows(values: np.ndarray, index: pd.DatetimeIndex, lookback: int):
    "All (input, calendar, target) windows of a series, as tensors."
    v = torch.tensor(values)
    x = v[:-H].unfold(0, lookback, 1)                 # [n, lookback]
    target = v[lookback:].unfold(0, H, 1)             # [n, H]
    n = min(len(x), len(target))
    first = index[lookback:lookback + n]              # timestamp of the first forecast hour
    cal = torch.tensor(np.column_stack([np.eye(24)[first.hour], np.eye(7)[first.dayofweek]]), dtype=torch.float32)
    return x[:n], cal, target[:n]


x, cal, t = make_windows(train_values, y.index[:first_test], 336)
print(f"{len(x):,} windows: inputs {tuple(x.shape)}, calendar {tuple(cal.shape)}, targets {tuple(t.shape)}")

30,704 windows: inputs (30704, 336), calendar (30704, 31), targets (30704, 24)

title: The Deep Learning Data Pipeline
text:
2. Normalisation
Each setting below trains three networks with different random seeds. The table shows their mean skill, the spread between the best and worst seed, and the skill of their averaged forecast (the seed ensemble). A difference smaller than the spread is not a difference.
Three options, all inside the model so the backtest sees raw kWh:








Option
Inputs and targets divided by
Effect




None
nothing
the network must learn the level itself


Global
the training mean and standard deviation
fixed scale; drift in the level still shows


Instance (RevIN)
each window’s own mean and standard deviation, undone on the output
every window looks “level zero”; the network learns shape, and the level is added back



RevIN (reversible instance normalisation; Kim et al., 2022) is the third option with a learnable affine step. It is the single trick most of the modern architectures on the next pages share, because it removes the distribution shift between training years and test months.


class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, lookback: int, norm: str, mean: float = 0.0, std: float = 1.0, hidden: int = 256):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm, self.mean, self.std = norm, mean, std
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(lookback + 31, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.1),
                                 nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, H))

    def forward(self, x, cal):
        if self.norm == "instance":
            mu, sd = x.mean(1, keepdim=True), x.std(1, keepdim=True) + 1e-3
        elif self.norm == "global":
            mu, sd = self.mean, self.std
        else:
            mu, sd = 0.0, 1.0
        out = self.net(torch.cat([(x - mu) / sd, cal], 1))
        return out * sd + mu


def train_mlp(lookback: int, norm: str, epochs: int = 15, seed: int = 0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    x, cal, t = make_windows(train_values, y.index[:first_test], lookback)
    model = MLP(lookback, norm, float(train_values.mean()), float(train_values.std())).to(DEVICE)
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
    x, cal, t = x.to(DEVICE), cal.to(DEVICE), t.to(DEVICE)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        for idx in torch.randperm(len(x), device=DEVICE).split(512):
            loss = (model(x[idx], cal[idx]) - t[idx]).abs().mean()  # L1 loss: the backtest scores absolute error
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
    model.eval()
    return model


def mlp_forecaster(model, lookback):
    def f(history, horizon):
        first = history.index[-1] + pd.Timedelta(hours=1)
        xi = torch.tensor(history.to_numpy(dtype=np.float32)[-lookback:])[None].to(DEVICE)
        ci = torch.tensor(np.concatenate([np.eye(24)[first.hour], np.eye(7)[first.dayofweek]]), dtype=torch.float32)[None].to(DEVICE)
        with torch.no_grad():
            return model(xi, ci)[0, :horizon].cpu().numpy()
    return f


SEEDS = (0, 1, 2)


def run(lookback, norm):
    "Train one network per seed; report the mean and spread of their skill, and score the seed ensemble."
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    models = [train_mlp(lookback, norm, seed=s) for s in SEEDS]
    singles = [score(backtest(y, mlp_forecaster(m, lookback)), y, exclude=FILLED)["skill"] for m in models]
    fs = [mlp_forecaster(m, lookback) for m in models]
    ensemble = score(backtest(y, lambda h, n: np.mean([f(h, n) for f in fs], axis=0)), y, exclude=FILLED)
    ensemble |= {"skill mean": float(np.mean(singles)), "skill spread": float(np.max(singles) - np.min(singles)),
                 "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0}
    del models, fs
    gc.collect()
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    return ensemble


norm_results = {norm: run(336, norm) for norm in ("none", "global", "instance")}
COLS = ["skill mean", "skill spread", "skill", "mase", "seconds"]
FMT = {"skill mean": "{:+.1%}", "skill spread": "{:.1%}", "skill": "{:+.1%}", "mase": "{:.3f}", "seconds": "{:.0f}"}

On this series, normalisation makes no measurable difference: the three means sit within a point of each other, inside the seed spread. That is a finding about the data, not about RevIN. The household series has no trend, its values sit near 1 kWh (already a scale a network trains well on), and the test months stay within the range of the training years. RevIN earns its place on series that drift, or when one network trains on many series at different scales, as the Global vs Local page showed for the scaler. It costs nothing, so the pages that follow keep it on.
The seed ensemble is the more useful result: averaging three networks that differ only in their random start adds one to two points of skill for free, because their errors are partly independent.

title: The Deep Learning Data Pipeline
text:
3. Lookback length
With instance normalisation fixed, the lookback is the next choice. Longer windows show more weeks of the routine, and more noise to fit.

Shorter is better, up to a point. One week of history gives the best and most stable network; two days is nearly as good; two and four weeks are worse, and the four-week networks disagree with each other the most (the largest seed spread). A longer window adds inputs faster than it adds information: the calendar features already say which weekday is coming, and the autocorrelation showed little beyond lag 168. With 30,000 training windows, the extra 500 inputs mostly give the network more noise to fit.
This small network, a two-layer MLP trained in seconds, is the best model on the scoreboard so far. Two things set it apart from the gradient-boosting models: it trains on a window ending at every hour (30,000 examples, against 1,280 daily rows on the regression page), and it predicts all 24 hours jointly from the full recent window, so the shape of the last day carries over into the next. The lesson for the rest of this section: before reaching for a bigger architecture, get the windows, the lookback and the ensemble right.

title: Multi-step Strategies
text:
A day-ahead forecast is 24 numbers. A regression model naturally predicts one. There are three standard ways to get 24:








Strategy
How hour h is forecast
Risk




Recursive (1 model)
predict hour 1, append it to the history as if observed, predict hour 2, …
errors compound: hour 24 rests on 23 guesses


Direct (24 models)
model h maps what is known at the origin straight to hour h
24 times the training; hours forecast independently


MIMO (1 model, 24 outputs)
all 24 hours at once from the same inputs
needs a model that outputs vectors (linear models, neural networks)



A fourth trick, used on the Feature Engineering page, sidesteps the choice: give one model only lags of at least 24 hours, so every input is known for every hour of the day ahead.

3. MIMO
LightGBM predicts one number, so the multi-output strategy uses ridge regression from the previous page: the last 336 hours plus the weekday, to all 24 hours at once.


x = train.to_numpy()
mids = [i for i in range(336, len(train) - 24 + 1) if train.index[i].hour == 0]
Xm = np.column_stack([np.stack([x[i - 336:i] for i in mids]), np.eye(7)[[train.index[i].dayofweek for i in mids]]])
mimo_model = Ridge(alpha=100.0).fit(Xm, np.stack([x[i:i + 24] for i in mids]))


def mimo(history, horizon):
    nxt = history.index[-1] + pd.Timedelta(hours=1)
    return mimo_model.predict(np.concatenate([history.to_numpy()[-336:], np.eye(7)[nxt.dayofweek]])[None])[0][:horizon]

title: Multi-step Strategies
text:
Error by hour ahead
The table hides the most important difference. Split the error by forecast step:


observed = lambda b: b[~FILLED.reindex(b.ds).to_numpy()]
by_step = pd.DataFrame({name: observed(bt).assign(ae=lambda d: (d.y - d.yhat).abs()).groupby("step").ae.mean()
                        for name, bt in bts.items()})
show(line_chart(by_step.index, {c: by_step[c] for c in by_step}, y_name="MAE (kWh)", height="360px", zoom=False))




        




Read the chart with one caveat: every origin is at midnight, so step h is also hour h of the day. All four curves rise towards the evening because evening hours are larger and more variable, not only because they are further ahead. Compare the curves with each other, not with themselves.

Recursive and direct start identical. At hour 1 both see the same last value; their errors match.
Then the recursive error grows faster. Over hours 13 to 24 it is about 10% above the direct strategy’s. Each step feeds a guess back in as lag1, and the model was trained on real values, not on its own guesses, so it trusts them too much. That is error compounding, measured.
“Lags of 24 h or more” is the mirror image. Its first hours are the worst of the four, because it cannot use the last observed value at all. From midday on it matches the direct strategy, because by then the direct models’ freshest inputs are hours old anyway.
MIMO ridge sits between them: it sees the last value, but as a linear model it uses it less well.

So the direct strategy’s whole advantage lies in the first few hours, which is where its 24 models earn their keep. If only the evening matters, as for a peak-demand forecast, one model with lags of 24 hours or more is almost as good and 24 times cheaper.

title: Hourly Time Series Forecasting using Facebook’s Prophet
text:
On this site’s backtest
The walkthrough above follows the original tutorial on a different dataset, and its cells do not run here. This section puts Prophet on the same backtest as every other model: the household series, 30 day-ahead windows, refitted at each origin on the last eight weeks, with daily and weekly seasonality and French public holidays.
Prophet (Taylor and Letham, 2018) fits a curve: a piecewise-linear trend plus Fourier seasonalities plus holiday effects, estimated with Stan. It was built for business series with strong human seasonality and missing data, and it is easy to use. Published comparisons have often found it behind simple baselines on general forecasting benchmarks, so it needs testing like anything else.


import logging
import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from dateutil.easter import easter
from prophet import Prophet

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, record, score
from ML_Timeseries.data import line_chart, load_household, show

# Prophet attaches its own INFO handler to cmdstanpy, so a level change is not enough.
logging.getLogger("cmdstanpy").disabled = True
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
holiday_dates = []
for yr in range(2006, 2011):
    e = pd.Timestamp(easter(yr))
    holiday_dates += [pd.Timestamp(f"{yr}-{md}") for md in ("01-01", "05-01", "05-08", "07-14", "08-15", "11-01", "11-11", "12-25")]
    holiday_dates += [e + pd.Timedelta(days=k) for k in (1, 39, 50)]
HOLIDAYS = pd.DataFrame({"holiday": "public holiday", "ds": holiday_dates})


def prophet_forecaster(history, horizon):
    train = pd.DataFrame({"ds": history.index[-24 * 7 * 8:], "y": history.iloc[-24 * 7 * 8:].to_numpy()})
    m = Prophet(daily_seasonality=True, weekly_seasonality=True, yearly_seasonality=False, holidays=HOLIDAYS)
    m.fit(train)
    future = m.make_future_dataframe(periods=horizon, freq="h", include_history=False)
    return m.predict(future)["yhat"].to_numpy()


bt = backtest(y, prophet_forecaster)
prophet_score = score(bt, y, exclude=FILLED)
_ = record("Prophet (daily + weekly + holidays)", "classical", prophet_score, notebook="03_Classical/08_Prophet")
print(f"Prophet: MASE {prophet_score['mase']:.3f}, skill {prophet_score['skill']:+.1%}, {prophet_score['seconds']:.0f} s for 30 fits")

Prophet: MASE 0.766, skill +3.9%, 3 s for 30 fits



w = bt.window.max()
last = bt[bt.window == w]
show(line_chart(last.ds.dt.strftime("%a %H:00"), {"actual": last.y, "Prophet": last.yhat}, y_name="kWh", height="320px", zoom=False))




        




Prophet lands level with the free forecasts on the Baselines page: about the same skill as the median of the same hour over the last four weeks, and far behind SARIMA, tuned Holt-Winters and gradient boosting. That is roughly what its design predicts. With a flat trend over eight weeks, Prophet’s forecast is a smooth daily-plus-weekly Fourier profile fitted to those weeks, which is a smoothed seasonal average. It has no short-term memory: unlike SARIMA’s AR terms, nothing in it says “today is running high, so tonight will too”.
Prophet earns its place elsewhere: long daily or weekly business series with several seasonalities, holidays, missing data and changepoints in the trend, where an analyst wants interpretable components and tunable knobs more than the last few percent of accuracy.

A vector autoregression VAR(p) forecasts several series together. Each series is a linear function of the last p values of every series:
\[\mathbf{y}_t = \mathbf{c} + A_1 \mathbf{y}_{t-1} + \dots + A_p \mathbf{y}_{t-p} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_t\]

title: VAR and Granger Causality
text:
1. Granger causality
Series A Granger-causes B (Granger, 1969) if A’s past improves the forecast of B beyond what B’s own past gives. The test fits two regressions of B, with and without lags of A, and F-tests the difference. It is a statement about predictive information, not about cause: two series driven by a third will Granger-cause each other.
Each cell below is the smallest p-value over lags 1 to 7 for “row Granger-causes column”.


pv = {}
for target in X:
    for source in X:
        if source == target:
            continue
        with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):  # the function prints every test
            res = grangercausalitytests(train[[target, source]], maxlag=7)
        pv[(source, target)] = min(res[k][0]["ssr_ftest"][1] for k in res)
granger = pd.Series(pv).unstack()
granger.style.format("{:.4f}", na_rep="")

Every circuit Granger-causes every other, at the 5% level and mostly far below it. The wiring did not do that. A common cause did: whether the household is at home and active. A busy day raises cooking, washing, hot water and lighting together; a holiday week lowers all four. Each circuit’s past is therefore a noisy measurement of that hidden activity level, and so it helps predict every other circuit.
This is the standard trap with Granger tests on observational data. The result is real and useful for forecasting (a busy kitchen yesterday does carry information), and it says nothing about intervening (switching off the kitchen would not lower the water heater’s use).

section: 2. Does the VAR forecast the total better?
text:
2. Does the VAR forecast the total better?
If the circuits carry information about each other, forecasting them jointly and summing might beat forecasting the total directly. Seven days ahead, 30 weekly windows over the last 210 days, fitted on the last year at each origin:


sel = VAR(train.iloc[-365:].to_numpy()).select_order(14)
print(f"VAR order chosen by AIC: {sel.aic}, by BIC: {sel.bic}")


def var_total(order):
    def f(history, horizon):
        hist = X.loc[:history.index[-1]].iloc[-365:].to_numpy()
        return VAR(hist).fit(order).forecast(hist[-order:], horizon).sum(axis=1)
    return f


def ar_total(history, horizon):
    return AutoReg(history.iloc[-365:].to_numpy(), lags=7).fit().forecast(horizon)


candidates = {"seasonal naive (7 days)": seasonal_naive(7), "AR(7) on the total": ar_total,
              f"VAR({sel.bic}) on the circuits, summed": var_total(sel.bic), "VAR(7) on the circuits, summed": var_total(7)}
daily_scores = pd.DataFrame({n: score(backtest(total, f, horizon=7, n_windows=30, step=7), total, m=7, exclude=filled)
                             for n, f in candidates.items()}).T[["mase", "skill", "mae"]]

The VAR does not beat a plain autoregression on the total. The circuits’ cross-information is real (section 1), but the total already contains it: when the household is busy, the total rises, and the total’s own lags carry that signal. The VAR spends 16 coefficients per lag to rediscover it from four noisier series, and the extra variance costs more than the information gains. AIC asked for 9 lags (144 coefficients from one year of days) and BIC for 2. BIC’s model forecasts worst of the three: two days of history cannot see the weekly cycle. Neither order reaches the plain AR on the total.
When does a VAR pay? When the extra series carry information the target does not: an upstream sensor that moves before the target does, a price that leads demand, a weather series. Splitting one quantity into its parts rarely helps forecast the sum. These are daily results on a 7-day horizon, so they are not on the hourly scoreboard.

title: Theta and Intermittent Demand
text:
The Theta method (Assimakopoulos and Nikolopoulos, 2000) won the M3 competition in 2000 on 3,003 series. It splits a deseasonalised series into two “theta lines”: one with the curvature removed (the linear trend) and one with the curvature doubled. It extrapolates the first, forecasts the second with simple exponential smoothing, averages the two and puts the season back. Hyndman and Billah (2003) later showed that this is equivalent to simple exponential smoothing with a drift equal to half the trend’s slope, which explains why it works: a damped compromise between “the level stays” and “the trend continues”.


import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.forecasting.theta import ThetaModel
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, mae, origins, record, rmse, score, seasonal_naive
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, line_chart, load_household, show

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page BLAS pools would oversubscribe the 4 cores.
_ = threadpool_limits(1)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", module="statsmodels")


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
NB = "03_Classical/04_Theta_Intermittent"
WINDOW = 24 * 7 * 8


def theta(history, horizon):
    res = ThetaModel(history.iloc[-WINDOW:].to_numpy(), period=24).fit()
    return np.asarray(res.forecast(horizon))


theta_score = score(backtest(y, theta), y, exclude=FILLED)
record("Theta (24 h season)", "classical", theta_score, notebook=NB)
print(f"Theta: MASE {theta_score['mase']:.3f}, skill {theta_score['skill']:+.1%}")

Theta: MASE 0.831, skill -4.4%


Theta loses slightly to seasonal naive here, for the same reason the default ETS fit does: its smoothing is fitted for one step ahead, and the house’s next hour is a poor guide to tomorrow evening. Theta’s strength is many short, trending, low-frequency series such as yearly and monthly business data, which is what M3 was made of. An hourly household load has no trend worth extrapolating over a day.

Theta’s strength is many short, trending, low-frequency series such as yearly and monthly business data, which is what M3 was made of. An hourly household load has no trend worth extrapolating over a day.

title: Theta and Intermittent Demand
text:
2. Intermittent demand
Some series are zero most of the time: spare-parts demand, hospital admissions for a rare condition, or this house’s kitchen circuit, which draws nothing in 86% of hours. Ordinary methods handle these badly. Exponential smoothing decays towards zero after every zero and jumps after every non-zero, so its forecast is mostly noise.
Croston’s method (1972) splits the series into two smaller ones and smooths each separately:

the size of each non-zero demand, \(z\);
the interval between non-zero demands, \(p\).

The forecast is the demand rate \(z / p\), a flat line: the method does not try to say when the next demand comes, only how much per period on average. Three refinements:








Method
Change
Why




SBA (Syntetos and Boylan, 2005)
multiply Croston by \(1 - \alpha/2\)
Croston’s ratio of two smoothed values is biased upwards


TSB (Teunter, Syntetos and Babai, 2011)
smooth the probability of a demand every period, instead of the interval
the forecast decays when demand stops, which matters for items going obsolete


ADIDA (Nikolopoulos et al., 2011)
aggregate to a coarser period (here: days), forecast that, then split it back
at the daily level the series is no longer intermittent



All four are a few lines of numpy.


def croston(x, alpha=0.1, sba=False):
    nz = np.flatnonzero(x > 0)
    if len(nz) == 0:
        return 0.0
    z, p, last = x[nz[0]], nz[0] + 1.0, nz[0]
    for i in nz[1:]:
        z += alpha * (x[i] - z)
        p += alpha * ((i - last) - p)
        last = i
    rate = z / p
    return rate * (1 - alpha / 2) if sba else rate


def tsb(x, alpha=0.1, beta=0.1):
    nz = np.flatnonzero(x > 0)
    if len(nz) == 0:
        return 0.0
    z, prob = x[nz[0]], 1.0 / (nz[0] + 1)
    for v in x[nz[0]:]:
        prob += beta * ((v > 0) - prob)
        if v > 0:
            z += alpha * (v - z)
    return prob * z


def adida(history, horizon, alpha=0.1):
    "Aggregate to days, smooth the daily total, spread it over the hours by the average hourly profile."
    x = history.iloc[-WINDOW:]
    daily = x.resample("D").sum()
    level = daily.iloc[0]
    for v in daily.iloc[1:]:
        level += alpha * (v - level)
    profile = x.groupby(x.index.hour).sum()
    profile = profile / profile.sum() if profile.sum() > 0 else pd.Series(1 / 24, index=range(24))
    hours = (x.index[-1] + pd.to_timedelta(np.arange(1, horizon + 1), "h")).hour
    return level * profile.reindex(hours).to_numpy()


flat = lambda rate_fn: (lambda h, n: np.repeat(rate_fn(h.iloc[-WINDOW:].to_numpy()), n))
methods = {
    "zero": lambda h, n: np.zeros(n),
    "seasonal naive (24 h)": seasonal_naive(24),
    "Croston": flat(croston),
    "SBA": flat(lambda x: croston(x, sba=True)),
    "TSB": flat(tsb),
    "ADIDA (daily, hourly profile)": adida,
}


Scoring a sparse series
The kitchen series is scored on the same 30 windows with three numbers. MAE and RMSE as usual, plus bias: total forecast over total actual, minus one. For a stock-keeping decision (how many spare parts, how much hot water) the total over the period matters more than the hour-by-hour match.


kitchen = hh["sub1_kwh"]
rows = {}
for name, f in methods.items():
    bt = backtest(kitchen, f)
    rows[name] = {"MAE": mae(bt.y, bt.yhat), "RMSE": rmse(bt.y, bt.yhat), "bias": bt.yhat.sum() / bt.y.sum() - 1}
inter = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
print(f"kitchen: zero in {(kitchen == 0).mean():.0%} of hours")
test_days = [kitchen.iloc[i:i + 24].sum() for i in origins(kitchen.index)]
avg_days = [kitchen.iloc[i - WINDOW:i].sum() / (WINDOW / 24) for i in origins(kitchen.index)]
print(f"the 30 test days used {1 - sum(test_days) / sum(avg_days):.0%} less than an average day of the 8 weeks before each")
inter.style.format({"MAE": "{:.4f}", "RMSE": "{:.4f}", "bias": "{:+.0%}"})

The table is the whole lesson of intermittent forecasting:

The zero forecast has the lowest MAE. In most hours the kitchen draws nothing, so “nothing” is the median, and MAE rewards the median. It is also useless: its bias is -100%, it never predicts the energy the kitchen actually uses.
Seasonal naive copies yesterday’s spikes into the right hours of today only by luck, so it pays for every misplaced spike twice: once where it predicted one and once where the real one came.
Croston and SBA predict a small flat rate. Their MAE is worse than zero’s and their RMSE slightly better. SBA’s correction lowers Croston’s rate and its bias, as the theory says it should.
TSB does worst of the rate methods here: it updates the demand probability every hour, so a few busy days before an origin push the whole next day up.
ADIDA is the best non-zero method on every measure. Forecasting the daily total is a much easier problem than forecasting sparse hours, and spreading it by the usual hourly profile puts the energy at meal times.
Every method over-forecasts the total. That is the data, not a bug: kitchen use is lumpy, with rare heavy cooking days, so a typical day is well below the average day. The 30 test days happened to use about a fifth less than the average day before them, so even a perfect estimate of the average would have over-forecast them.

So for a sparse series the metric decides the method. Optimise MAE and you will ship the zero forecast; optimise RMSE or bias and you will ship Croston or ADIDA. The Forecast Metrics page showed the same trap from the metric’s side: sMAPE scored this series as the easiest of the three.
These results are for the kitchen circuit, not the total, so they are not on the scoreboard.


bt_k = {n: backtest(kitchen, methods[n]) for n in ("Croston", "ADIDA (daily, hourly profile)")}

a_, b_ = bt_k["Croston"], bt_k["ADIDA (daily, hourly profile)"]
a_, b_ = a_[a_.window == w], b_[b_.window == w]
show(line_chart(a_.ds.dt.strftime("%a %H:00"), {"actual kitchen": a_.y, "Croston": a_.yhat, "ADIDA": b_.yhat},
                y_name="kWh", height="300px", zoom=False))

title: Exponential Smoothing (ETS)
text:
Exponential smoothing forecasts with a weighted average of the past in which the weights shrink geometrically: the last hour counts most, the one before a little less, and so on. One parameter, \(\alpha\) between 0 and 1, sets how fast the weights shrink. A large \(\alpha\) follows the data closely; a small one averages over a long memory.
Holt-Winters applies the same idea to three states at once. With an additive season of length \(m\):
\[\ell_t = \alpha\,(y_t - s_{t-m}) + (1-\alpha)\,\ell_{t-1}\]
\[s_t = \gamma\,(y_t - \ell_t) + (1-\gamma)\,s_{t-m}\]
\[\hat y_{t+h} = \ell_t + s_{t+h-m}\]
The level \(\ell\) is the deseasonalised average; the season \(s\) is a profile of \(m\) values, one per hour of the cycle, each updated only when its hour comes round. A trend state can be added the same way. The ETS framework (Error, Trend, Season; Hyndman et al., 2002) writes all these variants as state space models, which gives them likelihoods, prediction intervals and automatic model selection.


import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.exponential_smoothing.ets import ETSModel
from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, origins, record, score, seasonal_naive
from ML_Timeseries.data import line_chart, load_household, show

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page BLAS pools would oversubscribe the 4 cores.

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", module="statsmodels")

y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
NB = "03_Classical/02_ETS"

import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.exponential_smoothing.ets import ETSModel
from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, origins, record, score, seasonal_naive
from ML_Timeseries.data import line_chart, load_household, show

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page BLAS pools would oversubscribe the 4 cores.

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", module="statsmodels")


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
NB = "03_Classical/02_ETS"
WINDOW = 24 * 7 * 8  # each forecast fits on the last 8 weeks

title: Exponential Smoothing (ETS)
text:
1. The default fit
statsmodels estimates \(\alpha\) and \(\gamma\) by minimising the one-step-ahead squared error on the training window. Here that is the wrong objective, because the forecast is used 1 to 24 steps ahead.


fitted = []


def holt_winters(m, alpha=None, gamma=None):
    "Additive Holt-Winters on the last 8 weeks; smoothing estimated unless given."
    def f(history, horizon):
        model = ExponentialSmoothing(history.iloc[-WINDOW:].to_numpy(), seasonal="add", seasonal_periods=m,
                                     initialization_method="estimated")
        kw = {} if alpha is None else {"smoothing_level": alpha, "smoothing_seasonal": gamma}
        res = model.fit(**kw)
        fitted.append((res.params["smoothing_level"], res.params["smoothing_seasonal"]))
        return res.forecast(horizon)
    return f


default = {}
for m in (24, 168):
    fitted.clear()
    default[m] = score(backtest(y, holt_winters(m)), y, exclude=FILLED)
    a, g = np.median(fitted, axis=0)
    print(f"season {m:3d} h: skill {default[m]['skill']:+.1%}; median fitted alpha {a:.2f}, gamma {g:.2f}")
_ = record("Holt-Winters (24 h), default fit", "classical", default[24], notebook=NB)

season  24 h: skill -13.4%; median fitted alpha 0.59, gamma 0.00
season 168 h: skill -9.6%; median fitted alpha 0.62, gamma 0.00


Both lose to seasonal naive. The fitted \(\alpha\) is around 0.6: the level jumps most of the way to every new hour. The fitted \(\gamma\) is 0: the season profile is frozen at its initial estimate and never learns from the eight weeks it is given. For a one-step forecast that is sensible, because the next hour does look like this one (the lag-1 autocorrelation is 0.71). For a forecast of tomorrow evening, the level is then whatever the last hour before midnight happened to be, plus a season profile that was barely updated. The model is excellent at a question nobody asked.

title: Exponential Smoothing (ETS)
section: 2. Smoothing chosen for the real horizon
text:
2. Smoothing chosen for the real horizon
The fix is to choose \(\alpha\) and \(\gamma\) by the error that matters: 24-step forecasts on validation windows that end before the first test origin, exactly the honest procedure from leak 5. Then the chosen pair runs once on the test windows.


first_test = origins(y.index)[0]
val_y = y.iloc[:first_test]
grid = [(a, g) for a in (0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.3) for g in (0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3)]
val = {}
for m in (24, 168):
    for a, g in grid:
        val[(m, a, g)] = score(backtest(val_y, holt_winters(m, a, g)), val_y, exclude=FILLED)["mae"]
val = pd.Series(val, name="validation MAE")
best = {m: val[m].idxmin() for m in (24, 168)}
tuned = {m: score(backtest(y, holt_winters(m, *best[m])), y, exclude=FILLED) for m in (24, 168)}
for m in (24, 168):
    print(f"season {m:3d} h: chosen alpha {best[m][0]}, gamma {best[m][1]} -> test skill {tuned[m]['skill']:+.1%}")
m_best = max(tuned, key=lambda m: tuned[m]["skill"])
_ = record(f"Holt-Winters ({m_best} h), smoothing tuned for 24 steps", "classical", tuned[m_best], notebook=NB,
       notes=f"alpha {best[m_best][0]}, gamma {best[m_best][1]}, chosen on validation windows")

season  24 h: chosen alpha 0.005, gamma 0.05 -> test skill +12.3%
season 168 h: chosen alpha 0.005, gamma 0.2 -> test skill +7.1%


With the smoothing chosen for the real task, Holt-Winters swings from losing to seasonal naive to beating every baseline by a wide margin. (Choosing the pair on the test windows instead would have reported about 16%; the honest validation choice gives a little less, which is leak 5 measured again.) Nothing about the model changed; only the objective used to fit it. This is the most general lesson on this page: fit a forecaster on the horizon you will use it at. It applies equally to ARIMA, to tree models trained on one-step targets, and to neural networks.
A small \(\alpha\) makes the level a long average, so a single unusual hour barely moves it, and the season adapts slowly enough to average several weeks, much like the seasonal window median on the Baselines page.


bt_default = backtest(y, holt_winters(24))
bt_tuned = backtest(y, holt_winters(m_best, *best[m_best]))
w = bt_tuned.window.max()
a_, b_ = bt_default[bt_default.window == w], bt_tuned[bt_tuned.window == w]
show(line_chart(b_.ds.dt.strftime("%a %H:00"), {"actual": b_.y, "default fit": a_.yhat, "tuned for 24 steps": b_.yhat},
                y_name="kWh", height="320px", zoom=False))

title: Exponential Smoothing (ETS)
section: 3. Where ETS is at home: daily totals
text:
3. Where ETS is at home: daily totals
ETS was designed for series like monthly sales or daily totals: smooth, with one season, where the next value really does depend mostly on the recent level. The same method on this house’s daily energy, forecasting 7 days ahead over 30 weekly windows, with automatic estimation and a damped trend:


daily = load_household("D")["kwh"]


def ets_daily(history, horizon):
    model = ETSModel(history.iloc[-365:].to_numpy(), error="add", trend="add", damped_trend=True,
                     seasonal="add", seasonal_periods=7)
    return model.fit(disp=False).forecast(horizon)


bt_d = backtest(daily, ets_daily, horizon=7, n_windows=30, step=7)
daily_ets = score(bt_d, daily, m=7)
print(f"daily totals, 7 days ahead: ETS(A,Ad,A) skill {daily_ets['skill']:+.1%} against repeating last week")

daily totals, 7 days ahead: ETS(A,Ad,A) skill +19.0% against repeating last week


On daily totals the default fit works, because one step ahead and the forecast horizon are the same kind of question: tomorrow’s total depends on today’s level. This result is on a different series, so it is not on the hourly scoreboard.

title: Scoreboard
text:
Each forecasting page calls record from ML_Timeseries.backtest, which writes one JSON file per model into nbs/results/. This page reads them all. A page re-run updates its own row; nothing else changes.

MASE: mean absolute scaled error, the headline. Lower is better; 1.0 is as good as seasonal naive was on the history.
Skill: the share of seasonal naive’s error removed on the same test windows. Higher is better; 0 is the reference itself.
Seconds: total forecasting time across the 30 windows, including any refits, on a 4-core CPU or a 12 GB GPU.

The Backtesting page defines the household protocol and Benchmarks the M4 Hourly one. Forecast Metrics explains why these metrics.

title: Forecast Metrics
text:
A metric is a decision about which errors hurt. RMSE punishes one large miss more than many small ones. MAPE punishes a miss at 03:00, when the house uses almost nothing, far more than the same miss at 19:00. Pick the wrong metric and the “best” model is best at the wrong thing.
All the metrics below are implemented in ML_Timeseries.backtest and computed here on two seasonal naive backtests, so the differences come from the metrics, not the models:

daily: repeat yesterday (season 24 hours);
weekly: repeat the same day last week (season 168 hours).

Each runs on three series from the same house, which differ in scale and in how often they are zero.


import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, mae, mape, mase_scale, rmse, seasonal_naive, smape, wape
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, load_household, show


hh = load_household()
observed = ~hh["filled"]  # score only hours the meter recorded, as the backtest protocol does
series = {"total": hh["kwh"], "kitchen": hh["sub1_kwh"], "water heater + AC": hh["sub3_kwh"]}
for name, s in series.items():
    print(f"{name:18s} mean {s.mean():.3f} kWh, zero in {(s == 0).mean():.0%} of hours")

total              mean 1.089 kWh, zero in 0% of hours
kitchen            mean 0.067 kWh, zero in 86% of hours
water heater + AC  mean 0.387 kWh, zero in 23% of hours

All the metrics below are implemented in ML_Timeseries.backtest and computed here on two seasonal naive backtests, so the differences come from the metrics, not the models:

title: Forecast Metrics
text:
1. Scale-dependent: MAE and RMSE
\[\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum |y_t - \hat y_t|\]
\[\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum (y_t - \hat y_t)^2}\]
Both are in the units of the series (kWh here), which makes them easy to read and impossible to compare across series. MAE is minimised by forecasting the median; RMSE by forecasting the mean. RMSE is always at least MAE, and the gap grows with the size of the largest misses, so RMSE far above MAE means a few big errors dominate.

title: Forecast Metrics
text:
2. Percentage errors: MAPE and sMAPE
\[\text{MAPE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum \frac{|y_t - \hat y_t|}{|y_t|}\]
\[\text{sMAPE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum \frac{2\,|y_t - \hat y_t|}{|y_t| + |\hat y_t|}\]
Percentages look scale-free, which is why managers like them. They fail in two ways:

Division by zero. One hour with zero consumption makes MAPE infinite. The kitchen meter reads zero in most hours.
Asymmetry. sMAPE was designed to fix MAPE, and it is not symmetric either: for the same absolute miss, forecasting too low costs more than forecasting too high.



print(f"actual 1.0, forecast 1.5 (too high): sMAPE {smape([1.0], [1.5]):.3f}")
print(f"actual 1.0, forecast 0.5 (too low):  sMAPE {smape([1.0], [0.5]):.3f}")

actual 1.0, forecast 1.5 (too high): sMAPE 0.400
actual 1.0, forecast 0.5 (too low):  sMAPE 0.667

title: Forecast Metrics
section: 3. Scale-free and safe: WAPE and MASE
text:
3. Scale-free and safe: WAPE and MASE
\[\text{WAPE} = \frac{\sum |y_t - \hat y_t|}{\sum |y_t|}\]
\[\text{MASE} = \frac{\text{MAE}}{\frac{1}{T-m}\sum_{t>m} |y_t - y_{t-m}|}\]
WAPE divides total error by total demand, so a zero hour adds nothing to the denominator instead of exploding one term. It reads as “the forecast is off by 25% of what the house used”.
MASE (Hyndman and Koehler, 2006) divides by the error the seasonal naive forecast made on the training history. It is defined for any series with some variation, works across scales, and has a fixed meaning: 1.0 is as good as seasonal naive was in the past. The M4 competition used it alongside sMAPE.
Skill is the most direct comparison: 1 - MAE / MAE(reference), both on the same test windows. It answers “how much error did this model remove compared with doing nothing clever”.


rows = []
for name, s in series.items():
    for label, m in [("daily", 24), ("weekly", 168)]:
        bt = backtest(s, seasonal_naive(m))
        bt = bt[observed.reindex(bt.ds).to_numpy()]
        scale = mase_scale(s, 24)
        mase = bt.groupby("window").apply(lambda g: mae(g.y, g.yhat) / scale.loc[g.origin.iloc[0]], include_groups=False).mean()
        rows.append({"series": name, "reference": label, "MAE": mae(bt.y, bt.yhat), "RMSE": rmse(bt.y, bt.yhat),
                     "MAPE": mape(bt.y, bt.yhat), "sMAPE": smape(bt.y, bt.yhat), "WAPE": wape(bt.y, bt.yhat), "MASE": mase})
table = pd.DataFrame(rows)

Read the table by column:

MAE and RMSE rank the series by size, not by how predictable they are.
MAPE is infinite for both sub-meters, because each has zero hours in the test windows. A metric that cannot rank two models is useless.
sMAPE gives the kitchen the best score of the three series. In 86% of its hours both the actual and the forecast are zero, and those terms count as perfect. Yet WAPE shows that the kitchen forecasts’ total error is almost twice the kitchen’s total consumption. sMAPE rewards a series for being empty.
WAPE and MASE stay finite on every series, and on each one they agree about which reference is better: yesterday for the total and the water heater, last week for the kitchen.
MASE below 1 for seasonal naive itself is not a contradiction. The scale comes from the whole history, and the test period (summer into autumn) is calmer than the four-year average, so the same method makes smaller errors there.

title: Forecast Metrics
text:
4. Where MAPE puts its weight
Split the daily reference’s errors by hour of day. The left bar is each hour’s share of the total absolute error, which is where the energy actually went wrong. The right bar is each hour’s share of the MAPE sum. MAPE gives the night (00:00 to 05:00) more weight than its share of the error, and the evening peak (18:00 to 21:00) less, because a 0.2 kWh miss on a 0.3 kWh night is 67%, while the same miss on a 2 kWh evening is 10%. A model tuned for MAPE learns to get the night right, where little energy is at stake.


bt = backtest(hh["kwh"], seasonal_naive(24))
bt = bt[observed.reindex(bt.ds).to_numpy()].copy()
bt["abs_err"] = (bt.y - bt.yhat).abs()
bt["pct_err"] = bt.abs_err / bt.y
by_hour = bt.groupby(bt.ds.dt.hour)[["abs_err", "pct_err"]].sum()
by_hour = by_hour / by_hour.sum()
show(bar_chart([f"{h:02d}" for h in by_hour.index],
               {"share of absolute error": by_hour.abs_err, "share of MAPE": by_hour.pct_err},
               y_name="share", height="360px"))

Every choice made before a model sees the data changes what the model can learn, and most of them are made silently: a default mean() when resampling, a fillna borrowed from another project, a timezone added because it seemed tidy. title: Data Preparation
section: 1. Resampling: the aggregate decides what you can see
text:
1. Resampling: the aggregate decides what you can see
The meter reports one-minute average power. The forecasts on this site use energy per hour, which is the mean power over the hour. That is the right aggregate for energy, and the wrong one for peak demand: a 6 kW oven running for ten minutes and a 1 kW heater running for an hour use the same energy, and a meter that bills on peak power sees them very differently.


g = raw["active_kw"].resample("h")
peak_ratio = (g.max() / g.mean()).dropna()
print(f"hourly peak minute / hourly mean: median {peak_ratio.median():.2f}, 90th percentile {peak_ratio.quantile(0.9):.2f}")
day = raw.loc["2009-12-20", "active_kw"]
hourly_mean = day.resample("h").mean().reindex(day.index, method="ffill")
show(line_chart(day.index.strftime("%H:%M"), {"1-minute power": day, "hourly mean": hourly_mean}, y_name="kW", height="320px"))

hourly peak minute / hourly mean: median 1.76, 90th percentile 3.30





        




In a typical hour the peak minute is almost twice the hourly mean, and in one hour in ten it is more than three times. A forecast of hourly energy cannot answer a question about peak power. If the goal were sizing a battery inverter or forecasting a demand charge, the resampling would have to keep the maximum (resample("h").max()), and that is a different target with a different model.

title: Data Preparation
text:
2. Clock time and daylight saving
France changes its clocks twice a year. In local clock time, the hour from 02:00 to 03:00 on the last Sunday of March does not exist, and the hour from 02:00 to 03:00 on the last Sunday of October happens twice. Yet the raw file is a perfect one-minute grid with no gap and no duplicate. So which clock is it?
The household answers it. If the timestamps ignored daylight saving, the family’s routine (getting up, cooking dinner) would jump by an hour in the data at each change. Compare the average daily profile in the three weeks before and after each change, and find the shift that lines them up:


changes = ["2007-03-25", "2007-10-28", "2008-03-30", "2008-10-26", "2009-03-29", "2009-10-25", "2010-03-28", "2010-10-31"]
rows = []
for c in changes:
    t = pd.Timestamp(c)
    before = y[t - pd.Timedelta("21D"):t - pd.Timedelta("1h")]
    after = y[t + pd.Timedelta("1D"):t + pd.Timedelta("22D")]
    pb = before.groupby(before.index.hour).mean().to_numpy()
    pa = after.groupby(after.index.hour).mean().to_numpy()
    corr = {k: np.corrcoef(pb, np.roll(pa, k))[0, 1] for k in range(-2, 3)}
    rows.append({"clock change": c, "best shift (h)": max(corr, key=corr.get), "corr at 0": corr[0], "corr at +1": corr[1], "corr at -1": corr[-1]})
dst = pd.DataFrame(rows)
dst.style.format(precision=3).hide(axis="index")

The best alignment is a shift of zero at every change. The routine stays at the same clock time across the changes, so the timestamps are local wall-clock time. Because the grid is still regular, the logger must have dealt with each change somehow (inventing an hour in spring, merging one in autumn), and the dataset’s documentation does not say how. The practical rules that follow:

Keep these timestamps naive. Localising them fails at the first spring change, because the file contains a time that did not exist:



try:
    y.tz_localize("Europe/Paris")
except ValueError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, ":", str(e).split(".")[0])

ValueError : 2007-03-25 02:00:00 is a nonexistent time due to daylight savings time



Calendar features stay correct. “Hour of day” in naive local time is the hour the household lived by, which is what predicts its behaviour.
For your own data, store UTC and convert at the edges. A logger that records UTC never has a missing or duplicate hour, and converting to local time for calendar features is one line (tz_convert).

title: Data Preparation
section: 3. Filling gaps: test the method, do not assume it
text:
3. Filling gaps: test the method, do not assume it
The Datasets loader fills gaps of up to 3 hours by linear interpolation and longer ones from the same hour a week earlier. That rule should be measured, not trusted. The test: take 300 random stretches of complete data for each gap length, hide them, fill them with each method, and score the fill against the hidden truth.


rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
complete = hh_raw["kwh"].notna().to_numpy()
lengths = [1, 3, 6, 24, 72]
fill_rows = []
for L in lengths:
    starts = []
    while len(starts) < 300:
        i = int(rng.integers(400, len(y) - 400))
        if complete[i - 340:i + L + 340].all():
            starts.append(i)
    errs = {"linear": [], "yesterday (t-24)": [], "last week (t-168)": [], "loader default": []}
    for i in starts:
        truth = y.iloc[i:i + L].to_numpy()
        s = y.iloc[i - 400:i + L + 400].copy()
        s.iloc[400:400 + L] = np.nan
        errs["linear"].append(np.abs(s.interpolate().iloc[400:400 + L].to_numpy() - truth).mean())
        daily_fill = s.copy()
        for k in (1, 2, 3):
            daily_fill = daily_fill.fillna(s.shift(24 * k))
        errs["yesterday (t-24)"].append(np.abs(daily_fill.iloc[400:400 + L].to_numpy() - truth).mean())
        errs["last week (t-168)"].append(np.abs(s.shift(168).iloc[400:400 + L].to_numpy() - truth).mean())
        errs["loader default"].append(np.abs(fill_gaps(s).iloc[400:400 + L].to_numpy() - truth).mean())
    fill_rows.append({"gap (h)": L} | {k: np.mean(v) for k, v in errs.items()})
fills = pd.DataFrame(fill_rows).set_index("gap (h)")
show(bar_chart([f"{L} h" for L in fills.index], {c: fills[c] for c in fills.columns}, y_name="fill MAE (kWh)", height="360px"))

The crossover is between 6 and 24 hours. Up to 6 hours, the neighbours on either side are the best guide; beyond a day, interpolation draws a straight line through a night and an evening, and copying last week wins. Yesterday and last week are close; last week is slightly better on long gaps because it also gets the weekday right.
The loader’s threshold of 3 hours is conservative: at 6 hours, interpolation beats last week by a small margin. It stays, because 9 of the 16 real gaps are 1 to 3 hours long and the difference at 6 hours is under 5%.

title: Data Preparation
section: 4. Outliers: extreme is not the same as wrong
text:
4. Outliers: extreme is not the same as wrong
A robust way to flag unusual hours: compare each hour with the median of the same hour of the week, and scale by the median absolute deviation (MAD) of that hour of the week. This robust z-score is not pulled by the outliers themselves, unlike a mean and standard deviation.


how = y.index.dayofweek * 24 + y.index.hour
med = y.groupby(how).transform("median")
mad = (y - med).abs().groupby(how).transform("median") * 1.4826
z = (y - med) / mad
flag = z.abs() > 5
print(f"{flag.sum():,} hours ({flag.mean():.1%}) have |robust z| > 5; largest z {z.max():.0f} at {z.idxmax():%a %Y-%m-%d %H:00} ({y[z.idxmax()]:.2f} kWh)")
night = flag[y.index.hour.isin(range(0, 6))].mean()
print(f"share of night hours (00-05) flagged: {night:.1%}; share of other hours flagged: {flag[~y.index.hour.isin(range(0, 6))].mean():.1%}")

1,402 hours (4.1%) have |robust z| > 5; largest z 39 at Sat 2007-02-03 02:00 (3.50 kWh)
share of night hours (00-05) flagged: 12.7%; share of other hours flagged: 1.2%


Four percent of hours look extreme, and most of them are nights. A quiet night has a tiny MAD, so one load of washing at 02:00 scores a z of 40. That is a real event in the house, not a sensor error. Removing or clipping it would teach a model that nobody ever runs the washing machine at night, and the model would then be confidently wrong when someone does.
The rule this site follows: remove values that are physically impossible (negative energy, a sub-meter above the total), keep values that are merely rare, and handle rare values in the loss or the metric, not in the data. The loader’s assertion that sub-meters never exceed the total is the first kind of check.

title: Data Preparation
text:
5. Scaling and transforms
Two transforms matter for the models that follow.
Per-series scaling. The total, kitchen and water-heater series differ in mean by a factor of about 16. A global model trained on all of them at once (the machine learning and deep learning sections) would spend its capacity on the large series unless each is scaled by its own statistics first.
The log transform. Consumption is right-skewed: most hours are small and a few are large. log1p (log of 1 plus the value, safe at zero) makes the distribution closer to symmetric, which helps models that assume Gaussian errors. It works on the total and does little for the kitchen meter, whose skew comes from being zero most of the time; no smooth transform moves a spike of zeros. The cost: a model trained on the log predicts the median, not the mean, after transforming back, so its forecasts of total energy run low unless corrected.


stats = pd.DataFrame({name: {"mean kWh": s.mean(), "std kWh": s.std(), "skew": s.skew(), "skew after log1p": np.log1p(s).skew()}
                      for name, s in {"total": y, "kitchen": hh["sub1_kwh"], "water heater + AC": hh["sub3_kwh"]}.items()}).T

Filling gaps
Most models cannot take missing values, so the loader can fill them, and it marks every filled period in a boolean filled column. The backtest uses that flag to score forecasts only against hours the meter actually recorded. The fill rule depends on the gap length:

Short gaps (up to 3 periods): linear interpolation. Consumption changes little in three hours.
Long gaps: copy the value from one season earlier (168 hours, the same hour last week). Interpolating across two missing days would draw a straight line through two nights and two evenings, which no house ever does.

The Data Preparation notebook compares these choices. Here they are only the default.

Models
Auto Forecast: Automatic forecasting tools search for the best parameters and select the best possible model for a series of time series. These tools are useful for large collections of univariate time series. Includes automatic versions of: Arima, ETS, Theta, CES.
Exponential Smoothing: Uses a weighted average of all past observations where the weights decrease exponentially into the past. Suitable for data with no clear trend or seasonality. Examples: SES, Holt’s Winters, SSO.
Benchmark models: classical models for establishing baselines. Examples: Mean, Naive, Random Walk
Intermittent or Sparse models: suited for series with very few non-zero observations. Examples: CROSTON, ADIDA, IMAPA
Multiple Seasonalities: suited for signals with more than one clear seasonality. Useful for low-frequency data like electricity and logs. Examples: MSTL.
Theta Models: fit two theta lines to a deseasonalized time series, using different techniques to obtain and combine the two theta lines to produce the final forecasts. Examples: Theta, DynamicTheta

AutoARIMA:

Automatically selects the best ARIMA (AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average) model using an information criterion.

HoltWinters:

Triple exponential smoothing, Holt-Winters’ method is an extension of exponential smoothing for series that contain both trend and seasonality.

HistoricAverage: arthimetic mean

title: Decomposition and Stationarity
text:
Most forecasting methods assume a series is a sum of parts:
\[y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t\]

Trend \(T_t\): the slow level, here the household’s general consumption over months.
Seasonality \(S_t\): patterns that repeat on a fixed period. Here there are three: the day (24 hours), the week (168 hours) and the year.
Remainder \(R_t\): everything else, including the unpredictable.

Decomposing first tells you which parts a model must capture and how much of the series is predictable at all. If the remainder holds most of the variance, no model will forecast well, and the remainder sets the floor on error.


import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.signal import find_peaks
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import MSTL, STL
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf, adfuller, kpss, pacf

from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, line_chart, load_household, show


hh = load_household()
y = hh["kwh"]
year = y["2009-11-01":"2010-10-31"]
daily = load_household("D")["kwh"]
print(f"hourly: {len(y):,} points, one year for MSTL: {len(year):,}; daily: {len(daily):,}")
