title: Decomposition and Stationarity
text:
Most forecasting methods assume a series is a sum of parts:
\[y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t\]

Trend \(T_t\): the slow level, here the household’s general consumption over months.
Seasonality \(S_t\): patterns that repeat on a fixed period. Here there are three: the day (24 hours), the week (168 hours) and the year.
Remainder \(R_t\): everything else, including the unpredictable.

Decomposing first tells you which parts a model must capture and how much of the series is predictable at all. If the remainder holds most of the variance, no model will forecast well, and the remainder sets the floor on error.


import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.signal import find_peaks
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import MSTL, STL
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf, adfuller, kpss, pacf

from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, line_chart, load_household, show


hh = load_household()
y = hh["kwh"]
year = y["2009-11-01":"2010-10-31"]
daily = load_household("D")["kwh"]
print(f"hourly: {len(y):,} points, one year for MSTL: {len(year):,}; daily: {len(daily):,}")

hourly: 34,589 points, one year for MSTL: 8,760; daily: 1,442

title: Decomposition and Stationarity
text:
1. MSTL: several seasons at once
STL (Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess, Cleveland et al., 1990) splits a series into trend, one seasonal component and a remainder by repeated local regression. It handles a season whose shape drifts over time, which classical decomposition (a fixed average per hour) cannot. MSTL (Bandara et al., 2021) runs STL once per seasonal period, so the daily and weekly cycles get separate components.
Here it runs on one year of hourly data with periods of 24 and 168 hours.


mstl = MSTL(year, periods=(24, 168)).fit()
parts = pd.DataFrame({"trend": mstl.trend, "daily": mstl.seasonal["seasonal_24"],
                      "weekly": mstl.seasonal["seasonal_168"], "remainder": mstl.resid})
win = parts["2010-01-04":"2010-01-10"]
labels = win.index.strftime("%a %H:00")
show(line_chart(labels, {"actual": year.loc[win.index], "trend + daily + weekly": win.trend + win.daily + win.weekly},
                y_name="kWh", height="340px"))




        




The gap between the two lines is the remainder. This is an in-sample fit: MSTL lets the seasonal shapes drift week by week, so they follow the data more closely here than any forecast made in advance could. Even so, the misses are the sharp spikes, which are appliances switched on at times the calendar cannot predict. The two seasonal components on their own:

show(line_chart(labels, {"daily (24 h)": win.daily, "weekly (168 h)": win.weekly}, y_name="kWh", height="300px"))




        




How much each part matters is measured by its strength (Wang, Smith and Hyndman, 2006): one minus the remainder’s variance as a share of the component plus remainder. 0 means the component adds nothing over noise; 1 means it explains all the variation the remainder would otherwise hold.
\[F_S = \max\left(0,\ 1 - \frac{\operatorname{Var}(R_t)}{\operatorname{Var}(S_t + R_t)}\right)\]

def strength(component, remainder):
    return max(0.0, 1 - remainder.var() / (component + remainder).var())


annual = STL(daily, period=365, robust=True).fit()
strengths = pd.Series({
    "daily (24 h)": strength(parts.daily, parts.remainder),
    "weekly (168 h)": strength(parts.weekly, parts.remainder),
    "annual (on daily totals)": strength(annual.seasonal, annual.resid),
}, name="strength")
print(f"remainder std {parts.remainder.std():.3f} kWh of total std {year.std():.3f} kWh")
strengths.round(3)

remainder std 0.462 kWh of total std 0.812 kWh


daily (24 h)                0.568
weekly (168 h)              0.277
annual (on daily totals)    0.582
Name: strength, dtype: float64


The daily cycle is the strongest part of the hourly series, the weekly cycle is weaker, and the annual cycle shows clearly on daily totals (winter heating and lighting). The remainder’s standard deviation is more than half the series’ own: an hour in this house is noisy, because a kettle, an oven or a water heater switches on when someone decides to use it. Any hourly model will leave a large share of the error unexplained.

title: Decomposition and Stationarity
section: 2. The periodogram: which periods carry power
text:
2. The periodogram: which periods carry power
A discrete Fourier transform rewrites the series as a sum of sine waves. The periodogram is the power of each wave. A seasonal period shows as a peak, and so do its harmonics (period / 2, period / 3, …), because a daily cycle with a sharp morning and evening peak is not a sine wave and needs several to draw.


x = y.to_numpy() - y.mean()
power = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) ** 2
period = 1 / np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), d=1.0)[1:]
power = power[1:]
band = (period >= 4) & (period <= 400)
peaks, _ = find_peaks(power[band])
cand = pd.DataFrame({"period_h": period[band][peaks], "power": power[band][peaks]}).sort_values("power", ascending=False)
top = []
for p, pw in cand.itertuples(index=False):
    if all(abs(p - q) / q > 0.03 for q, _ in top):
        top.append((p, pw))
    if len(top) == 8:
        break
top = pd.DataFrame(top, columns=["period_h", "power"])
top["share"] = top.power / top.power.sum()
show(bar_chart([f"{p:.0f} h" for p in top.period_h], {"share of peak power": top.share}, height="320px"))




        




The two largest peaks are 12 and 24 hours: the day and its first harmonic (a morning peak and an evening peak, 12 hours apart). Next come 6 hours (the second harmonic), then the week (168 hours) and its own harmonic at 84 hours. These are the periods MSTL was given, found here from the data alone. The FFT finds the seasons; the decomposition then separates them.

title: Decomposition and Stationarity
text:
3. Autocorrelation
The autocorrelation function (ACF) is the correlation between the series and itself shifted by k hours. It is the most direct view of which lags a model should use. The partial autocorrelation (PACF) removes what shorter lags already explain, so it shows which lags add new information.


lags = np.arange(0, 401)
a = acf(y, nlags=400, fft=True)
show(line_chart(lags, {"ACF": a}, y_name="correlation", height="320px"))




        





p = pacf(y, nlags=48)
print("ACF at 1, 12, 24, 168, 336 h:", {k: round(float(a[k]), 3) for k in (1, 12, 24, 168, 336)})
print("largest PACF after lag 1:", {int(k): round(float(p[k]), 3) for k in np.argsort(-np.abs(p[2:]))[:4] + 2})

ACF at 1, 12, 24, 168, 336 h: {1: 0.713, 12: 0.239, 24: 0.436, 168: 0.463, 336: 0.431}
largest PACF after lag 1: {23: 0.162, 22: 0.145, 10: 0.107, 47: 0.101}


Three things to read from it:

Lag 1 is by far the highest. The next hour looks like this hour. That is useless for a day-ahead forecast, which must start from lag 24.
Lag 168 beats lag 24, slightly. Over four years, the same hour last week correlates a little better with this hour than the same hour yesterday, because a weekly lag matches both the hour of the day and the day of the week. Correlation over the whole series is not forecast accuracy over a test period, though: on the Baselines page, copying last week loses to copying yesterday, because a week-old copy also carries a week-old level.
The peaks decay slowly. Lag 336 (two weeks) is still about as strong as lag 168. The seasonal pattern is stable, which favours models that average several past seasons over ones that copy one.

title: Decomposition and Stationarity
text:
4. Stationarity: ADF and KPSS
A series is stationary when its mean, variance and autocorrelation do not change over time. ARIMA-type models assume it after differencing, so the classical workflow tests for it first. Two tests ask opposite questions:








Test
Null hypothesis
Small p-value means




ADF (augmented Dickey-Fuller)
the series has a unit root (a random walk part, never returns to a mean)
no unit root


KPSS (Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin)
the series is stationary around a constant level
not stationary



Used together they separate three cases: both say stationary; both say a unit root, so difference it; or they disagree, which usually means stationary around something the test does not model, such as seasonality.


cases = {"hourly, one year": year, "daily totals": daily,
         "daily, differenced": daily.diff().dropna(), "daily, minus last week": daily.diff(7).dropna()}
rows = []
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")  # KPSS warns when its p-value is outside its lookup table (0.01 to 0.1)
    for name, s in cases.items():
        rows.append({"series": name, "ADF p": adfuller(s, autolag="AIC")[1], "KPSS p": kpss(s, regression="c", nlags="auto")[1]})
tests = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("series")
tests.style.format("{:.3f}")






 
ADF p
KPSS p


series
 
 




hourly, one year
0.000
0.010


daily totals
0.005
0.100


daily, differenced
0.000
0.100


daily, minus last week
0.000
0.100





Reading the table:

Daily totals: ADF rejects a unit root and KPSS does not reject stationarity. Daily consumption returns to its level; it is not a random walk, so differencing it would only add noise.
Hourly: ADF rejects a unit root, and KPSS rejects stationarity too. The two disagree because the hourly series has a strong, deterministic daily cycle, which KPSS reads as a changing mean. The fix is to model the seasonality (seasonal terms, Fourier terms, seasonal lags), not to difference.
KPSS reports p-values only between 0.01 and 0.1 (it interpolates a table), so 0.010 means “0.01 or less” and 0.100 means “0.1 or more”.

Stationarity tests matter most for ARIMA. Tree models and neural networks do not assume stationarity, but they still forecast badly outside the range they were trained on, so a trend still has to be handled.

What this means for the models







Finding
Consequence




Daily and weekly seasons, with harmonics
Fourier terms at 24 h and 168 h are good features; averaging several aligned past weeks beats copying one


Lag 168, 24 and 336 all similar
Use several seasonal lags, not one


Large remainder
Expect skill well below 50% against seasonal naive for any model


No unit root, deterministic seasons
Model seasonality explicitly; avoid differencing the level


Annual cycle on daily totals
A model trained on summer will under-forecast winter; the backtest’s test span (June to November) runs into the start of winter

title: Feature Engineering
text:
A tree model or a linear model cannot read a time series. It reads rows. Feature engineering builds, for each hour to forecast, a row of numbers that are known at the forecast origin and that carry information about that hour.
Every feature here obeys the rule from Backtesting and Leakage: it is computed from history plus an empty future, so a feature that would need a future value comes out empty instead of leaking. The model is the same throughout (scikit-learn’s histogram gradient boosting, trained once on everything before the first origin), so every change in score comes from the features.

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page OpenMP pools on 4 cores made the gradient-boosting pages 30x slower.

title: Feature Engineering
text:
2. One group at a time
Each step adds one group to the previous set, trains the model and runs the full 30-window backtest. Sub-meter values are cut at the origin too: the forecaster sees hh.loc[:origin], nothing later.


def gbm_forecaster(groups):
    train = y.iloc[:cut]
    model = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=300, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=0)
    model.fit(make_features(train, groups, hh).iloc[700:], train.iloc[700:])

    def f(history, horizon):
        ext = pd.concat([history, pd.Series(np.nan, index=future_index(history, horizon))])
        return model.predict(make_features(ext, groups, hh.loc[:history.index[-1]]).iloc[-horizon:])
    return f


steps = [("seasonal lags", ()), ("+ calendar", ("calendar",)), ("+ Fourier", ("calendar", "fourier")),

Reading the steps:

Seasonal lags alone already beat seasonal naive, because the model can weigh four past seasons instead of copying one.
The calendar is the largest single gain. Hour and day of week let the model learn the household’s routine directly instead of inferring it from lags, and the holiday flag catches days that look like Sundays.
Fourier terms add a little, mostly through the annual pair: four lags cannot know it is November.
Rolling statistics add almost nothing on top. The same-hour average they include is close to what the lags and calendar already give.
Sub-meters do not help. Knowing that the kitchen was busy yesterday says little about the total tomorrow beyond what the total itself says. An exogenous series earns its place only when it carries information the target does not, such as a weather forecast for heating load.

The best set goes on the scoreboard as the first machine learning row.

title: Feature Engineering
section: 3. Features of a whole series: catch22
text:
3. Features of a whole series: catch22
The features above describe one hour. Some tasks need features of a whole series or a whole window: classifying a day, clustering households, spotting an unusual week. catch22 (Lubba et al., 2019) is a set of 22 such features, chosen from thousands of candidate features in the hctsa library because together they classify time series nearly as well as the full set. They measure distribution shape, autocorrelation, entropy and how the series moves between levels. tsfresh is the large alternative: hundreds of features with built-in significance tests, slower and more prone to overfitting on small data.
Here catch22 runs on each day’s 24-hour profile (via sktime). The question: do the 22 numbers alone tell a weekday from a weekend?


start = y.index[y.index.hour == 0][0]
days = y[start:]
n = len(days) // 24
profiles = days.to_numpy()[:n * 24].reshape(n, 1, 24)
day_index = days.index[::24][:n]
weekend = (day_index.dayofweek >= 5).astype(int)
F = Catch22(col_names="short_str_feat").fit_transform(profiles)
print(f"{F.shape[0]} days x {F.shape[1]} catch22 features")

1440 days x 22 catch22 features



clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))
acc = cross_val_score(clf, F.fillna(0), weekend, cv=5).mean()
base = 1 - weekend.mean()
print(f"weekday/weekend accuracy from catch22 alone: {acc:.1%} (always guessing weekday: {base:.1%})")
d = (F[weekend == 1].mean() - F[weekend == 0].mean()) / F.std()
d.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).head(5).rename("standardised difference").round(2)

weekday/weekend accuracy from catch22 alone: 75.0% (always guessing weekday: 71.5%)


transition_matrix    0.70
centroid_freq        0.66
ami_timescale        0.56
acf_timescale        0.54
whiten_timescale     0.46
Name: standardised difference, dtype: float64


The 22 shape features beat the base rate, but not by much. The features that differ most between weekend and weekday measure timescales and frequency content (how fast the profile changes), not level. Most catch22 features ignore when in the day something happens, on purpose. That is the trade-off of shape features: they are robust to shifts in time, which is good for clustering households and bad for telling Saturday from Tuesday. For this site’s forecasting task, the hour-level features in sections 1 and 2 do the work.

title: Backtesting and Leakage
text:
A forecast is used at one moment, with only the past available. An honest evaluation must recreate that moment many times: pick a point in time (the origin), give the model only the data before it, ask for the next 24 hours, and score the answer against what actually happened. Repeat for many origins and average.
This is a rolling-origin backtest. The ordinary machine learning recipe (shuffle the rows, hold out 20%) breaks it, because a shuffled test row has its own neighbours, one hour before and one hour after, in the training set. The model then interpolates instead of forecasting. Section 5 measures how much that flatters the score.



Rolling-origin backtest

title: Backtesting and Leakage
text:
1. The protocol
Every single-series page uses the same protocol, so scores compare across pages:



Setting
Value
Why




Target
hourly household energy, kWh (gap-filled)
the Datasets page


Horizon
24 hours from midnight
a day-ahead forecast, the common operational case


Windows
30 origins, 5 days apart
5 and 7 share no factor, so the origins cycle through every weekday


Test span
the last 150 days (late June to late November 2010)
summer into winter, with the annual peak just starting


History
everything before the origin
a model may refit at each origin or train once before the first


Scored hours
only hours the meter recorded
49 of the 720 test hours were gap-filled (one whole day copied from the week before); they are forecast but not scored, because a forecast scored against a copy of last week rewards any model that copies last week



Excluding the filled hours matters more than it sounds. Scored against all 720 hours, repeating last week earns +2% skill against repeating yesterday; scored only on recorded hours, it earns -4.5%. One gap-filled day, copied from the week before, was worth six points to any model that copies last week. That is a sixth leak, through the data preparation rather than the model.
The test span covers one part of the year only. A model that is good in summer and bad in winter will look better than it is. That is a known limit of this protocol, accepted to keep runs short.

title: Backtesting and Leakage
text:
2. Running a backtest
A forecaster is any function f(history, horizon) that returns horizon numbers. history is a pd.Series that ends one step before the origin, so a forecaster cannot see the future even by mistake. backtest calls it once per origin and returns one row per forecast hour.
future_index gives the timestamps a forecaster is asked about, for models that need calendar features.

    horizon:int=24, n_windows:int=30, step:int=120

Rolling-origin backtest: one row per (window, forecast hour) with y and yhat. Total seconds in .attrs.

title: Backtesting and Leakage
text:
3. The reference: seasonal naive
The seasonal naive forecast repeats the last observed season: tomorrow at 18:00 equals today at 18:00. It costs nothing, and it is the bar every other model must clear. A model that cannot beat it has learned nothing useful about the series.

Forecaster that repeats the last m observations.

title: Backtesting and Leakage
text:
4. Scores
The Forecast Metrics page explains each metric and when it misleads. score reports all of them for one backtest:

MASE (mean absolute scaled error) is the headline. It divides each window’s mean absolute error by the mean absolute error of the seasonal naive forecast inside that window’s history. Below 1 means better than seasonal naive was on the past.
Skill is 1 - MAE / MAE(seasonal naive) on the same test windows. Positive means the model beat the reference where it mattered; 0.2 means 20% less error.

exclude takes a boolean series (the loader’s filled flag) and drops those hours from every metric, for the model and the reference alike.

title: Backtesting and Leakage
text:
7. Five ways an evaluation leaks
Each example builds a gradient-boosted tree model (scikit-learn’s HistGradientBoostingRegressor) twice: once with the bug, once without. The bug always makes the score look better. That is what makes leakage dangerous: nothing fails, the number just improves.
The honest model uses only features that exist at the origin:

lags of 24, 25, 48, 168 and 336 hours (every lag is at least the 24-hour horizon, so its value is known before the forecast starts);
hour of day and day of week.

It trains once on everything before the first origin.


from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_val_score

from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page OpenMP pools on 4 cores made the gradient-boosting pages 30x slower.
_ = threadpool_limits(1)


SAFE_LAGS = [24, 25, 48, 168, 336]


def features(s: pd.Series, lags=SAFE_LAGS, extra: dict | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    X = pd.DataFrame({f"lag{l}": s.shift(l) for l in lags}, index=s.index)
    X["hour"], X["dow"] = s.index.hour, s.index.dayofweek
    for k, v in (extra or {}).items():
        X[k] = v
    return X


def gbm(**kw):
    return HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=200, learning_rate=0.08, random_state=0, **kw)


cut = origins(y.index)[0]
train_y = y.iloc[:cut]


def honest_forecaster(model, make_features):
    "Forecast by computing features on history plus an empty future, so no future value can leak in."
    def f(history, horizon):
        ext = pd.concat([history, pd.Series(np.nan, index=future_index(history, horizon))])
        return model.predict(make_features(ext).iloc[-horizon:])
    return f


scored_ds = bt.ds[~FILLED.reindex(bt.ds).to_numpy()].to_numpy()


def test_rows_mae(model, X_full):
    "The buggy way: build features on the whole series, then score the test rows."
    p = model.predict(X_full)
    idx = scored_ds
    return mae(y.loc[idx], pd.Series(p, index=y.index).loc[idx])


X_train = features(train_y).iloc[336:]
base = gbm().fit(X_train, train_y.iloc[336:])
honest_bt = backtest(y, honest_forecaster(base, features))
honest = score(honest_bt, y, exclude=FILLED)
print(f"honest gradient boosting: MAE {honest['mae']:.3f}, skill {honest['skill']:+.1%}")

honest gradient boosting: MAE 0.464, skill +11.1%



Bug 1: shuffled cross-validation
The model is scored with 5-fold cross-validation on shuffled training rows. Each held-out hour has its neighbours in the training folds.
Fix: score with the rolling-origin backtest.

cv_mae = -cross_val_score(gbm(), X_train, train_y.iloc[336:], cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0),
                          scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error").mean()
leaks = [{"bug": "1. shuffled cross-validation", "leaky MAE": cv_mae, "honest MAE": honest["mae"]}]
print(f"shuffled CV MAE {cv_mae:.3f} vs backtest MAE {honest['mae']:.3f}")

shuffled CV MAE 0.493 vs backtest MAE 0.464


Here the shuffled score is worse, not better. The two numbers measure different periods: cross-validation averages over four years including the winters, and the backtest covers summer and autumn, when consumption is lower and easier. So comparing the two tells you nothing, which is the point. A shuffled score cannot even be compared with the real one.
The honest comparison holds the period fixed: train on the same rows, then score the backtest’s own test hours by shuffled cross-validation over all rows including the test period.

X_all = features(y).iloc[336:]
y_all = y.iloc[336:]
test_mask = X_all.index.isin(scored_ds)
oof = np.zeros(len(X_all))
for tr, te in KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0).split(X_all):
    oof[te] = gbm().fit(X_all.iloc[tr], y_all.iloc[tr]).predict(X_all.iloc[te])
cv_test_mae = mae(y_all[test_mask], oof[test_mask])
leaks[0]["leaky MAE"] = cv_test_mae
print(f"shuffled CV on the test hours: MAE {cv_test_mae:.3f} vs backtest MAE {honest['mae']:.3f}")

shuffled CV on the test hours: MAE 0.453 vs backtest MAE 0.464


On the same hours, shuffling flatters the score, but only by a few percent. The leak is small here because no feature is closer than 24 hours, so a test hour’s direct neighbours never appear as inputs. Add lag1 to the features (as most tutorials do) and shuffled cross-validation scores the model on interpolation instead, which bug 2 shows is worth about 30%.


Bug 2: lags shorter than the horizon
lag1 (the previous hour) is the strongest feature any hourly model can have. For a 24-hour forecast it exists only for the first hour; for hour 18 it would be the value at hour 17, which is still in the future at the origin. Building the feature table on the whole series and then splitting hands the model those future values.
Fix: use only lags of at least the horizon, or forecast recursively and feed predictions back in.

short = lambda s: features(s, lags=[1, 2, 3] + SAFE_LAGS)
m2 = gbm().fit(short(train_y).iloc[336:], train_y.iloc[336:])
leaky2 = test_rows_mae(m2, short(y))
honest2 = score(backtest(y, honest_forecaster(m2, short)), y, exclude=FILLED)["mae"]
leaks.append({"bug": "2. lags shorter than the horizon", "leaky MAE": leaky2, "honest MAE": honest2})
print(f"lag1-3 with future values: MAE {leaky2:.3f}; same model with only the past: MAE {honest2:.3f}")

lag1-3 with future values: MAE 0.325; same model with only the past: MAE 0.467




Bug 3: a rolling window that includes the target
s.rolling(24).mean() at hour t averages hours t-23 to t, so it contains the value being predicted. This is the most common leak in feature engineering code, because pandas aligns the window to its right edge by default.
Fix: shift by the horizon before rolling: s.shift(24).rolling(24).mean().

roll_leak = lambda s: features(s, extra={"roll24": s.rolling(24).mean()})
roll_safe = lambda s: features(s, extra={"roll24": s.shift(24).rolling(24).mean()})
m3 = gbm().fit(roll_leak(train_y).iloc[336:], train_y.iloc[336:])
leaky3 = test_rows_mae(m3, roll_leak(y))
m3s = gbm().fit(roll_safe(train_y).iloc[336:], train_y.iloc[336:])
honest3 = score(backtest(y, honest_forecaster(m3s, roll_safe)), y, exclude=FILLED)["mae"]
leaks.append({"bug": "3. rolling mean includes the target", "leaky MAE": leaky3, "honest MAE": honest3})
print(f"unshifted rolling mean: MAE {leaky3:.3f}; shifted: MAE {honest3:.3f}")

unshifted rolling mean: MAE 0.403; shifted: MAE 0.453




Bug 4: a statistic computed on the whole series
An hour-of-week profile (the average consumption for each of the 168 hours of the week) is a strong feature. Computed over the whole series, it includes the test period’s own average, which is information about the answers.
Fix: compute every statistic, scaler and encoder on the training rows only.

how = lambda idx: idx.dayofweek * 24 + idx.hour
prof_all = y.groupby(how(y.index)).mean()
prof_train = train_y.groupby(how(train_y.index)).mean()
prof_feat = lambda prof: (lambda s: features(s, extra={"profile": prof.reindex(how(s.index)).to_numpy()}))
m4 = gbm().fit(prof_feat(prof_all)(train_y).iloc[336:], train_y.iloc[336:])
leaky4 = test_rows_mae(m4, prof_feat(prof_all)(y))
m4s = gbm().fit(prof_feat(prof_train)(train_y).iloc[336:], train_y.iloc[336:])
honest4 = score(backtest(y, honest_forecaster(m4s, prof_feat(prof_train))), y, exclude=FILLED)["mae"]
leaks.append({"bug": "4. statistic computed on all data", "leaky MAE": leaky4, "honest MAE": honest4})
print(f"profile from all data: MAE {leaky4:.3f}; from training only: MAE {honest4:.3f}")

profile from all data: MAE 0.462; from training only: MAE 0.462


The leak is almost invisible here, because the test period is only 150 of about 1,440 days, so it barely moves a four-year average. The same bug is serious when the test period is a large share of the data, or when the statistic tracks a trend (a min-max scaler on a growing series, for example).


Bug 5: tuning on the test windows
Six settings of the model are tried, and the one with the lowest backtest score is reported. That score is optimistic: the choice itself used the test data. With enough settings, a lucky one always wins.
Fix: choose on validation windows that end before the first test origin, then score the chosen setting once on the test windows.

grid = [dict(max_iter=it, learning_rate=lr) for it in (50, 200, 600) for lr in (0.03, 0.15)]
val_y = y.iloc[:cut]
fit_cut = origins(val_y.index)[0]


def fit_eval(params, series, cut_at):
    m = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0, **params).fit(features(series.iloc[:cut_at]).iloc[336:], series.iloc[336:cut_at])
    return m


def observed_mae(b):
    b = b[~FILLED.reindex(b.ds).to_numpy()]
    return mae(b.y, b.yhat)


test_scores = [observed_mae(backtest(y, honest_forecaster(fit_eval(p, y, cut), features))) for p in grid]
val_scores = [observed_mae(backtest(val_y, honest_forecaster(fit_eval(p, val_y, fit_cut), features))) for p in grid]
leaky5, honest5 = min(test_scores), test_scores[int(np.argmin(val_scores))]
leaks.append({"bug": "5. tuning on the test windows", "leaky MAE": leaky5, "honest MAE": honest5})
print(f"best of {len(grid)} on test: MAE {leaky5:.3f}; chosen on validation: MAE {honest5:.3f}")

best of 6 on test: MAE 0.462; chosen on validation: MAE 0.462


Here validation picked the same setting the test windows would have, so the two scores match. That is luck, not safety: the leaky procedure can only ever report a score equal to or better than the honest one, and the gap grows with every setting tried.


Summary
The “flattery” column is how much lower the leaky error is than the honest one. Bugs 2 and 3 are the dangerous kind: they make a model that beats seasonal naive by about 11% look like it beats it by 23 to 38%. Bugs 1, 4 and 5 are small on this data for the reasons given above, and much larger on others. All five share one property: the leaky number is never worse than the honest one, so a leak only ever makes results look better.

leak_table = pd.DataFrame(leaks)
leak_table["flattery"] = 1 - leak_table["leaky MAE"] / leak_table["honest MAE"]
leak_table.style.format({"leaky MAE": "{:.3f}", "honest MAE": "{:.3f}", "flattery": "{:.0%}"}).hide(axis="index")

What this unlocks
Every later page calls backtest, score and record, so a new model is three lines away from a comparable number. The honest gradient-boosting model above is not recorded here; the machine learning section builds it properly.

title: Benchmarks
text:
One dataset can make any method look good. A benchmark fixes many datasets, a split and a metric in advance, so that results from different papers compare. Each one also bakes in choices that decide what “best” means, and a leaderboard number is only meaningful once you know them.








Benchmark
What it is
Headline metric




M4 (2018)
100,000 series, yearly to hourly, fixed horizons
sMAPE and MASE, combined as OWA (overall weighted average) against a naive method


Monash (2021)
a few dozen public datasets in one format, a common pretraining source
MASE per dataset


ETT / long-horizon (2021)
ETTh1/h2/m1/m2, Electricity, Traffic, Weather; horizons 96 to 720
MSE and MAE on z-normalised data


GIFT-Eval (2024)
23 datasets, 144,000 series, 177 million points, built to test foundation models
MASE and CRPS over seasonal naive, geometric mean


fev-bench (2025)
tasks from the AutoGluon team, many with covariates
win rate and skill score against a reference





import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import mase_scale, record, smape
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, fetch, load_m4_hourly, show

from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page OpenMP pools on 4 cores made the gradient-boosting pages 30x slower.

title: Benchmarks
text:
One dataset can make any method look good. A benchmark fixes many datasets, a split and a metric in advance, so that results from different papers compare. Each one also bakes in choices that decide what “best” means, and a leaderboard number is only meaningful once you know them.








Benchmark
What it is
Headline metric




M4 (2018)
100,000 series, yearly to hourly, fixed horizons
sMAPE and MASE, combined as OWA (overall weighted average) against a naive method


Monash (2021)
a few dozen public datasets in one format, a common pretraining source
MASE per dataset


ETT / long-horizon (2021)
ETTh1/h2/m1/m2, Electricity, Traffic, Weather; horizons 96 to 720
MSE and MAE on z-normalised data


GIFT-Eval (2024)
23 datasets, 144,000 series, 177 million points, built to test foundation models
MASE and CRPS over seasonal naive, geometric mean


fev-bench (2025)
tasks from the AutoGluon team, many with covariates
win rate and skill score against a reference





import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import mase_scale, record, smape
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, fetch, load_m4_hourly, show

from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page OpenMP pools on 4 cores made the gradient-boosting pages 30x slower.
_ = threadpool_limits(1)

title: Benchmarks
text:
1. How to read a leaderboard
Five questions decide whether a leaderboard number means what it seems to:

Normalised to what? GIFT-Eval divides each model’s error by seasonal naive’s error on the same series, then takes the geometric mean, so 0.7 means 30% less error than seasonal naive on a typical series. A raw average would let one large series dominate.
Zero-shot or trained? A foundation model scored zero-shot has never seen the test series. A model trained per dataset has. Leaderboards mark the two separately; compare like with like.
Was the test data in the pretraining corpus? Many foundation models pretrain on public archives that overlap the benchmark. GIFT-Eval marks entries with possible test leakage; fev-bench replaces a leaky model’s scores on the overlapping datasets. An unflagged result from an overlapping corpus is the same bug as leak 4, at the scale of a whole corpus.
Point or probabilistic? CRPS rewards a good spread of outcomes; MASE only the median. A model can top one ranking and sit mid-table on the other.
When was it read? Leaderboards change monthly. A ranking quoted without a date is not evidence. In September 2026, one paper counted 129 entries on GIFT-Eval.

title: Benchmarks
text:
2. ETTh1: the long-horizon protocol
ETT (Electricity Transformer Temperature, from the Informer paper, 2021) records a power transformer in China every hour for two years. OT, the oil temperature, is the target. The long-horizon literature fixes the protocol:

Split: the first 12 months train, the next 4 validate, the next 4 test.
Scale: z-normalise with the training mean and standard deviation; report errors on that scale.
Windows: every possible test window, one step apart. Each test input may reach back into the validation period.
Horizons: 96, 192, 336 and 720 steps. This page uses 96 with a 336-step lookback.

The data comes from the fev benchmark’s public copy on Hugging Face (0.5 MB).


ETT_URL = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/autogluon/fev_datasets/resolve/main/ETT/1H/train-00000-of-00001.parquet"
ett = pd.read_parquet(fetch(ETT_URL, "ett_1h.parquet"))
row = ett.set_index("id").loc["ETTh1"]
ot = pd.Series(np.asarray(row["OT"], dtype=float), index=pd.DatetimeIndex(row["timestamp"]), name="OT")
print(f"ETTh1 OT: {len(ot):,} hours from {ot.index[0]:%Y-%m-%d} to {ot.index[-1]:%Y-%m-%d}")

ETTh1 OT: 17,420 hours from 2016-07-01 to 2018-06-26



H, L = 96, 336
n_train, n_val, n_test = 12 * 30 * 24, 4 * 30 * 24, 4 * 30 * 24
mu, sd = ot.iloc[:n_train].mean(), ot.iloc[:n_train].std()
z = ((ot - mu) / sd).to_numpy()


def windows(start, stop):
    "Input/target pairs whose targets start in [start, stop - H]."
    idx = np.arange(start, stop - H + 1)
    X = np.stack([z[i - L:i] for i in idx])
    Y = np.stack([z[i:i + H] for i in idx])
    return X, Y


X_tr, Y_tr = windows(L, n_train)
X_te, Y_te = windows(n_train + n_val, n_train + n_val + n_test)
print(f"{len(X_tr):,} training windows, {len(X_te):,} test windows")

8,209 training windows, 2,785 test windows


Three forecasters, from nothing to a single linear layer:

Seasonal naive (24 h): repeat the last day four times.
Last value: hold the last observation flat for 96 hours.
Linear: one ridge regression from the 336 inputs to the 96 outputs. This is DLinear (2023) without its trend split, the model that showed many published transformers did not beat a linear map on this benchmark.



forecasts = {
    "Seasonal naive (24 h)": np.tile(X_te[:, -24:], H // 24),
    "Last value": np.repeat(X_te[:, -1:], H, axis=1),
    "Linear (ridge, 336 to 96)": Ridge(alpha=10.0).fit(X_tr, Y_tr).predict(X_te),
}
ett_scores = pd.DataFrame({name: {"MSE": np.mean((Y_te - f) ** 2), "MAE": np.mean(np.abs(Y_te - f))}
                           for name, f in forecasts.items()}).T
ett_scores.round(3)

show(bar_chart(ett_scores.index, {"MSE": ett_scores.MSE, "MAE": ett_scores.MAE}, height="320px"))




        




Two things to take from the numbers. First, holding the last value flat is as good as copying the last day (slightly better here): oil temperature drifts slowly, and its daily cycle is weak compared with the drift over four days. Second, one linear layer cuts the error of both baselines by about a fifth. Any model claimed to be state of the art on ETTh1 has to beat that layer, and papers from 2021 and 2022 often reported transformers that did not.

title: Benchmarks
text:
3. M4 Hourly: the competition protocol
M4 scores each of the 414 hourly series on its fixed 48-hour test horizon, then averages across series:

sMAPE in percent (the M4 definition multiplies by 100);
MASE with a 24-hour season, scaled by each series’ own training history.

Averaging scale-free errors across series is what makes 414 series of very different sizes comparable.


m4_train, m4_test = load_m4_hourly()
rows = []
for uid, g in m4_train.groupby("unique_id", sort=False):
    hist = g.y.to_numpy()
    actual = m4_test.loc[m4_test.unique_id == uid, "y"].to_numpy()
    yhat = np.resize(hist[-24:], 48)
    scale = np.mean(np.abs(hist[24:] - hist[:-24]))
    rows.append({"unique_id": uid, "smape": 100 * smape(actual, yhat), "mase": np.mean(np.abs(actual - yhat)) / scale})
m4_scores = pd.DataFrame(rows)
m4_snaive = {"mase": m4_scores.mase.mean(), "smape": m4_scores.smape.mean(), "skill": 0.0}
record("Seasonal naive (24 h)", "baseline", m4_snaive, notebook="02_Evaluation/02_Benchmarks", dataset="m4_hourly")
pd.Series(m4_snaive).round(3)

mase      1.193
smape    13.912
skill     0.000
dtype: float64


The average hides a wide spread. Most series sit between MASE 0.5 and 1.8, but a few reach 6, where yesterday says almost nothing about tomorrow. A method can win on the mean by doing well on those few, which is why M4 also reported ranks and why GIFT-Eval uses a geometric mean.

m4_scores.mase.describe(percentiles=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9]).round(3)

title: Benchmarks
text:
What this unlocks
The M4 Hourly seasonal naive row is now on the scoreboard as the reference for the global models. The household protocol from Backtesting is this site’s own benchmark: one series, scored the same way on every page.

title: Baselines
text:
A baseline answers one question: how much of this problem is solved before any modelling? On many real series a well-chosen baseline is hard to beat, and a complex model that loses to it is worse than useless, because it looks sophisticated. The M competitions repeatedly found simple methods near the top.
Every baseline here is a few lines of numpy and runs on the same backtest as every other model.







Baseline
Forecast for each of the next 24 hours




Naive
the last observed hour


Mean
the mean of the last four weeks


Drift
the last value, plus the average change per hour over the last four weeks


Seasonal naive (24 h)
the same hour yesterday (already on the scoreboard as the reference)


Seasonal naive (168 h)
the same hour on the same weekday last week


Seasonal window mean / median
the mean or median of the same hour over the last four weeks





import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, record, score, seasonal_naive
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, line_chart, load_household, show


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
NB = "03_Classical/01_Baselines"
FOUR_WEEKS = 24 * 28


def naive(history, horizon):
    return np.repeat(history.iloc[-1], horizon)


def mean(history, horizon):
    return np.repeat(history.iloc[-FOUR_WEEKS:].mean(), horizon)


def drift(history, horizon):
    x = history.iloc[-FOUR_WEEKS:].to_numpy()
    slope = (x[-1] - x[0]) / (len(x) - 1)
    return x[-1] + slope * np.arange(1, horizon + 1)


def seasonal_window(stat, weeks=4):
    "The `stat` (mean or median) of the same hour of the week over the last `weeks` weeks."
    def f(history, horizon):
        x = history.to_numpy()
        past = np.stack([x[len(x) - 168 * k:len(x) - 168 * k + horizon] for k in range(1, weeks + 1)])
        return stat(past, axis=0)
    return f

Results


baselines = {
    "Naive": naive,
    "Mean (4 weeks)": mean,

show(bar_chart(order.index, {"skill vs seasonal naive (24 h)": order.skill}, horizontal=True, height="380px"))




        




What the ranking says:

Naive, mean and drift lose to seasonal naive. They ignore the daily cycle, which is most of the predictable signal. Drift is the worst: a straight line through a series that goes up and down every day.
Last week loses to yesterday. The autocorrelation is slightly higher at lag 168 than at lag 24 over the whole four years, yet on these test windows copying one week ago is worse. A week-old copy gets the weekday right but carries a level that is seven days stale, and in late summer and autumn the level moves. (Before gap-filled hours were excluded from scoring, last week appeared to win; see the backtest protocol.)
Averaging four weeks beats copying either. One week contains that week’s accidents: a late dinner, a guest, a load of washing. The average of four keeps the routine and dilutes the accidents. Mean and median are almost tied. The median has the better MASE, because it ignores a single unusual week entirely; the mean has the clearly better RMSE, because one large miss costs it less than it costs a median that sits on a spike. That is the rule from Forecast Metrics in action: the median minimises absolute error, the mean minimises squared error.

A four-week seasonal window is the strongest free forecast for this house. Every model on the later pages should be compared with about +4% skill, not 0%.

title: Baselines
text:
One window, four forecasts
The last test window shows the difference. Copying a single day reproduces that day’s peaks wherever they happened to fall; the four-week median draws the usual shape at the usual height.


w = bts["Naive"].window.max()
pick = ["Naive", "Seasonal naive (24 h)", "Seasonal naive (168 h)", "Seasonal window median (4 weeks)"]
last = bts[pick[0]][bts[pick[0]].window == w]
show(line_chart(last.ds.dt.strftime("%a %H:00"),
                {"actual": last.y} | {p: bts[p][bts[p].window == w].yhat for p in pick},
                y_name="kWh", height="340px", zoom=False))

title: Baselines
section: Why a median of past weeks is hard to beat
text:
Why a median of past weeks is hard to beat
The household’s consumption is a routine plus noise. The routine repeats every week; the noise does not. Any forecast that averages several aligned past weeks estimates the routine and throws away noise, and the remainder from the decomposition is more than half the series’ spread, so most of what is left cannot be forecast from the past alone. Better models win by adapting the routine faster (a warm week, a holiday) or by using other information (the calendar, the weather), not by finding a hidden pattern in the noise.

title: ARIMA
text:
ARIMA(p, d, q) combines three ideas:

AR(p), autoregression: the next value is a weighted sum of the last p values, plus noise.
I(d), integration: difference the series d times first, to remove a unit root (a random-walk component).
MA(q), moving average: the next value also depends on the last q forecast errors, so the model corrects itself after a surprise.

\[y_t = c + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \phi_i\, y_{t-i} + \sum_{j=1}^{q} \theta_j\, \varepsilon_{t-j} + \varepsilon_t\]
Seasonal ARIMA, written \((p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_m\), adds the same three terms at multiples of the season \(m\): a seasonal AR term at lag 24 says “this hour depends on the same hour yesterday”. The stationarity tests found no unit root, so \(d = 0\) and \(D = 0\) here; the seasonality is modelled by seasonal AR and MA terms rather than removed by differencing.


import itertools
import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf, pacf
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, future_index, origins, record, score
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, line_chart, load_household, show

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page BLAS pools would oversubscribe the 4 cores.
_ = threadpool_limits(1)
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", module="statsmodels")


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
NB = "03_Classical/03_ARIMA"
FIT = 24 * 21  # each forecast fits on the last 3 weeks
first_test = origins(y.index)[0]
dev = y.iloc[first_test - FIT:first_test]  # the 3 weeks before the first test origin, for identification

title: ARIMA
section: 1. Identification from the ACF and PACF
text:
1. Identification from the ACF and PACF
The classical (Box-Jenkins) recipe reads the order off two plots of the training data:

an AR(p) process has a PACF that cuts off after lag p and an ACF that decays;
an MA(q) process has an ACF that cuts off after lag q and a PACF that decays;
seasonal terms show the same patterns at lags 24, 48, …



lag = np.arange(0, 73)
show(line_chart(lag, {"ACF": acf(dev, nlags=72), "PACF": pacf(dev, nlags=72)}, y_name="correlation", height="320px", zoom=False))




        




The PACF has one large spike at lag 1 and a smaller one at lag 23, the hour just before the same hour yesterday; everything else is small. The ACF decays and rises again towards 24 and 48. That suggests one or two short AR terms plus a seasonal term at 24. Real series rarely match the textbook patterns cleanly, so the plots narrow the search rather than settle it: something like \((1\text{-}2, 0, 0\text{-}1)(0\text{-}1, 0, 0\text{-}1)_{24}\).

title: ARIMA
text:
2. Choosing the order by AIC
Automatic ARIMA (Hyndman and Khandakar’s auto.arima, and its Python ports) searches orders and keeps the one with the lowest AIC (Akaike information criterion): the fit’s log-likelihood, penalised by the number of parameters. Here a small grid over the candidates above, fitted on the same three weeks:


aic, orders = {}, {}
for p, q, P, Q in itertools.product((1, 2), (0, 1), (0, 1), (0, 1)):
    if P == Q == 0:
        continue
    name = f"({p},0,{q})({P},0,{Q})24"
    orders[name] = ((p, 0, q), (P, 0, Q, 24))
    aic[name] = SARIMAX(dev.to_numpy(), order=orders[name][0], seasonal_order=orders[name][1]).fit(disp=False).aic
aic = pd.Series(aic).sort_values()
chosen = aic.index[0]
print(f"lowest AIC: {chosen}")
aic.head(5).round(1)

lowest AIC: (2,0,1)(1,0,1)24


(2,0,1)(1,0,1)24    751.4
(1,0,0)(1,0,1)24    759.7
(1,0,1)(1,0,1)24    760.0
(2,0,0)(1,0,1)24    761.0

title: ARIMA
text:
3. Checking the residuals: Ljung-Box
If the model has captured the structure, its residuals should look like white noise: no autocorrelation left. The Ljung-Box test asks whether the first k residual autocorrelations are jointly zero. A small p-value means structure remains.


order, seasonal = orders[chosen]
fit = SARIMAX(dev.to_numpy(), order=order, seasonal_order=seasonal).fit(disp=False)
lb = acorr_ljungbox(fit.resid[24:], lags=[1, 24, 48, 168])
lb.round(3)








lb_stat
lb_pvalue

24

The residuals pass at every lag tested: no autocorrelation is left that the test can detect. Two cautions before reading that as “the model is good”:

White residuals are not small residuals. They mean the model has used all the linear structure in these three weeks. The decomposition already showed that most of an hour’s variation is unpredictable appliance use; Ljung-Box cannot tell you how large that part is.
Three weeks hold only three weekly cycles, so the test has almost no power at lag 168. A weekly pattern can be there and still pass. A seasonal ARIMA handles one season well; a second, much longer one (168 lags) makes the state space large and the fit slow. Section 5 adds it another way.

title: ARIMA
text:
4. The backtest
The chosen order is refitted on the last three weeks at every origin, then forecasts 24 hours.


def sarima(history, horizon):
    res = SARIMAX(history.iloc[-FIT:].to_numpy(), order=order, seasonal_order=seasonal).fit(disp=False)
    return res.forecast(horizon)


bt = backtest(y, sarima)
arima_score = score(bt, y, exclude=FILLED)
record(f"SARIMA {chosen}", "classical", arima_score, notebook=NB, notes="order by AIC on the 3 weeks before the test; refit on 3 weeks per window")
print(f"SARIMA {chosen}: MASE {arima_score['mase']:.3f}, skill {arima_score['skill']:+.1%}, {arima_score['seconds']:.0f} s for 30 fits")

SARIMA (2,0,1)(1,0,1)24: MASE 0.670, skill +17.2%, 20 s for 30 fits

title: ARIMA
section: 5. A second season with Fourier terms
text:
5. A second season with Fourier terms
Dynamic harmonic regression keeps the seasonal ARIMA for the daily cycle and adds the weekly cycle as regressors: sine and cosine pairs at the 168-hour period. Four pairs give a smooth weekly shape with 8 parameters instead of 168. The Fourier terms are known for any future hour, so they are legitimate inputs to a forecast.


T0 = y.index[0]


def fourier(index, period=168, pairs=4):
    t = (index - T0) / pd.Timedelta("1h")
    return np.column_stack([f(2 * np.pi * k * t / period) for k in range(1, pairs + 1) for f in (np.sin, np.cos)])


def dhr(history, horizon):
    x = history.iloc[-FIT:]
    res = SARIMAX(x.to_numpy(), exog=fourier(x.index), order=order, seasonal_order=seasonal).fit(disp=False)
    return res.forecast(horizon, exog=fourier(future_index(history, horizon)))


dev_fit = SARIMAX(dev.to_numpy(), exog=fourier(dev.index), order=order, seasonal_order=seasonal).fit(disp=False)
lb_dhr = acorr_ljungbox(dev_fit.resid[24:], lags=[24, 168])
print("Ljung-Box p-values with weekly Fourier terms:", lb_dhr.lb_pvalue.round(4).to_dict())
bt_dhr = backtest(y, dhr)
dhr_score = score(bt_dhr, y, exclude=FILLED)
record(f"SARIMA {chosen} + weekly Fourier", "classical", dhr_score, notebook=NB, notes="4 Fourier pairs at 168 h as regressors")
print(f"with weekly Fourier terms: MASE {dhr_score['mase']:.3f}, skill {dhr_score['skill']:+.1%}")

Ljung-Box p-values with weekly Fourier terms: {24: 0.893, 168: 0.7869}
with weekly Fourier terms: MASE 0.695, skill +14.0%


The weekly terms make the forecast slightly worse. Three weeks of history give each of the eight Fourier coefficients only three weekly cycles to learn from, so they mostly fit that period’s accidents, and the extra variance costs more than the weekly signal gains. A longer fit window would give the Fourier terms more to learn from and make every fit slower. On this series the seasonal AR term at lag 24 plus two short-term AR terms already capture most of what a day-ahead forecast can use, which matches the autocorrelation finding that lag 24 and lag 168 carry similar information.


w = bt.window.max()
a_, b_ = bt[bt.window == w], bt_dhr[bt_dhr.window == w]
show(line_chart(a_.ds.dt.strftime("%a %H:00"), {"actual": a_.y, "SARIMA": a_.yhat, "SARIMA + weekly Fourier": b_.yhat},
                y_name="kWh", height="320px", zoom=False))

title: State Space Models and the Kalman Filter
text:
A state space model separates what you want to know from what you can measure:
The state equation says how the hidden state evolves:
\[x_t = F\,x_{t-1} + w_t, \quad w_t \sim N(0, Q)\]
The observation equation says what the meter reads:
\[y_t = H\,x_t + v_t, \quad v_t \sim N(0, R)\]
For this house, the hidden state could be the household’s underlying consumption level and its daily and weekly profile; the observation is that plus the appliance noise of each hour. ETS and ARIMA are both special cases with particular choices of \(F\), \(H\), \(Q\) and \(R\), which is how statsmodels fits them.
The Kalman filter (Kalman, 1960) tracks the state through two steps per observation:

Predict: push the state estimate and its uncertainty through \(F\). Uncertainty grows by \(Q\).
Update: compare the prediction with the new observation and move the estimate by the Kalman gain \(K\) times the error. \(K\) is large when the state is uncertain and the meter is precise, small when the meter is noisy.

This is the same filter that fuses wheel odometry and IMU readings in a robot (the EKF in ROS 2’s robot_localization is its nonlinear extension). Here the “sensor” is the meter and the “pose” is the household’s consumption level.

title: State Space Models and the Kalman Filter
section: 1. A Kalman filter in twelve lines
text:
1. A Kalman filter in twelve lines
The simplest state space model is the local level: the state is one number, a level that wanders as a random walk, observed with noise.
\[\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + w_t \qquad y_t = \ell_t + v_t\]
So \(F = H = 1\), and the filter is scalar arithmetic. Run on the daily totals with a level noise \(Q\) and a measurement noise \(R\):


def kalman_local_level(obs, Q, R, level0=None, P0=1e6):
    "Scalar Kalman filter for a local level model; returns filtered levels and gains."
    level = obs[0] if level0 is None else level0
    P = P0
    levels, gains = [], []
    for z in obs:
        P = P + Q                   # predict: the level may have moved, so uncertainty grows
        K = P / (P + R)             # gain: trust the observation in proportion to our uncertainty
        level = level + K * (z - level)  # update: move towards the observation
        P = (1 - K) * P             # the observation reduced the uncertainty
        levels.append(level)
        gains.append(K)
    return np.array(levels), np.array(gains)


x = daily.to_numpy()
R = np.var(np.diff(x)) / 2      # a rough split of the day-to-day variance into noise...
Q = R / 50                      # ...and a level that moves slowly relative to it
levels, gains = kalman_local_level(x, Q, R)
show(line_chart(daily.index.date, {"daily kWh": x, "Kalman level": levels}, y_name="kWh", height="340px"))
crumbs: State Space Models and the Kalman Filter

title: State Space Models and the Kalman Filter
section: 2. Exponential smoothing is a Kalman filter
text:
2. Exponential smoothing is a Kalman filter
Watch the gain. It starts near 1 (the first observations are all the filter has) and settles to a constant within a few weeks. Once it is constant, the update step reads
\[\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + K\,(y_t - \ell_{t-1})\]
\[\ell_t = K\,y_t + (1-K)\,\ell_{t-1},\]
which is simple exponential smoothing with \(\alpha = K\). The steady-state gain has a closed form in the noise ratio \(q = Q/R\):
\[K_\infty = \frac{-q + \sqrt{q^2 + 4q}}{2}\]
So the smoothing parameter of SES is not an arbitrary knob: it encodes a belief about how much the level moves compared with how noisy the readings are. Fitting \(\alpha\) is estimating that ratio.


q = Q / R
k_inf = (-q + np.sqrt(q * q + 4 * q)) / 2
ses_level, ses_levels = levels[59], []
for z in x[60:]:                    # simple exponential smoothing, started from the filter's day-59 level
    ses_level = k_inf * z + (1 - k_inf) * ses_level
    ses_levels.append(ses_level)
gap = np.max(np.abs(np.array(ses_levels) - levels[60:]))
print(f"steady-state gain from the formula: {k_inf:.5f}; from the filter after 60 days: {gains[60]:.5f}")
print(f"largest difference between SES (alpha = K) and the Kalman level after day 60: {gap:.2e} kWh")

steady-state gain from the formula: 0.13177; from the filter after 60 days: 0.13177
largest difference between SES (alpha = K) and the Kalman level after day 60: 5.68e-08 kWh


The two agree to rounding error. Every exponential smoothing method is the steady state of a Kalman filter for some state space model; Holt-Winters is the filter for a level, a trend and a seasonal state. The Kalman form adds three things the plain recursion lacks: a likelihood (so the noise ratio can be estimated), prediction intervals, and a principled way to handle missing observations: skip the update step and let the uncertainty grow.
crumbs: State Space Models and the Kalman Filter

title: State Space Models and the Kalman Filter
text:
3. Missing data for free
A gap is just several predict steps without an update. The filter’s uncertainty widens across the gap and the estimate carries on; no imputation is needed. On the real 121-hour gap in the raw data, a structural model with a daily season, fitted around the gap:


raw = load_household(clean=False)["kwh"]
gaps = raw.isna()
run = (gaps != gaps.shift()).cumsum()
longest = gaps.groupby(run).sum().idxmax()
gap_idx = raw.index[(run == longest) & gaps]
around = raw[gap_idx[0] - pd.Timedelta("7D"):gap_idx[-1] + pd.Timedelta("2D")]
uc_gap = UnobservedComponents(around.to_numpy(), level="local level",
                              freq_seasonal=[{"period": 24, "harmonics": 4}]).fit(disp=False)
smoothed = uc_gap.smoothed_state[0] + uc_gap.smoothed_state[1]
show(line_chart(around.index.strftime("%d %b %H:00"), {"observed": around.to_numpy(), "Kalman smoother": smoothed},
                y_name="kWh", height="320px"))
print(f"gap of {len(gap_idx)} hours from {gap_idx[0]:%Y-%m-%d %H:00}, filled by the smoother without any imputation step")

gap of 121 hours from 2010-08-17 21:00, filled by the smoother without any imputation step


The smoother (a backward pass after the forward filter) uses observations on both sides of the gap, so it reconnects the level smoothly and keeps the daily cycle running through it. That is the model-based gap filling the Data Preparation page set aside.
crumbs: State Space Models and the Kalman Filter

title: State Space Models and the Kalman Filter
section: 4. A structural model on the backtest
text:
4. A structural model on the backtest
statsmodels’ UnobservedComponents builds the state space model from named parts, the “structural” approach of Harvey (1989):

a local level;
a daily season and a weekly season, each as a few Fourier harmonics (6 for the day, 3 for the week), which keeps the state small;
an AR(1) term for short-lived departures, such as an evening that runs high.

It is refitted by maximum likelihood on the last three weeks at each origin.


def structural(history, horizon):
    model = UnobservedComponents(history.iloc[-24 * 21:].to_numpy(), level="local level", autoregressive=1,
                                 freq_seasonal=[{"period": 24, "harmonics": 6}, {"period": 168, "harmonics": 3}])
    return model.fit(disp=False).forecast(horizon)


uc_score = score(backtest(y, structural), y, exclude=FILLED)
record("Structural model (level + daily + weekly + AR1)", "classical", uc_score, notebook=NB)
print(f"structural model: MASE {uc_score['mase']:.3f}, skill {uc_score['skill']:+.1%}")

structural model: MASE 0.733, skill +9.4%


The structural model beats seasonal naive and the default ETS fit, and stays below SARIMA. Its seasons are smooth (a few harmonics), which loses the sharp edges of the morning and evening peaks that SARIMA’s lag-24 term copies directly. Its strengths are elsewhere: every component is interpretable, it handles gaps natively, and it gives a likelihood for comparing designs.







Model family
State space view




Simple exponential smoothing
steady-state Kalman filter of a local level


Holt-Winters, ETS
level, trend and seasonal states, single error source


ARIMA
lagged values and errors as the state vector


Structural (this page)
named components, each with its own noise

title: GARCH: Forecasting the Variance
text:
Every model so far forecasts the expected value. Many decisions also need the uncertainty: how much reserve to hold, how wide a band to plan within. If the uncertainty itself changes, calm periods followed by turbulent ones, a constant-width interval is too wide in calm weeks and too narrow in turbulent ones.
ARCH (autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity; Engle, 1982) and its generalisation GARCH (Bollerslev, 1986) model the variance of tomorrow’s error as a function of recent errors and recent variance:
\[\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha\, \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta\, \sigma_{t-1}^2\]
A large surprise yesterday (\(\varepsilon_{t-1}^2\)) raises today’s variance; \(\beta\) makes the effect persist. \(\alpha + \beta\) close to 1 means volatility comes in long spells. GARCH is the standard tool in finance, where returns are calm for months and then turbulent; Engle shared the 2003 Nobel prize in economics for ARCH.

import pandas as pd

from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import het_arch

import warnings

title: GARCH: Forecasting the Variance
section: 1. The series: weekly changes in daily consumption
text:
1. The series: weekly changes in daily consumption
GARCH models the errors of a mean model, so the series should have no strong predictable level left. The change in daily consumption against the same weekday last week removes the weekly cycle and most of the annual level. What remains is the week-on-week surprise, in kWh.


daily = load_household("D")["kwh"]
r = (daily - daily.shift(7)).dropna()
lm_p = het_arch(r.to_numpy(), nlags=7)[1]
print(f"{len(r)} days; Engle's ARCH test (7 lags): p = {lm_p:.1e}")

1435 days; Engle's ARCH test (7 lags): p = 2.4e-65


Engle’s test regresses the squared series on its own lags. A tiny p-value means large changes cluster with large changes: the variance is predictable.

title: GARCH: Forecasting the Variance
text:
2. GARCH(1,1) with an AR(7) mean
The arch library fits the mean (an AR(7), to use the last week of changes) and the variance equation together by maximum likelihood.


fit = arch_model(r, mean="AR", lags=7, vol="GARCH", p=1, q=1).fit(disp="off")
a, b = fit.params["alpha[1]"], fit.params["beta[1]"]
print(f"alpha {a:.3f}, beta {b:.3f}, persistence alpha + beta = {a + b:.3f}")
vol = fit.conditional_volatility
by_month = vol.groupby(vol.index.month).mean()
show(bar_chart(["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"],
               {"mean conditional volatility (kWh)": by_month.to_numpy()}, height="300px"))

alpha 0.086, beta 0.862, persistence alpha + beta = 0.949





        




Persistence near 0.95 means a turbulent spell decays slowly, with a half-life of about two weeks. The monthly averages show where the turbulence lives: winter. Heating, lighting and more time indoors make winter days both larger and more variable, so a forecast for a January day should carry a wider band than one for August.


show(line_chart(r.index.date, {"weekly change (kWh)": r.to_numpy(), "+2 sigma": 2 * vol.to_numpy(), "-2 sigma": -2 * vol.to_numpy()},
                y_name="kWh", height="340px"))

title: GARCH: Forecasting the Variance
text:
3. Are the intervals better?
The test that matters: one-step-ahead 90% intervals over the last 300 days, from a GARCH model and from the same AR(7) mean with constant variance. Both are refitted every 30 days on the data before. A good interval covers about 90% of outcomes and is as narrow as possible.


Z90 = 1.645
test_idx = range(len(r) - 300, len(r))
hits = {"constant variance": [], "GARCH(1,1)": []}
width = {k: [] for k in hits}
for i in test_idx:
    if (i - test_idx[0]) % 30 == 0:
        params = {"GARCH(1,1)": arch_model(r.iloc[:i], mean="AR", lags=7, vol="GARCH", p=1, q=1).fit(disp="off").params,
                  "constant variance": arch_model(r.iloc[:i], mean="AR", lags=7, vol="Constant").fit(disp="off").params}
    for name, vol_kind in (("GARCH(1,1)", "GARCH"), ("constant variance", "Constant")):
        model = arch_model(r.iloc[:i + 1], mean="AR", lags=7, vol=vol_kind, **({"p": 1, "q": 1} if vol_kind == "GARCH" else {}))
        fc = model.fix(params[name]).forecast(horizon=1, start=i - 1, reindex=False)
        mu, sd = fc.mean.iloc[0, 0], np.sqrt(fc.variance.iloc[0, 0])
        hits[name].append(abs(r.iloc[i] - mu) <= Z90 * sd)
        width[name].append(2 * Z90 * sd)
cover = pd.DataFrame({"coverage of 90% interval": {k: np.mean(v) for k, v in hits.items()},
                      "mean width (kWh)": {k: np.mean(v) for k, v in width.items()}})
cover.style.format({"coverage of 90% interval": "{:.1%}", "mean width (kWh)": "{:.1f}"})






 
coverage of 90% interval
mean width (kWh)




constant variance
94.3%
25.8


GARCH(1,1)
91.3%
22.5





The constant-variance interval over-covers: it is wide enough for winter all year, so in summer it is far wider than it needs to be. GARCH’s intervals land closer to the nominal 90% and are narrower on average, because they tighten in calm spells and widen when turbulence starts. Same mean forecast, more useful band.
The Probabilistic Forecasting and Conformal Prediction pages take this further, with quantile models and conformal intervals that need no distributional assumption.

title: Forecasting as Regression
text:
Any regression model can forecast once the series is rewritten as rows. Each row is one moment in the past, playing the role of a forecast origin:

inputs: what was known at that moment (recent values, the calendar of the hours ahead);
target: what happened next.

Training on thousands of such rows teaches the model the mapping from “what I knew” to “what came next”. This reduction of forecasting to regression is what lets scikit-learn, LightGBM or a neural network forecast at all. Three choices define it:



Choice
Options
This page




Window
how far back the inputs reach
336 hours (two weeks)


Target
one step, one specific step, or all 24 at once
all 24 at once (one row per day)


Split
which rows train and which test
rows before the first origin train; the backtest tests



The split is where most mistakes happen. Rows overlap: the row for Tuesday’s forecast and the row for Wednesday’s share 312 of their 336 inputs. A random split puts near-copies of each test row in the training set, which is leak 1. Every row in training must end before every row in testing begins.

title: Forecasting as Regression
text:
1. Building the table
One row per midnight in the training data: the 336 hours before it, a one-hot encoding of the weekday being forecast, and the 24 hours that followed as a 24-column target.


def daily_rows(s: pd.Series):
    "Inputs (last WINDOW values + weekday one-hot) and 24-hour targets for every midnight with a full window."
    x = s.to_numpy()
    mids = [i for i in range(WINDOW, len(s) - H + 1) if s.index[i].hour == 0]
    X = np.stack([x[i - WINDOW:i] for i in mids])
    dow = np.eye(7)[[s.index[i].dayofweek for i in mids]]
    Y = np.stack([x[i:i + H] for i in mids])
    return np.column_stack([X, dow]), Y


X_train, Y_train = daily_rows(train)
print(f"{X_train.shape[0]} training rows, {X_train.shape[1]} inputs each, {Y_train.shape[1]} targets each")


def as_forecaster(model):
    def f(history, horizon):
        nxt = history.index[-1] + pd.Timedelta(hours=1)
        row = np.concatenate([history.to_numpy()[-WINDOW:], np.eye(7)[nxt.dayofweek]])
        return model.predict(row[None])[0][:horizon]
    return f

1280 training rows, 343 inputs each, 24 targets each

title: Forecasting as Regression
text:
2. A linear model: ridge regression
With all 24 hours as targets, one ridge regression is 24 linear autoregressions sharing their inputs: each output hour is a weighted sum of the last two weeks plus a weekday offset. The ridge penalty keeps 343 weights per output from fitting noise. This multi-output form is called MIMO (multiple input, multiple output).


ridge = Ridge(alpha=100.0).fit(X_train, Y_train)
ridge_score = score(backtest(y, as_forecaster(ridge)), y, exclude=FILLED)
_ = record("Ridge, 336 h window to 24 h (MIMO)", "machine learning", ridge_score, notebook=NB)
print(f"ridge: MASE {ridge_score['mase']:.3f}, skill {ridge_score['skill']:+.1%}")

ridge: MASE 0.701, skill +12.4%


It is tempting to read the weights as “what the model learned”. They resist that reading. For the 19:00 output, the largest weights sit at scattered lags, with alternating signs, not on the seasonal lags the autocorrelation highlights:


lag_to_target = np.arange(WINDOW, 0, -1) + 19  # input k hours before midnight is k + 19 hours before 19:00
w19 = pd.Series(ridge.coef_[19][:WINDOW], index=lag_to_target)
top = w19.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).head(6)
print("largest weights for the 19:00 output, by lag in hours:", {int(lag): round(float(w19[lag]), 3) for lag in top.index})

largest weights for the 19:00 output, by lag in hours: {348: -0.121, 212: -0.117, 38: -0.106, 158: 0.106, 326: 0.104, 349: 0.092}



show(line_chart(lag_to_target, {"weight on the input at this lag": w19.to_numpy()}, y_name="weight", height="300px"))




        




The inputs are strongly correlated with their neighbours (hour t looks like hour t-1), so many different weight patterns give nearly the same forecast, and ridge picks one that spreads weight in positive and negative pairs. The forecast is reliable; the individual coefficients are not. Interpreting a model of correlated lags needs tools built for it, such as permutation importance on grouped features, which the production section returns to.

title: Forecasting as Regression
section: 3. A tree model on the same table
text:
3. A tree model on the same table
Gradient boosting cannot output 24 numbers at once, so MultiOutputRegressor trains one model per output hour. Same rows, same split, nonlinear model:


gbm = MultiOutputRegressor(HistGradientBoostingRegressor(max_iter=150, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=0)).fit(X_train, Y_train)
gbm_score = score(backtest(y, as_forecaster(gbm)), y, exclude=FILLED)
_ = record("Gradient boosting, 336 h window to 24 h (one model per hour)", "machine learning", gbm_score, notebook=NB)
print(f"gradient boosting on the raw window: MASE {gbm_score['mase']:.3f}, skill {gbm_score['skill']:+.1%}")

gradient boosting on the raw window: MASE 0.655, skill +18.1%


Gradient boosting on the same raw table beats ridge by a wide margin, and edges past both the engineered-feature model from Feature Engineering and SARIMA: it is the best model on the scoreboard so far. Two differences explain it. It trains one model per output hour, so each hour gets its own mapping (the direct strategy, compared properly on the next page). And trees can act on the recent level nonlinearly (“if yesterday evening ran high, raise tonight”), where ridge can only add up weighted past values.
The cost is 24 models instead of one, and about 40 seconds of training on one core instead of under one second.

title: Global vs Local Models
text:
Approach
Trained on
Typical models




Local
one series at a time, one parameter set each
ARIMA, ETS, a small LightGBM per series


Global
all series pooled, one shared parameter set
one LightGBM or neural network for everything



Classical statistics is local by habit: each series gets its own model. The M4 (2018) and M5 (2020) competitions changed practice. The M5 winners were global LightGBM models, and M4’s winner was a hybrid with global parameters. A global model sees far more examples of “what a daily cycle looks like” or “what happens after a spike” than any single series can show it, which is the same reason a foundation model trained on many datasets can forecast a series it has never seen.
Pooling only works if the series look alike to the model. M4 Hourly mixes series whose levels differ by orders of magnitude, so each one must first be put on a common scale. That is the job of the target transforms.
This page uses Nixtla’s mlforecast, which builds the lag features, applies the transforms per series, trains one model, and forecasts recursively. The Nixtla MLForecast walkthrough covers its API.


import time

import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from mlforecast import MLForecast
from mlforecast.lag_transforms import RollingMean, SeasonalRollingMean
from mlforecast.target_transforms import Differences, LocalStandardScaler
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import record, smape
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, load_m4_hourly, show

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page OpenMP pools would oversubscribe the 4 cores.
_ = threadpool_limits(1)


train, test = load_m4_hourly()
NB = "04_Machine_Learning/03_Global_vs_Local"
LAGS = list(range(1, 25)) + [48, 72, 96, 120, 144, 168]
LAG_TRANSFORMS = {24: [SeasonalRollingMean(season_length=24, window_size=7)], 1: [RollingMean(window_size=24)]}
H = 48


def m4_scores(fc: pd.DataFrame, col: str) -> dict:
    "The M4 protocol: per-series sMAPE (percent) and MASE (24 h season), averaged over the 414 series."
    rows = []
    for uid, g in train.groupby("unique_id", sort=False):
        hist = g.y.to_numpy()
        actual = test.loc[test.unique_id == uid, "y"].to_numpy()
        pred = fc.loc[fc.unique_id == uid, col].to_numpy()
        rows.append((100 * smape(actual, pred), np.mean(np.abs(actual - pred)) / np.mean(np.abs(hist[24:] - hist[:-24]))))
    r = np.array(rows)
    return {"mase": float(r[:, 1].mean()), "smape": float(r[:, 0].mean())}

title: Global vs Local Models
text:
1. Global: one model for 414 series
30 lags (the last day hour by hour, then each day back to a week), two rolling means, and two per-series transforms applied before training and undone after forecasting:

Differences([24]): subtract the same hour yesterday, so the model learns day-on-day changes, which look alike across series far more than levels do.
LocalStandardScaler: divide each series by its own standard deviation, so a 10 MW series and a 10 kW series contribute equally.



def global_model(transforms, name):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    mf = MLForecast(models={"lgbm": lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=500, learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=127, min_child_samples=50,
                                                       verbose=-1, n_jobs=1, random_state=0)},
                    freq=1, lags=LAGS, lag_transforms=LAG_TRANSFORMS, target_transforms=transforms)
    mf.fit(train, static_features=[])
    sc = m4_scores(mf.predict(H), "lgbm") | {"seconds": time.perf_counter() - t}
    print(f"{name}: MASE {sc['mase']:.3f}, sMAPE {sc['smape']:.2f}, {sc['seconds']:.0f} s")
    return sc


glob = global_model([Differences([24]), LocalStandardScaler()], "global, differenced and scaled")

global, differenced and scaled: MASE 0.887, sMAPE 11.68, 14 s

title: Global vs Local Models
text:
2. Local: one model per series
The same features, transforms and model family, but 414 separate fits. Each local model sees 700 or 960 hours; the global model saw all of them at once. The local trees are smaller (15 leaves instead of 127), because a large tree fitted to one short series memorises it.


t = time.perf_counter()
local_fc = []
for uid, g in train.groupby("unique_id", sort=False):

                                                       verbose=-1, n_jobs=1, random_state=0)},
                    freq=1, lags=LAGS, lag_transforms=LAG_TRANSFORMS, target_transforms=[Differences([24]), LocalStandardScaler()])
    mf.fit(g, static_features=[])
    local_fc.append(mf.predict(H))
loc = m4_scores(pd.concat(local_fc), "lgbm") | {"seconds": time.perf_counter() - t}
print(f"local, one model per series: MASE {loc['mase']:.3f}, sMAPE {loc['smape']:.2f}, {loc['seconds']:.0f} s")

local, one model per series: MASE 0.933, sMAPE 12.09, 60 s

3. What the transforms are worth
The same global model, trained on raw levels, and on scaled but undifferenced series:

glob_scaled = global_model([LocalStandardScaler()], "global, scaled only")

global, scaled only: MASE 1.303, sMAPE 10.96, 12 s



res = pd.DataFrame({"global, differenced + scaled": glob, "local, differenced + scaled": loc,
                    "global, scaled only": glob_scaled, "global, raw levels": glob_raw}).T

Three results, in order of importance:

The transforms matter more than the model. On raw levels the global model’s MASE is about four times worse: the loss is dominated by the few largest series, and the small ones are fitted badly. A model is only global in a useful sense once the series are on a common scale.
With the same features, global beats local on both metrics, and trains four times faster (one model instead of 414). Against seasonal naive (MASE 1.193, sMAPE 13.91) it removes about a quarter of the scaled error.
The metric picks the transform. Scaling without differencing gives the best sMAPE of all four and a poor MASE. MASE divides by each series’ day-on-day change, so it rewards a model trained on day-on-day changes; sMAPE is a percentage of the level, so it rewards getting levels right. Decide the metric before tuning anything, as the Forecast Metrics page argued.

The household scoreboard has one series, so global models enter it only indirectly: the deep learning and foundation model sections test models that were trained on many series.

title: RNN, LSTM and DeepAR
text:
A recurrent neural network (RNN) keeps a hidden state \(h_t\) and updates it with each new value: \(h_t = f(h_{t-1}, y_t)\). After reading the lookback window, the state summarises it, and a decoder turns the state into the forecast. Plain RNNs forget quickly, because the gradient through many steps shrinks or explodes. The LSTM (long short-term memory; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) adds gates that decide what to keep, forget and output, which lets it carry information across hundreds of steps.
DeepAR (Salinas et al., Amazon, 2020) made recurrent forecasting practical at scale. Three ideas:

it is global: one LSTM trained on many related series;
it is probabilistic: the network outputs the parameters of a distribution for each step (here a Student’s t), not one number, and is trained by maximising the likelihood;
it is autoregressive: at forecast time it samples a value, feeds it back as the next input and continues, so a forecast is a set of sampled paths.

Both models here come from Nixtla’s neuralforecast (the NeuralForecast walkthrough covers the library). They see only the series, a one-week lookback, and train once on everything before the first test origin.
This page trains on the GPU, so it does not run in CI: it carries skip_exec and stores its outputs.


import gc
import logging
import time
import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
from neuralforecast import NeuralForecast
from neuralforecast.losses.pytorch import DistributionLoss, MAE
from neuralforecast.models import LSTM, DeepAR

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, origins, record, score
from ML_Timeseries.data import line_chart, load_household, show, to_long

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
for name in ("pytorch_lightning", "lightning", "lightning.pytorch", "lightning_fabric"):
    logging.getLogger(name).setLevel(logging.ERROR)


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
NB = "05_Deep_Learning/02_RNN_LSTM_DeepAR"
INPUT, H = 168, 24
train = to_long(y.iloc[:origins(y.index)[0]])
TRAINER = dict(random_seed=0, enable_progress_bar=False, enable_model_summary=False, logger=False,
               accelerator="gpu" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu", devices=1)


def fit_and_score(model, col):
    "Train once before the first origin, then forecast every window from its own history."
    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    nf = NeuralForecast(models=[model], freq="h")
    nf.fit(train)
    fit_s = time.perf_counter() - t0

    def f(history, horizon):
        out = nf.predict(df=to_long(history.iloc[-(INPUT + 48):]))
        return out[col if col in out else col.split("-")[0]].to_numpy()[:horizon]

    bt = backtest(y, f)
    sc = score(bt, y, exclude=FILLED) | {"seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0, "fit seconds": fit_s,
                                          "peak VRAM GB": torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9}
    del nf
    gc.collect()
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    return sc, bt
