text:
1. LSTM
A two-layer LSTM encoder reads the week; an MLP decoder maps the final state to all 24 hours at once. Trained on mean absolute error, like the scores.


lstm_score, lstm_bt = fit_and_score(

title: RNN, LSTM and DeepAR
text:
2. DeepAR
DeepAR outputs a Student’s t distribution per hour. The point forecast scored here is the median of its sampled paths, the value that minimises absolute error.


deepar_score, deepar_bt = fit_and_score(
    DeepAR(h=H, input_size=INPUT, lstm_n_layers=2, lstm_hidden_size=128, trajectory_samples=200,
           loss=DistributionLoss(distribution="StudentT", level=[80, 90]), valid_loss=MAE(),
           max_steps=1000, scaler_type="robust", **TRAINER), "DeepAR-median")
_ = record("DeepAR (neuralforecast, median)", "deep learning", {k: deepar_score[k] for k in ("mase", "skill", "mae", "rmse", "wape", "smape", "seconds")}, notebook=NB)
print(f"DeepAR: skill {deepar_score['skill']:+.1%}, fit {deepar_score['fit seconds']:.0f} s, peak VRAM {deepar_score['peak VRAM GB']:.2f} GB")

DeepAR: skill +20.3%, fit 74 s, peak VRAM 3.23 GB



w = lstm_bt.window.max()
a_, b_ = lstm_bt[lstm_bt.window == w], deepar_bt[deepar_bt.window == w]
show(line_chart(a_.ds.dt.strftime("%a %H:00"), {"actual": a_.y, "LSTM": a_.yhat, "DeepAR (median)": b_.yhat},
                y_name="kWh", height="320px", zoom=False))




        




Both recurrent models do well here: each beats SARIMA and every gradient-boosting model on the scoreboard. DeepAR edges the LSTM slightly, at six times the training time and eight times the GPU memory, because sampling 200 paths per window is expensive. Its real product is the distribution; the median alone is only a by-product. The Probabilistic Forecasting page shows how to score a distribution (pinball loss, CRPS, coverage).
So why did the field move on from recurrence? Not because it forecasts badly on a task like this. An RNN reads its window one step at a time, so training cannot run in parallel along the time axis, and very long lookbacks are slow and unstable to train. On a 168-step window and a 24-step horizon that cost is small. On the long-horizon benchmarks with lookbacks of 512 steps and horizons of 720, models that look at the whole window at once (the MLPs and transformers on the next two pages) train faster and forecast better.

title: Transformers for Time Series: PatchTST, iTransformer and TFT
text:
A transformer lets every input token attend to every other, so a long-range dependency (this hour and the same hour last week) is one step away instead of 168. The first time-series transformers (Informer, Autoformer, FEDformer, 2021 and 2022) treated each time step as a token. A single hourly reading carries almost no meaning on its own, so attention between individual readings learned little, and the DLinear paper showed a linear layer matching them.
The models since then fix the tokenisation:








Model
Token
Idea




PatchTST (Nie et al., 2023)
a patch of consecutive steps (here 16 hours)
like words instead of letters: a patch has a shape worth attending to. Each series is handled independently (“channel independence”)


iTransformer (Liu et al., 2024)
a whole variable’s history
attention runs across variables, not across time; useful when many related series move together


TFT (Lim et al., Google, 2021)
time steps, with gating and variable selection
built for many covariates: static, past-only and known-future inputs, with interpretable attention weights



Same protocol as the previous pages (univariate, one-week lookback, trained once before the first origin), so iTransformer sees a single variable, which removes its main advantage; it is included to show that. GPU page, so skip_exec with stored outputs.

Both pay for it: TFT trains for over two minutes and peaks above 4 GB of GPU memory, against seconds and megabytes for DLinear. iTransformer, given a single series, has one token to attend to, so its attention does nothing and it behaves like an MLP; on many related series it would be a different model.
The DLinear test. On this task the linear model’s MASE is about 7% above the best transformer’s, so the gap is wider than the 2023 paper’s headline would suggest. Three reasons, all about the setting rather than the models: the horizon is short (24 steps, where DLinear’s paper used 96 to 720), so there is less long-range structure for a linear map to exploit; the series is noisy and spiky, which rewards nonlinear models that can react to the shape of the last evening; and no model here sees the calendar, so the nonlinear models must infer the weekday from the window itself. Across the whole deep learning section, the most accurate model is still the small calendar-aware MLP ensemble from the data pipeline page. Inputs and training setup moved the score more than the choice of architecture did.

title: Chronos-2 Zero-Shot
text:
Every model on this site so far was trained on this house. A foundation model is trained once, on a very large and varied corpus of time series, and then forecasts a new series from its context alone: zero-shot. It has learned what daily cycles, weekly cycles, trends, spikes and level shifts generally look like, and recognises them in a context it has never seen.
Chronos-2 (Amazon, October 2025) is an encoder-only transformer with about 120 million parameters. It reads the context in patches, forecasts quantiles for every horizon step at once, and adds group attention: several related series (or a target and its covariates) attend to each other, so it can use past-only covariates, known-future covariates and related series in the same forward pass. In spring 2026 it ranked first on GIFT-Eval; the comparison page has the current standings.
It runs through Amazon’s chronos-forecasting package, because no general-purpose library loads it. That package is installed in the root environment only, and imported only on these GPU pages, which carry skip_exec and stored outputs (an exception recorded in the repo’s coding conventions). The weights are Apache-2.0.


import gc
import logging
import time
import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
from chronos import Chronos2Pipeline

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, future_index, record, score
from ML_Timeseries.data import line_chart, load_household, show

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
logging.disable(logging.WARNING)


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
NB = "06_Foundation_Models/01_Chronos2_Zero_Shot"
CTX = 2048  # hours of context given to the model: about 12 weeks
pipe = Chronos2Pipeline.from_pretrained("amazon/chronos-2", device_map="cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
print(f"Chronos-2: {sum(p.numel() for p in pipe.model.parameters()) / 1e6:.0f} M parameters")


def median(out):
    "Chronos-2 returns (quantiles, mean); quantiles[i] is [variates, horizon, levels]."
    return out[0][0][0, :, 0].cpu().numpy()


def run(name, f):
    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    bt = backtest(y, f)
    sc = score(bt, y, exclude=FILLED) | {"seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0, "peak VRAM GB": torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9}
    print(f"{name}: skill {sc['skill']:+.1%}, MASE {sc['mase']:.3f}, {sc['seconds']:.1f} s for 30 forecasts")
    return sc, bt

title: Chronos-2 Zero-Shot
text:
1. Univariate, zero-shot
The model gets the last 2,048 hours and nothing else: no training, no tuning, no features.


def univariate(history, horizon):
    x = torch.tensor(history.to_numpy(dtype=np.float32)[-CTX:])
    return median(pipe.predict_quantiles([x], prediction_length=horizon, quantile_levels=[0.5]))


uni_score, uni_bt = run("Chronos-2, univariate", univariate)
_ = record("Chronos-2, zero-shot", "foundation model", {k: uni_score[k] for k in ("mase", "skill", "mae", "rmse", "wape", "smape", "seconds")},
           notebook=NB, notes="no training; 2,048 h context")

Chronos-2, univariate: skill +21.7%, MASE 0.645, 0.9 s for 30 forecasts

title: Chronos-2 Zero-Shot
Chronos-2 Zero-Shot
section: 3. With the sub-meters as past covariates
text:
3. With the sub-meters as past covariates
The three sub-meters are known up to the origin but not after it, so they go in as past-only covariates. Group attention lets the model look across the four series.


SUBS = ["sub1_kwh", "sub2_kwh", "sub3_kwh"]


def with_submeters(history, horizon):
    x = history.iloc[-CTX:]
    past = {c: hh[c].loc[x.index].to_numpy(np.float32) for c in SUBS} | calendar(x.index)
    item = {"target": x.to_numpy(np.float32), "past_covariates": past, "future_covariates": calendar(future_index(history, horizon))}
    return median(pipe.predict_quantiles([item], prediction_length=horizon, quantile_levels=[0.5]))


sub_score, _ = run("Chronos-2, + calendar + sub-meters", with_submeters)

Chronos-2, + calendar + sub-meters: skill +21.7%, MASE 0.639, 1.4 s for 30 forecasts



w = uni_bt.window.max()
last = uni_bt[uni_bt.window == w]
show(line_chart(last.ds.dt.strftime("%a %H:00"), {"actual": last.y, "Chronos-2 (zero-shot)": last.yhat},
                y_name="kWh", height="320px", zoom=False))




        




With no training at all, Chronos-2 beats SARIMA, every gradient-boosting model and every library deep learning model on the scoreboard. Only the two hand-built networks from the deep learning section, trained on this house, do better. Thirty forecasts take about a second on the GPU.
Neither kind of covariate helps. The calendar adds nothing because the model already reads the daily and weekly rhythm from twelve weeks of context, the same reason sub-meter lags added nothing to gradient boosting: the information is already in the target’s own history. Covariates pay when they carry something the target cannot, such as a weather forecast for a heating load or a price signal.
The practical meaning: for a new meter with a few months of data and no time to build a model, a zero-shot forecast from a foundation model is a strong default on day one.

title: Fine-Tuning Chronos-2
text:
A zero-shot forecast uses only what the model learned from its pretraining corpus. Fine-tuning continues training on the target data, so the model can adapt to this house’s particular routine. Two forms:

full fine-tuning updates every weight (here 119 million);
LoRA (low-rank adaptation) freezes the weights and trains small low-rank corrections added to some layers; far fewer parameters and less memory, usually a little less gain.

The risk is the usual one: a model fitted to a few years of one house can forget the general patterns that made it good. A small learning rate and few steps limit that. The setting is fixed in advance (300 steps at a learning rate of 1e-5, batch 32) and not tuned on the test windows; the fine-tuning data is everything before the first test origin, exactly what every other model on the scoreboard trained on.
GPU page, so skip_exec with stored outputs. Checkpoints go to a temporary folder and are deleted afterwards.


import gc
import logging
import tempfile
import time
import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
from chronos import Chronos2Pipeline

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, origins, record, score
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, line_chart, load_household, show

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
logging.disable(logging.WARNING)


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
NB = "06_Foundation_Models/03_Fine_Tuning"
CTX, H = 2048, 24
train = y.iloc[:origins(y.index)[0]].to_numpy(np.float32)
base = Chronos2Pipeline.from_pretrained("amazon/chronos-2", device_map="cuda")


def forecaster(pipe):
    def f(history, horizon):
        x = torch.tensor(history.to_numpy(dtype=np.float32)[-CTX:])
        return pipe.predict_quantiles([x], prediction_length=horizon, quantile_levels=[0.5])[0][0][0, :, 0].cpu().numpy()
    return f


def fine_tune(steps, lr=1e-5, mode="full"):
    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        tuned = base.fit([train], prediction_length=H, num_steps=steps, learning_rate=lr, batch_size=32,
                         context_length=CTX, finetune_mode=mode, output_dir=d)
    return tuned, time.perf_counter() - t0, torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9

        return pipe.predict_quantiles([x], prediction_length=horizon, quantile_levels=[0.5])[0][0][0, :, 0].cpu().numpy()

def fine_tune(steps, lr=1e-5, mode="full"):
    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        tuned = base.fit([train], prediction_length=H, num_steps=steps, learning_rate=lr, batch_size=32,
                         context_length=CTX, finetune_mode=mode, output_dir=d)
    return tuned, time.perf_counter() - t0, torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9

title: Probabilistic Forecasting
text:
A point forecast says “1.2 kWh at 19:00”. A decision usually needs more: how high could it plausibly go (to size a battery, or to warn before a peak), how low (to schedule a flexible load). A probabilistic forecast answers with a distribution, most often summarised by quantiles: the 90% quantile is the value the outcome stays below 90% of the time. Two quantiles make an interval: the 5% and 95% quantiles bound a 90% prediction interval.
Three questions judge such a forecast:

Calibration: does the 90% interval contain the outcome about 90% of the time? Too often means too wide; too rarely means overconfident.
Sharpness: among calibrated forecasts, narrower is better. An interval from 0 to 10 kWh always covers and says nothing.
A single score that rewards both: the pinball loss and CRPS.

title: Probabilistic Forecasting
text:
1. The pinball loss and CRPS
The pinball loss of a quantile forecast \(q_\tau\) at level \(\tau\) is
\[L_\tau(y, q) = \begin{cases} \tau\,(y - q) & y \ge q \\ (1 - \tau)\,(q - y) & y < q \end{cases}\]
For the 90% quantile, an outcome above it costs 0.9 per unit of miss; one below costs only 0.1. Minimising it in expectation gives exactly the true 90% quantile, which is why quantile regression trains on it. At \(\tau = 0.5\) it is half the absolute error.
The CRPS (continuous ranked probability score) is the pinball loss integrated over every level from 0 to 1, times two. It reduces to the absolute error for a point forecast, so it compares probabilistic and point forecasts on the same scale. With a finite set of quantiles, the average pinball loss over those levels approximates it; GIFT-Eval’s CRPS is computed this way.

title: Probabilistic Forecasting
text:
2. Two ways to get quantiles

Empirical seasonal quantiles: take the same hour of the week over the last k weeks and read off their quantiles. The probabilistic version of the seasonal window baseline.
Quantile regression: train one LightGBM model per level on the pinball loss, with the shared features. Each model learns its quantile as a function of the hour, the weekday and the recent level.



import lightgbm as lgb
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import future_index
from ML_Timeseries.data import line_chart, load_household, show
from ML_Timeseries.features import make_features

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page OpenMP pools would oversubscribe the 4 cores.
_ = threadpool_limits(1)


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
train = y.iloc[:origins(y.index)[0]]


def empirical(weeks):
    def f(history, horizon):
        x = history.to_numpy()
        past = np.stack([x[len(x) - 168 * k:len(x) - 168 * k + horizon] for k in range(1, weeks + 1)])
        return np.quantile(past, LEVELS, axis=0).T
    return f


X_train = make_features(train).iloc[700:]
quantile_models = {l: lgb.LGBMRegressor(objective="quantile", alpha=l, n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05,
                                        num_leaves=31, verbose=-1, n_jobs=1, random_state=0).fit(X_train, train.iloc[700:])
                   for l in LEVELS}


def quantile_gbm(history, horizon):
    ext = pd.concat([history.iloc[-800:], pd.Series(np.nan, index=future_index(history, horizon))])
    X = make_features(ext).iloc[-horizon:]
    return np.column_stack([quantile_models[l].predict(X) for l in LEVELS])


methods = {"empirical, 4 weeks": empirical(4), "empirical, 8 weeks": empirical(8), "quantile LightGBM": quantile_gbm}
qbs = {name: quantile_backtest(y, f, exclude=FILLED) for name, f in methods.items()}
prob = pd.DataFrame({name: summarise(qb) for name, qb in qbs.items()}).T
prob.style.format({"crps": "{:.3f}", "median MAE": "{:.3f}", "cover 90%": "{:.1%}", "width 90%": "{:.2f}",

Four weeks of history cannot make a 90% interval. The 5% and 95% quantiles of four values sit between the smallest and largest of them, so the “90%” band covers only about half the outcomes. Eight weeks helps but is still far off. An empirical quantile needs many samples per tail; this is the same small-sample problem that makes the 4-week median a fine point forecast and a poor interval.
Quantile regression comes close: its 90% interval covers 86% and its 80% interval 76%, a little narrow in both cases, with the best CRPS by a wide margin. It is slightly overconfident because each quantile model learned the spread of the training years, and the test months turn out a little more variable. The Conformal Prediction page corrects exactly that.
The CRPS ranks the three methods the same way as the median MAE, and it also rewards the quantile model’s calibration: two forecasts with similar medians can differ a lot in CRPS when one of them has honest tails.

title: Anomaly Detection
text:
For a meter, the anomalies worth finding are usually faults, not unusual behaviour. The Data Preparation page showed that this house’s extreme hours are real appliance use; flagging them would only teach an operator to ignore the alarms. Three fault types matter in practice:








Fault
What the data shows
Injected




Spike
one hour 3 kWh too high (a bad reading, a double count)
8


Dropout
six hours of exactly zero (meter or link down, filled with zeros)
8


Stuck meter
twelve hours repeating the last good value
8



To measure detection, 24 such faults are injected at random positions into the test months (June to November 2010), with a fixed random seed. An event counts as found if any of its hours is flagged. The cost side is the number of flags on clean hours per week.


import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, line_chart, load_household, show

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page OpenMP pools would oversubscribe the 4 cores.
_ = threadpool_limits(1)


hh = load_household()
y = hh["kwh"]
hist = y[:"2010-05-31"]                 # detectors learn from here
test = y["2010-06-01":"2010-11-25"].copy()
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
starts = sorted(rng.choice(np.arange(200, len(test) - 200), 24, replace=False))
kinds = ["spike"] * 8 + ["dropout"] * 8 + ["stuck"] * 8
rng.shuffle(kinds)
x, events = test.copy(), []
for s, kind in zip(starts, kinds):
    if kind == "spike":
        span = [s]
        x.iloc[s] += 3.0
    elif kind == "dropout":
        span = list(range(s, s + 6))
        x.iloc[span] = 0.0
    else:
        span = list(range(s, s + 12))
        x.iloc[span] = x.iloc[s - 1]
    events.append((kind, x.index[span]))
injected = pd.Series(False, index=x.index)
for _, idx in events:
    injected[idx] = True
print(f"{len(events)} faults injected over {len(x) / 168:.0f} weeks; {injected.sum()} faulty hours")


def evaluate(flags: pd.Series) -> dict:
    flags = flags.reindex(x.index).fillna(False).astype(bool)
    found = {k: [] for k in ("spike", "dropout", "stuck")}
    for kind, idx in events:
        found[kind].append(bool(flags[idx].any()))
    return {"recall": np.mean(sum(found.values(), [])), **{f"{k} recall": np.mean(v) for k, v in found.items()},
            "false flags per week": (flags & ~injected).sum() / (len(x) / 168)}

24 faults injected over 25 weeks; 152 faulty hours

title: Anomaly Detection
section: 1. Four detectors that know nothing about faults
text:
1. Four detectors that know nothing about faults

Robust z-score: distance from the median of the same hour of the week, in units of its median absolute deviation, flagged above 5.
Forecast residual: the seasonal window median as the expected value; flag when the actual differs by more than the 99.5% quantile of historical week-on-week changes.
Isolation forest (Liu et al., 2008): an ensemble of random trees that isolates points with few splits; anomalies are easy to isolate. Fitted on rolling six-hour window features of the history, contamination 1%.
Spike score: how far an hour rises above both its neighbours, flagged above the 99.9% quantile of the history’s own spike scores.



how = lambda idx: idx.dayofweek * 24 + idx.hour
med = hist.groupby(how(hist.index)).median()
mad = (hist - med.reindex(how(hist.index)).to_numpy()).abs().groupby(how(hist.index)).median() * 1.4826
z = (x - med.reindex(how(x.index)).to_numpy()) / mad.reindex(how(x.index)).to_numpy()

full = pd.concat([hist, x])
expected = pd.Series([np.median([full.iloc[i - 168 * k] for k in range(1, 5)]) for i in range(len(hist), len(full))], index=x.index)
resid_thr = np.quantile((hist - hist.shift(168)).abs().dropna(), 0.995)


def window_features(s, reference):
    r = s.rolling(6, center=True, min_periods=1)
    return pd.DataFrame({"value": s, "mean": r.mean(), "std": r.std(), "min": r.min(), "max": r.max(),
                         "zeros": (s == 0).rolling(6, center=True, min_periods=1).sum(),
                         "repeats": (s.diff() == 0).rolling(6, center=True, min_periods=1).sum(),
                         "vs expected": s - reference}).fillna(0)


iso = IsolationForest(n_estimators=200, contamination=0.01, random_state=0)
iso.fit(window_features(hist.iloc[-8000:], hist.shift(168).iloc[-8000:]))
iso_flags = pd.Series(iso.predict(window_features(x, expected)) == -1, index=x.index)

spike = x - np.maximum(x.shift(1), x.shift(-1))
spike_thr = np.quantile((hist - np.maximum(hist.shift(1), hist.shift(-1))).dropna(), 0.999)

detectors = {"robust z-score > 5": z.abs() > 5, "forecast residual": (x - expected).abs() > resid_thr,
             "isolation forest": iso_flags, "spike score": spike > spike_thr}
results = {name: evaluate(f) for name, f in detectors.items()}

The rules catch every dropout and every stuck meter with no false alarms at all, and together with the spike score they find 23 of the 24 faults at about one false flag every ten weeks. The one miss is a spike at 19:00 on 2 October, just before an hour that was itself 3.9 kWh, so it barely rose above its neighbours.
This is the general shape of operational anomaly detection. Generic detectors (scores, residuals, isolation forests) find what is rare; faults are often not rare in value, only impossible in structure. Write down what each fault looks like, encode it as a rule, and keep the generic detectors for what is left. They earn their place on faults nobody anticipated, which is also why their false flags need a human to look at them.
The same structural thinking applies to the Phisaver brief’s anomaly goal: a dead sub-meter, a reversed CT clamp (negative readings) or a sudden constant offset are each one rule, and each would beat a model.

title: The Matrix Profile: Motifs and Discords
text:
The matrix profile (Yeh, Keogh and colleagues, 2016) takes every subsequence of length m in a series and records the distance to its nearest neighbour, the most similar subsequence anywhere else (excluding overlaps with itself). From that one array:

the smallest values are motifs: shapes that recur almost exactly, such as the household’s standard weekday;
the largest values are discords: windows with no close match anywhere, the most unusual stretches of the year.

It has no parameters beyond m, needs no training, and the STUMPY library computes it exactly for a year of hourly data in seconds. The distance is usually computed on z-normalised windows (each window rescaled to mean 0, standard deviation 1), so it compares shapes regardless of level; the raw distance compares values.
Here m = 24: every day-long window of one year of hourly data, about 8,700 of them.


import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import stumpy

from ML_Timeseries.data import line_chart, load_household, show


hh = load_household()["2009-11-01":"2010-10-31"]
year, filled = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"].to_numpy()
M = 24


def top_windows(profile, k, largest=True):
    "Indices of the k most extreme windows, at least one window length apart."
    order = np.argsort(-profile if largest else profile)
    picks = []
    for i in order:
        if all(abs(i - j) >= M for j in picks):
            picks.append(i)
        if len(picks) == k:
            break
    return picks


mp = stumpy.stump(year.to_numpy(), m=M)
profile = mp[:, 0].astype(float)
print(f"{len(profile):,} windows; nearest-neighbour distance from {profile.min():.2f} to {profile.max():.2f}")

title: The Matrix Profile: Motifs and Discords
text:
The matrix profile (Yeh, Keogh and colleagues, 2016) takes every subsequence of length m in a series and records the distance to its nearest neighbour, the most similar subsequence anywhere else (excluding overlaps with itself). From that one array:

the smallest values are motifs: shapes that recur almost exactly, such as the household’s standard weekday;
the largest values are discords: windows with no close match anywhere, the most unusual stretches of the year.

It has no parameters beyond m, needs no training, and the STUMPY library computes it exactly for a year of hourly data in seconds. The distance is usually computed on z-normalised windows (each window rescaled to mean 0, standard deviation 1), so it compares shapes regardless of level; the raw distance compares values.
Here m = 24: every day-long window of one year of hourly data, about 8,700 of them.


import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import stumpy

from ML_Timeseries.data import line_chart, load_household, show


hh = load_household()["2009-11-01":"2010-10-31"]
year, filled = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"].to_numpy()
M = 24


def top_windows(profile, k, largest=True):
    "Indices of the k most extreme windows, at least one window length apart."
    order = np.argsort(-profile if largest else profile)
    picks = []
    for i in order:
        if all(abs(i - j) >= M for j in picks):
            picks.append(i)
        if len(picks) == k:
            break
    return picks


mp = stumpy.stump(year.to_numpy(), m=M)
profile = mp[:, 0].astype(float)
print(f"{len(profile):,} windows; nearest-neighbour distance from {profile.min():.2f} to {profile.max():.2f}")

8,737 windows; nearest-neighbour distance from 0.00 to 4.14

title: The Matrix Profile: Motifs and Discords
section: 1. The motif: the shape this house repeats
text:
1. The motif: the shape this house repeats
The window with the closest match anywhere in the year, plotted with that match:


i = top_windows(profile, 1, largest=False)[0]
j = int(mp[i, 1])
print(f"motif: {year.index[i]:%a %d %b %H:00} and its match {year.index[j]:%a %d %b %H:00}, distance {profile[i]:.2f}")
hours = [f"+{h} h" for h in range(M)]
show(line_chart(hours, {f"{year.index[i]:%a %d %b %H:00}": year.iloc[i:i + M], f"{year.index[j]:%a %d %b %H:00}": year.iloc[j:j + M]},
                y_name="kWh", height="300px", zoom=False))

motif: Thu 19 Aug 11:00 and its match Thu 12 Aug 11:00, distance 0.00





        




A distance of zero means an exact copy, and households do not repeat themselves to the watt-hour. This one is not the household at all: the Datasets loader filled the 121-hour gap from 17 to 22 August 2010 by copying the same hours a week earlier, and the matrix profile found the copy. That is a useful property in its own right: an exact or near-exact motif in meter data is a strong hint of duplicated, imputed or replayed readings.
Excluding every window that touches a filled hour gives the household’s real most-repeated shape:


touches_filled = np.array([filled[k:k + M].any() for k in range(len(profile))])
clean = profile.copy()
clean[touches_filled | touches_filled[mp[:, 1].astype(int)]] = np.inf
i2 = top_windows(clean, 1, largest=False)[0]
j2 = int(mp[i2, 1])
print(f"best motif among recorded hours: {year.index[i2]:%a %d %b %H:00} and {year.index[j2]:%a %d %b %H:00}, distance {profile[i2]:.2f}")
show(line_chart(hours, {f"{year.index[i2]:%a %d %b %H:00}": year.iloc[i2:i2 + M], f"{year.index[j2]:%a %d %b %H:00}": year.iloc[j2:j2 + M]},

title: The Matrix Profile: Motifs and Discords
text:
3. Shape versus size
Would the matrix profile catch a heater left on? Add 2.5 kWh to every hour from 10:00 to 18:00 on three ordinary days (20 kWh extra each, nearly doubling those days), recompute, and see where those days rank among all 8,700 windows, with z-normalised and with raw distances:


heater = year.copy()
days = [pd.Timestamp(d) for d in ("2010-01-13", "2010-04-21", "2010-08-04")]
for d in days:
    heater[d + pd.Timedelta(hours=10):d + pd.Timedelta(hours=17)] += 2.5
ranks = {}
for label, norm in (("z-normalised (shape)", True), ("raw (value)", False)):
    p = stumpy.stump(heater.to_numpy(), m=M, normalize=norm)[:, 0].astype(float)
    ranks[label] = [int((p > p[heater.index.get_loc(d + pd.Timedelta(hours=10)) - 4:heater.index.get_loc(d + pd.Timedelta(hours=10)) + 4].max()).sum()) + 1
                    for d in days]
rank_table = pd.DataFrame(ranks, index=[d.strftime("%d %b %Y") for d in days])
rank_table.index.name = "heater day"
rank_table

Shape and size are different questions. A heater left on all day nearly doubles a day’s energy, yet with z-normalised distances those days are unremarkable: adding a constant block to the middle of a day leaves its shape close to many real days. With raw distances they rise to the top 1 to 3% of all windows, but still not into the top five, because this house has dozens of genuinely unusual days (four of the five discords above are summer evenings and nights unlike any other).
So the matrix profile is the right tool for “is this shape new?”: a new appliance with its own cycle, a changed routine, a meter replaying old data. For “is this too much energy?”, a forecast with an interval (the probabilistic pages) or a plain rule answers more directly. And the discords are a good list to show a person: each one is an unusual day worth a look, which is exactly what an exploratory tool should produce.

title: Hierarchical Reconciliation
text:
Many series come in hierarchies: a house and its circuits, a region and its substations, a company and its stores. Forecast every node separately and the forecasts will not add up: the forecast for the house will differ from the sum of the forecasts for its circuits. A planner then has to choose which number to believe.
Reconciliation makes the forecasts coherent: every parent equals the sum of its children. The modern view (Hyndman et al., 2011; Wickramasuriya, Athanasopoulos and Hyndman, 2019) writes every method the same way. Stack the base forecasts of all nodes in a vector \(\hat y\), and let the summing matrix \(S\) map the bottom-level series to all nodes. A reconciliation method is a matrix \(P\) that maps the base forecasts to bottom-level forecasts; the coherent forecasts are then
\[\tilde y = S\,P\,\hat y\]

Bottom-up: \(P\) keeps the bottom-level forecasts. Uses only the leaves.
Top-down: \(P\) splits the total by historical proportions. Uses only the total.
OLS: \(P = (S^\top S)^{-1} S^\top\). Uses all levels with equal weight.
WLS: \(P = (S^\top W^{-1} S)^{-1} S^\top W^{-1}\), with \(W\) the diagonal of the base forecasts’ error variances. Weights each level by its accuracy.
MinT: the same formula with \(W\) the full error covariance (shrunk), so it also uses how the levels’ errors move together.

MinT (“minimum trace”) minimises the total variance of the coherent forecast errors, and it is optimal when \(W\) is known.
Here the hierarchy is this house: the total and its four parts (kitchen, laundry, water heater and AC, everything else). Nixtla’s hierarchicalforecast library implements all of these; at five nodes, the matrix algebra is shorter written out.


import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import origins
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, load_household, show


hh = load_household()
FILLED = hh["filled"].to_numpy()
O = origins(hh.index)
NODES = ["kwh", "sub1_kwh", "sub2_kwh", "sub3_kwh", "other_kwh"]
LABELS = ["total", "kitchen", "laundry", "heater + AC", "other"]
S = np.vstack([np.ones(4), np.eye(4)])  # total = sum of the four leaves; each leaf is itself
values = {c: hh[c].to_numpy() for c in NODES}
print("summing matrix S (rows: total, kitchen, laundry, heater + AC, other):")
print(S.astype(int))


def base_forecasts(o):
    "Seasonal window median (same hour, last 4 weeks) for every node: a 5 x 24 array."
    return np.stack([np.median(np.stack([values[c][o - 168 * k:o - 168 * k + 24] for k in range(1, 5)]), axis=0) for c in NODES])


def actuals(o):
    return np.stack([values[c][o:o + 24] for c in NODES])

title: Hierarchical Reconciliation
section: 1. The base forecasts do not add up
text:
1. The base forecasts do not add up
Every node gets the same simple base forecast, the seasonal window median. The median of a sum is not the sum of the medians, so the forecasts disagree:


gaps = [np.abs(base_forecasts(o)[0] - base_forecasts(o)[1:].sum(axis=0)).max() for o in O]
print(f"largest gap between the total forecast and the sum of its parts: {max(gaps):.2f} kWh in one hour")

largest gap between the total forecast and the sum of its parts: 0.91 kWh in one hour

title: Hierarchical Reconciliation
text:
2. Reconciling
The error covariance \(W\) comes from the base forecasts’ errors on the 60 days before the first test origin. A full 5 x 5 covariance estimated from data is noisy, so MinT uses the standard shrinkage towards its diagonal (half and half here).


history = [O[0] - 24 * k for k in range(1, 61)]
residuals = np.concatenate([actuals(o) - base_forecasts(o) for o in history], axis=1)
W = np.cov(residuals)
W_shrunk = 0.5 * np.diag(np.diag(W)) + 0.5 * W
proportions = np.array([hh[c].iloc[:O[0]].sum() for c in NODES[1:]])
proportions = proportions / proportions.sum()


def P_matrix(method):
    if method == "bottom-up":
        return np.hstack([np.zeros((4, 1)), np.eye(4)])
    if method == "top-down":
        return np.hstack([proportions[:, None], np.zeros((4, 4))])
    Winv = np.linalg.inv({"OLS": np.eye(5), "WLS": np.diag(np.diag(W)), "MinT (shrink)": W_shrunk}[method])
    return np.linalg.inv(S.T @ Winv @ S) @ S.T @ Winv


METHODS = ["base (incoherent)", "bottom-up", "top-down", "OLS", "WLS", "MinT (shrink)"]
rows, incoherence = {}, {}
for m in METHODS:
    errs, worst = [], 0.0
    for o in O:
        Yhat = base_forecasts(o)
        R = Yhat if m.startswith("base") else S @ P_matrix(m) @ Yhat
        keep = ~FILLED[o:o + 24]
        errs.append(np.abs(R - actuals(o))[:, keep])
        worst = max(worst, np.abs(R[0] - R[1:].sum(axis=0)).max())
    E = np.concatenate(errs, axis=1)
    rows[m] = dict(zip(LABELS, E.mean(axis=1)))
    incoherence[m] = worst
mae = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
mae["max incoherence (kWh)"] = pd.Series(incoherence)
mae.style.format("{:.4f}")

Every reconciled forecast is coherent to rounding error, so the planner’s dilemma is gone. Which method to use depends on which level matters:

Bottom-up is best for the total, about 4% better than forecasting the total directly, and by construction it leaves the circuits unchanged. The sum of the circuits’ medians is simply a better point forecast of the total than the total’s own median; for skewed, spiky parts the two differ, and on these windows the sum of the parts is closer.
WLS and MinT improve the total by about 3% but make the sparse circuits slightly worse: they move every node towards a compromise, and the kitchen’s near-zero forecasts are pulled up by the total. MinT adds nothing over WLS here; with five nodes and 60 days, the off-diagonal covariances are mostly noise and the shrinkage discards them.
Top-down is worst for the circuits: one fixed share per circuit cannot know that the kitchen peaks at dinner and the water heater at night.
OLS ignores that the circuits’ errors differ in size, and is worse than WLS on four of the five nodes.

The textbook result (MinT is optimal) assumes mean forecasts and well-estimated covariances. These are median forecasts of spiky series with a short calibration history, so the simplest coherent method wins on the level that usually matters. With hundreds of nodes, such as a utility’s substations and feeders, the covariance carries real information and MinT’s advantage returns.

title: Drift and Retraining
text:
Every model on this site so far trained once, before the first test origin, and then forecast five months without learning anything new. A deployed model faces two decisions:

Retraining schedule: how often to refit, and on how much history (everything so far, or a sliding window of recent data).
Drift monitoring: how to notice that the data has changed enough to matter, before the error does.

The model is LightGBM with the shared features, the same at every refit.


import time

import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, future_index, origins, score
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, line_chart, load_household, show
from ML_Timeseries.features import make_features

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page OpenMP pools would oversubscribe the 4 cores.
_ = threadpool_limits(1)


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
O = origins(y.index)
X = make_features(y)
PARAMS = dict(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=31, verbose=-1, n_jobs=1, random_state=0)

Every model on this site so far trained once, before the first test origin, and then forecast five months without learning anything new. A deployed model faces two decisions:

Retraining schedule: how often to refit, and on how much history (everything so far, or a sliding window of recent data).
Drift monitoring: how to notice that the data has changed enough to matter, before the error does.

The model is LightGBM with the shared features, the same at every refit.


import time

import lightgbm as lgb
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from threadpoolctl import threadpool_limits

from ML_Timeseries.backtest import backtest, future_index, origins, score
from ML_Timeseries.data import bar_chart, line_chart, load_household, show
from ML_Timeseries.features import make_features

# nbdev-test runs pages in parallel; per-page OpenMP pools would oversubscribe the 4 cores.
_ = threadpool_limits(1)


hh = load_household()
y, FILLED = hh["kwh"], hh["filled"]
O = origins(y.index)
X = make_features(y)
PARAMS = dict(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, num_leaves=31, verbose=-1, n_jobs=1, random_state=0)

title: Drift and Retraining
text:
1. Retraining schedules
Five schedules. At each refit the model sees only data before the current origin.


def schedule(every_days, window_days=None):
    models = {}

    def f(history, horizon):
        o = len(history)
        key = (o - O[0]) // (24 * every_days) if every_days else 0
        if key not in models:
            end = o if every_days else O[0]
            start = max(700, end - window_days * 24) if window_days else 700
            models[key] = lgb.LGBMRegressor(**PARAMS).fit(X.iloc[start:end], y.iloc[start:end])
        ext = pd.concat([history.iloc[-800:], pd.Series(np.nan, index=future_index(history, horizon))])
        return models[key].predict(make_features(ext).iloc[-horizon:])
    return f


SCHEDULES = {"train once": (0, None), "every 30 days, all history": (30, None), "every 5 days, all history": (5, None),
             "every 5 days, last 365 days": (5, 365), "every 5 days, last 90 days": (5, 90)}
rows = {}
for name, (every, window) in SCHEDULES.items():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    sc = score(backtest(y, schedule(every, window)), y, exclude=FILLED)
    rows[name] = {"skill": sc["skill"], "MASE": sc["mase"], "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0}
sched = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
show(bar_chart(sched.index, {"skill vs seasonal naive": sched.skill}, horizontal=True, height="300px"))

Refitting helps, a little. Going from one model to a refit every five days adds about one point of skill, for twenty times the training compute. Monthly refits capture half of that gain at a fifth of the cost.
Forgetting hurts, a lot. Training only on the last 365 days costs three points; the last 90 days costs six. Recent data is not more relevant here, it is less complete: the annual cycle needs more than a year of history to be learned at all, and a model fitted on summer has never seen a winter evening. “Retrain on recent data” is common advice for drifting series; for a strongly seasonal one it is the wrong default. Keep all history and refit on a fixed schedule, unless monitoring shows the old data has become misleading.

title: Drift and Retraining
text:
2. Measuring drift: PSI
The population stability index (PSI) compares two distributions binned by the reference’s deciles:
\[\text{PSI} = \sum_{i} (p_i - q_i)\,\ln\frac{p_i}{q_i}\]
where \(q_i\) and \(p_i\) are the shares of the reference and the new data in bin i. A common rule of thumb from credit scoring: below 0.1 is stable, 0.1 to 0.25 is a moderate shift, above 0.25 is a large one.
The question that matters for a seasonal series is compared with what? Each test month is compared twice: with the whole previous year, and with the same month a year earlier.


def psi(reference, new, bins=10):
    edges = np.quantile(reference, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1))
    edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    q = np.clip(np.histogram(reference, edges)[0] / len(reference), 1e-4, None)
    p = np.clip(np.histogram(new, edges)[0] / len(new), 1e-4, None)
    return float(np.sum((p - q) * np.log(p / q)))


previous_year = y["2009-06-01":"2010-05-31"].to_numpy()
months = pd.period_range("2010-06", "2010-11", freq="M")
drift = pd.DataFrame({
    "PSI vs previous 12 months": [psi(previous_year, y[str(m)].to_numpy()) for m in months],
    "PSI vs same month last year": [psi(y[str(m - 12)].to_numpy(), y[str(m)].to_numpy()) for m in months],
}, index=[m.strftime("%b %Y") for m in months])
show(bar_chart(drift.index, {c: drift[c] for c in drift}, y_name="PSI", height="320px"))

Against the previous twelve months, August 2010 looks like a severe shift (PSI 0.89). Against August 2009 it is moderate (0.16). Most of the “drift” is the calendar: August is a holiday month in France, and this household’s August always looks unlike its year. A drift monitor that compares with the last twelve months would page someone every summer for something entirely expected.
July 2010 is different: it is far from the previous year and from July 2009 (0.32). That is a genuine change in behaviour, and it matches the matrix profile, where three of the five most unusual windows of the year fell in July 2010.
Practical rules that follow:

Compare like with like: same season, same weekday mix, or residuals of a seasonal model, never raw values against an all-year baseline.
Monitor the error, not only the inputs. Input drift that does not raise the forecast error needs no action; the backtest machinery run on each new week is the most direct monitor there is.
Tie retraining to the schedule, and drift to an investigation. A refit cannot fix a broken meter or a new tenant; a person looking at the data can.

# Search for the best theta parameter, by trying 50 different values

text:
Covariates: using external data
past_covariates are series not necessarily known ahead of the forecast time. Those can for instance represent things that have to be measured and are not known upfront. Models do not use the future values of past_covariates when making forecasts.
future_covariates are series which are known in advance, up to the forecast horizon. This can represent things such as calendar information, holidays, weather forecasts, etc. Models that accept future_covariates will look at the future values (up to the forecast horizon) when making forecasts.

Types of distributions
The likelihood has to be compatible with the domain of your time series’ values. For instance PoissonLikelihood can be used on discrete positive values, ExponentialLikelihood can be used on real positive values, and BetaLikelihood on real values in (0,1)
It is also possible to use QuantileRegression to apply a quantile loss and fit some desired quantiles directly.

title: Darts
text:
Ensembling models
Ensembling is about combining the forecasts produced by several models, in order to obtain a final - and hopefully better forecast.
For instance, in our example of a less naive model above, we manually combined a naive seasonal model with a naive drift model. Here, we will show how models forecasts can be automatically combined, naively using a NaiveEnsembleModel, or learned using RegressionEnsembleModel.
It is of course also possible to use past and/or future_covariates with ensemble model but they will be passed only to the models supporting them when calling fit() and predict().

title: Darts
text:
Naive Ensembling

from darts.models import NaiveEnsembleModel


models = [NaiveDrift(), NaiveSeasonal(12)]

ensemble_model = NaiveEnsembleModel(forecasting_models=models)

backtest = ensemble_model.historical_forecasts(
    series_air, start=0.6, forecast_horizon=3, verbose=True
)

print("MAPE = %.2f" % (mape(backtest, series_air)))
series_air.plot()
backtest.plot()




MAPE = 11.88

title: Darts
text:
Learned Ensembling
As expected in this case, the naive ensemble doesn’t give great results (although in some cases it could!)
We can sometimes do better if we see the ensembling as a supervised regression problem: given a set of forecasts (features), find a model that combines them in order to minimise errors on the target. This is what the RegressionEnsembleModel does. It accepts three parameters:
forecasting_models is a list of forecasting models whose predictions we want to ensemble.

regression_train_n_points is the number of time steps to use for fitting the “ensemble regression” model (i.e., the inner model that combines the forecasts).

regression_model is, optionally, a sklearn-compatible regression model or a Darts RegressionModel to be used for the ensemble regression. If not specified, a linear regression is used. Using a sklearn model is easy out-of-the-box, but using a RegressionModel allows to potentially take arbitrary lags of the individual forecasts as inputs of the regression model.
Once these elements are in place, a RegressionEnsembleModel can be used like a regular forecasting model:

from darts.models import RegressionEnsembleModel


models = [NaiveDrift(), NaiveSeasonal(12)]

ensemble_model = RegressionEnsembleModel(
    forecasting_models=models, regression_train_n_points=12
)

backtest = ensemble_model.historical_forecasts(
    series_air, start=0.6, forecast_horizon=3, verbose=True
)

print("MAPE = %.2f" % (mape(backtest, series_air)))
series_air.plot()
backtest.plot()




MAPE = 4.85










ensemble_model.fit(series_air)
ensemble_model.regression_model.model.coef_#|eval: false

array([0.0136882, 1.0980103], dtype=float32)



from darts.models import LinearRegressionModel


quantiles = [0.25, 0.5, 0.75]

models = [NaiveDrift(), NaiveSeasonal(12)]

regression_model = LinearRegressionModel(
    quantiles=quantiles,
    lags_future_covariates=[0],
    likelihood="quantile",
    fit_intercept=False,
)

ensemble_model = RegressionEnsembleModel(
    forecasting_models=models,
    regression_train_n_points=12,
    regression_model=regression_model,
)

backtest = ensemble_model.historical_forecasts(
    series_air, start=0.6, forecast_horizon=3, num_samples=500, verbose=True
)

print("MAPE = %.2f" % (mape(backtest, series_air)))
series_air.plot()
backtest.plot()




MAPE = 4.79

title: Nixtla - StatsForecasting
section: Train multiple models for many series
text:
Train multiple models for many series
StatsForecast can train many models on many time series efficiently.

Start by importing and instantiating the desired models. StatsForecast offers a wide variety of models grouped in the following categories:

Auto Forecast: Automatic forecasting tools search for the best parameters and select the best possible model for a series of time series. These tools are useful for large collections of univariate time series. Includes automatic versions of: Arima, ETS, Theta, CES.
Exponential Smoothing: Uses a weighted average of all past observations where the weights decrease exponentially into the past. Suitable for data with no clear trend or seasonality. Examples: SES, Holt’s Winters, SSO.
Benchmark models: classical models for establishing baselines. Examples: Mean, Naive, Random Walk
Intermittent or Sparse models: suited for series with very few non-zero observations. Examples: CROSTON, ADIDA, IMAPA
Multiple Seasonalities: suited for signals with more than one clear seasonality. Useful for low-frequency data like electricity and logs. Examples: MSTL.
Theta Models: fit two theta lines to a deseasonalized time series, using different techniques to obtain and combine the two theta lines to produce the final forecasts. Examples: Theta, DynamicTheta

Here you can check the complete list of models .
For this example we will use:

AutoARIMA: Automatically selects the best ARIMA (AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average) model using an information criterion. Ref: AutoARIMA.
HoltWinters: triple exponential smoothing, Holt-Winters’ method is an extension of exponential smoothing for series that contain both trend and seasonality. Ref: HoltWinters
SeasonalNaive: Memory Efficient Seasonal Naive predictions. Ref: SeasonalNaive
HistoricAverage: arthimetic mean. Ref: HistoricAverage.
DynamicOptimizedTheta: The theta family of models has been shown to perform well in various datasets such as M3. Models the deseasonalized time series. Ref: DynamicOptimizedTheta.

Import and instantiate the models. Setting the season_length argument is sometimes tricky. This article on Seasonal periods) by the master, Rob Hyndmann, can be useful.

from statsforecast.models import (
    AutoARIMA,
    HoltWinters,
    CrostonClassic as Croston, 
    HistoricAverage,
    DynamicOptimizedTheta as DOT,
    SeasonalNaive,
    MSTL
)


# Create a list of models and instantiation parameters
models = [
    AutoARIMA(season_length=24),
    HoltWinters(),
    Croston(),
    SeasonalNaive(season_length=24),
    HistoricAverage(),
    DOT(season_length=24),
    MSTL
]

We fit the models by instantiating a new StatsForecast object with the following parameters:

models: a list of models. Select the models you want from models and import them.
freq: a string indicating the frequency of the data. (See pandas available frequencies.)
n_jobs: n_jobs: int, number of jobs used in the parallel processing, use -1 for all cores.
fallback_model: a model to be used if a model fails.

Any settings are passed into the constructor. Then you call its fit method and pass in the historical data frame.

# Instantiate StatsForecast class as sf
sf = StatsForecast(
    df=Y_df, 
    models=models,
    freq='H', 
    n_jobs=-1,
    fallback_model = SeasonalNaive(season_length=7)
)







Note



StatsForecast achieves its blazing speed using JIT compiling through Numba. The first time you call the statsforecast class, the fit method should take around 5 seconds. The second time -once Numba compiled your settings- it should take less than 0.2s.


The forecast method takes two arguments: forecasts next h (horizon) and level.

h (int): represents the forecast h steps into the future. In this case, 12 months ahead.
level (list of floats): this optional parameter is used for probabilistic forecasting. Set the level (or confidence percentile) of your prediction interval. For example, level=[90] means that the model expects the real value to be inside that interval 90% of the times.

The forecast object here is a new data frame that includes a column with the name of the model and the y hat values, as well as columns for the uncertainty intervals. Depending on your computer, this step should take around 1min. (If you want to speed things up to a couple of seconds, remove the AutoModels like ARIMA and Theta)






Note



The forecast method is compatible with distributed clusters, so it does not store any model parameters. If you want to store parameters for every model you can use the fit and predict methods. However, those methods are not defined for distrubed engines like Spark, Ray or Dask.



forecasts_df = sf.forecast(h=48, level=[90])

text:
Evaluate the model’s performance
In previous steps, we’ve taken our historical data to predict the future. However, to asses its accuracy we would also like to know how the model would have performed in the past. To assess the accuracy and robustness of your models on your data perform Cross-Validation.
With time series data, Cross Validation is done by defining a sliding window across the historical data and predicting the period following it. This form of cross-validation allows us to arrive at a better estimation of our model’s predictive abilities across a wider range of temporal instances while also keeping the data in the training set contiguous as is required by our models.
The following graph depicts such a Cross Validation Strategy:


Cross-validation of time series models is considered a best practice but most implementations are very slow. The statsforecast library implements cross-validation as a distributed operation, making the process less time-consuming to perform. If you have big datasets you can also perform Cross Validation in a distributed cluster using Ray, Dask or Spark.
In this case, we want to evaluate the performance of each model for the last 2 days (n_windows=2), forecasting every second day (step_size=48). Depending on your computer, this step should take around 1 min.






Tip



Setting n_windows=1 mirrors a traditional train-test split with our historical data serving as the training set and the last 48 hours serving as the testing set.


The cross_validation method from the StatsForecast class takes the following arguments.

df: training data frame
h (int): represents h steps into the future that are being forecasted. In this case, 24 hours ahead.
step_size (int): step size between each window. In other words: how often do you want to run the forecasting processes.
n_windows(int): number of windows used for cross validation. In other words: what number of forecasting processes in the past do you want to evaluate.


crossvaldation_df = sf.cross_validation(
    df=Y_df,
    h=24,
    step_size=24,
    n_windows=2
  )

The crossvaldation_df object is a new data frame that includes the following columns:

unique_id index: (If you dont like working with index just run forecasts_cv_df.resetindex())
ds: datestamp or temporal index
cutoff: the last datestamp or temporal index for the n_windows. If n_windows=1, then one unique cuttoff value, if n_windows=2 then two unique cutoff values.
y: true value
"model": columns with the model’s name and fitted value.

Next, we will evaluate the performance of every model for every series using common error metrics like Mean Absolute Error (MAE) or Mean Square Error (MSE) Define a utility function to evaluate different error metrics for the cross validation data frame.
First import the desired error metrics from mlforecast.losses. Then define a utility function that takes a cross-validation data frame as a metric and returns an evaluation data frame with the average of the error metric for every unique id and fitted model and all cutoffs.

from utilsforecast.losses import mse
from utilsforecast.evaluation import evaluate


def evaluate_cross_validation(df, metric):
    models = df.drop(columns=['unique_id', 'ds', 'cutoff', 'y']).columns.tolist()
    evals = []
    # Calculate loss for every unique_id and cutoff.    
    for cutoff in df['cutoff'].unique():
        eval_ = evaluate(df[df['cutoff'] == cutoff], metrics=[metric], models=models)
        evals.append(eval_)
    evals = pd.concat(evals)
    evals = evals.groupby('unique_id').mean(numeric_only=True) # Averages the error metrics for all cutoffs for every combination of model and unique_id
    evals['best_model'] = evals.idxmin(axis=1)
    return evals







Warning



You can also use Mean Average Percentage Error (MAPE), however for granular forecasts, MAPE values are extremely hard to judge and not useful to assess forecasting quality.

text:
Select the best model for every unique series
Define a utility function that takes your forecast’s data frame with the predictions and the evaluation data frame and returns a data frame with the best possible forecast for every unique_id.

def get_best_model_forecast(forecasts_df, evaluation_df):
    df = forecasts_df.set_index('ds', append=True).stack().to_frame().reset_index(level=2) # Wide to long 
    df.columns = ['model', 'best_model_forecast'] 
    df = df.join(evaluation_df[['best_model']])
    df = df.query('model.str.replace("-lo-90|-hi-90", "", regex=True) == best_model').copy()
    df.loc[:, 'model'] = [model.replace(bm, 'best_model') for model, bm in zip(df['model'], df['best_model'])]
    df = df.drop(columns='best_model').set_index('model', append=True).unstack()
    df.columns = df.columns.droplevel()
    df = df.reset_index(level=1)
    return df

Create your production-ready data frame with the best forecast for every unique_id.

title: Neural Forecast
text:
3. Model Training

Fit the models
Using the NeuralForecast.fit method you can train a set of models to your dataset. You can define the forecasting horizon (12 in this example), and modify the hyperparameters of the model. For example, for the LSTM we changed the default hidden size for both encoder and decoders.

from neuralforecast import NeuralForecast
from neuralforecast.models import LSTM, NHITS, RNN


horizon = 12

# Try different hyperparmeters to improve accuracy.
models = [LSTM(h=horizon,                    # Forecast horizon
               max_steps=500,                # Number of steps to train
               scaler_type='standard',       # Type of scaler to normalize data
               encoder_hidden_size=64,       # Defines the size of the hidden state of the LSTM
               decoder_hidden_size=64,),     # Defines the number of hidden units of each layer of the MLP decoder
          NHITS(h=horizon,                   # Forecast horizon
                input_size=2 * horizon,      # Length of input sequence
                max_steps=100,               # Number of steps to train
                n_freq_downsample=[2, 1, 1]) # Downsampling factors for each stack output
          ]
nf = NeuralForecast(models=models, freq='M')
nf.fit(df=Y_df)

title: Neural Save and Load Models
text:
Saving and loading trained Deep Learning models has multiple valuable uses. These models are often costly to train; storing a pre-trained model can help reduce costs as it can be loaded and reused to forecast multiple times. Moreover, it enables Transfer learning capabilities, consisting of pre-training a flexible model on a large dataset and using it later on other data with little to no training. It is one of the most outstanding 🚀 achievements in Machine Learning 🧠 and has many practical applications.
In this notebook we show an example on how to save and load NeuralForecast models.
The two methods to consider are: 1. NeuralForecast.save: Saves models into disk, allows save dataset and config. 2. NeuralForecast.load: Loads models from a given path.
You can run these experiments using GPU with Google Colab.

text:
4. Save models
To save all the trained models use the save method. This method will save both the hyperparameters and the learnable weights (parameters).
The save method has the following inputs:

path: directory where models will be saved.
model_index: optional list to specify which models to save. For example, to only save the NHITS model use model_index=[2].
overwrite: boolean to overwrite existing files in path. When True, the method will only overwrite models with conflicting names.
save_dataset: boolean to save Dataset object with the dataset.


nf.save(path='./checkpoints/test_run/',
        model_index=None, 
        overwrite=True,
        save_dataset=True)

For each model, two files are created and stored:

[model_name]_[suffix].ckpt: Pytorch Lightning checkpoint file with the model parameters and hyperparameters.
[model_name]_[suffix].pkl: Dictionary with configuration attributes.

Where model_name corresponds to the name of the model in lowercase (eg. nhits). We use a numerical suffix to distinguish multiple models of each class. In this example the names will be automlp_0, nbeats_0, and nhits_0.






Important



The Auto models will be stored as their base model. For example, the AutoMLP trained above is stored as an MLP model, with the best hyparparameters found during tuning.

title: Statistical, Machine Learning and Neural Forecasting methods
text:
Statistical, Machine Learning, and Neural Forecasting Methods In this tutorial, we will explore the process of forecasting on the M5 dataset by utilizing the most suitable model for each time series. We’ll accomplish this through an essential technique known as cross-validation. This approach helps us in estimating the predictive performance of our models, and in selecting the model that yields the best performance for each time series.
The M5 dataset comprises of hierarchical sales data, spanning five years, from Walmart. The aim is to forecast daily sales for the next 28 days. The dataset is broken down into the 50 states of America, with 10 stores in each state.
In the realm of time series forecasting and analysis, one of the more complex tasks is identifying the model that is optimally suited for a specific group of series. Quite often, this selection process leans heavily on intuition, which may not necessarily align with the empirical reality of our dataset.
In this tutorial, we aim to provide a more structured, data-driven approach to model selection for different groups of series within the M5 benchmark dataset. This dataset, well-known in the field of forecasting, allows us to showcase the versatility and power of our methodology.
We will train an assortment of models from various forecasting paradigms:
StatsForecast
MLForecast
Machine Learning: Leveraging ML models like LightGBM, XGBoost, and LinearRegression can be advantageous due to their capacity to uncover intricate patterns in data. We’ll use the MLForecast library for this purpose.
NeuralForecast
Deep Learning: DL models, such as Transformers (AutoTFT) and Neural Networks (AutoNHITS), allow us to handle complex non-linear dependencies in time series data. We’ll utilize the NeuralForecast library for these models.
Using the Nixtla suite of libraries, we’ll be able to drive our model selection process with data, ensuring we utilize the most suitable models for specific groups of series in our dataset.

title: Statistical, Machine Learning and Neural Forecasting methods
text:
StatsForecast
StatsForecast is a comprehensive library providing a suite of popular univariate time series forecasting models, all designed with a focus on high performance and scalability.
Here’s what makes StatsForecast a powerful tool for time series forecasting:

Collection of Local Models: StatsForecast provides a diverse collection of local models that can be applied to each time series individually, allowing us to capture unique patterns within each series.
Simplicity: With StatsForecast, training, forecasting, and backtesting multiple models become a straightforward process, requiring only a few lines of code. This simplicity makes it a convenient tool for both beginners and experienced practitioners.
Optimized for Speed: The implementation of the models in StatsForecast is optimized for speed, ensuring that large-scale computations are performed efficiently, thereby reducing the overall time for model training and prediction.
Horizontal Scalability: One of the distinguishing features of StatsForecast is its ability to scale horizontally. It is compatible with distributed computing frameworks such as Spark, Dask, and Ray. This feature allows it to handle large datasets by distributing the computations across multiple nodes in a cluster, making it a go-to solution for large-scale time series forecasting tasks.

StatsForecast receives a list of models to fit each time series. Since we are dealing with Daily data, it would be benefitial to use 7 as seasonality.

# Import necessary models from the statsforecast library
from statsforecast.models import (
    # SeasonalNaive: A model that uses the previous season's data as the forecast
    SeasonalNaive,
    # Naive: A simple model that uses the last observed value as the forecast
    Naive,
    # HistoricAverage: This model uses the average of all historical data as the forecast
    HistoricAverage,
    # CrostonOptimized: A model specifically designed for intermittent demand forecasting
    CrostonOptimized,
    # ADIDA: Adaptive combination of Intermittent Demand Approaches, a model designed for intermittent demand
    ADIDA,
    # IMAPA: Intermittent Multiplicative AutoRegressive Average, a model for intermittent series that incorporates autocorrelation
    IMAPA,
    # AutoETS: Automated Exponential Smoothing model that automatically selects the best Exponential Smoothing model based on AIC
    AutoETS
)
from statsforecast.utils import ConformalIntervals

/home/ben/mambaforge/envs/cfast/lib/python3.11/site-packages/statsforecast/core.py:25: TqdmExperimentalWarning: Using `tqdm.autonotebook.tqdm` in notebook mode. Use `tqdm.tqdm` instead to force console mode (e.g. in jupyter console)
  from tqdm.autonotebook import tqdm


We fit the models by instantiating a new StatsForecast object with the following parameters:

models: a list of models. Select the models you want from models and import them.
freq: a string indicating the frequency of the data. (See panda’s available frequencies.)
n_jobs: int, number of jobs used in the parallel processing, use -1 for all cores.
fallback_model: a model to be used if a model fails. Any settings are passed into the constructor. Then you call its fit method and pass in the historical data frame.


intervals = ConformalIntervals(h=horizon, n_windows=2)
models = [
    SeasonalNaive(season_length=7),
    Naive(),
    HistoricAverage(),
    CrostonOptimized(),
    ADIDA(),
    IMAPA(),
    AutoETS(season_length=7)
]


# Instantiate the StatsForecast class
sf = StatsForecast(
    models=models,  # A list of models to be used for forecasting
    freq='D',  # The frequency of the time series data (in this case, 'D' stands for daily frequency)
    n_jobs=10,  # The number of CPU cores to use for parallel execution (-1 means use all available cores)
    verbose = True
)

The forecast method takes two arguments: forecasts next h (horizon) and level.

h (int): represents the forecast h steps into the future. In this case, 12 months ahead.
level (list of floats): this optional parameter is used for probabilistic forecasting. Set the level (or confidence percentile) of your prediction interval. For example, level=[90] means that the model expects the real value to be inside that interval 90% of the times.

The forecast object here is a new data frame that includes a column with the name of the model and the y hat values, as well as columns for the uncertainty intervals.
This block of code times how long it takes to run the forecasting function of the StatsForecast class, which predicts the next 28 days (h=28). The level is set to [90], meaning it will compute the 90% prediction interval. The time is calculated in minutes and printed out at the end.

from time import time

# Get the current time before forecasting starts, this will be used to measure the execution time
init = time()

# Call the forecast method of the StatsForecast instance to predict the next 28 days (h=28) 
# Level is set to [90], which means that it will compute the 90% prediction interval
fcst_df = sf.forecast(df=df, 
                      h=horizon,
                      level=[90],
                      prediction_intervals=intervals
                     )

# Get the current time after the forecasting ends
end = time()

# Calculate and print the total time taken for the forecasting in minutes
print(f'Forecast Minutes: {(end - init) / 60}')

title: Statistical, Machine Learning and Neural Forecasting methods
text:
MLForecast
MLForecast is a powerful library that provides automated feature creation for time series forecasting, facilitating the use of global machine learning models. It is designed for high performance and scalability.
Key features of MLForecast include:

Support for sklearn models: MLForecast is compatible with models that follow the scikit-learn API. This makes it highly flexible and allows it to seamlessly integrate with a wide variety of machine learning algorithms.
Simplicity: With MLForecast, the tasks of training, forecasting, and backtesting models can be accomplished in just a few lines of code. This streamlined simplicity makes it user-friendly for practitioners at all levels of expertise.
Optimized for speed: MLForecast is engineered to execute tasks rapidly, which is crucial when handling large datasets and complex models.
Horizontal Scalability: MLForecast is capable of horizontal scaling using distributed computing frameworks such as Spark, Dask, and Ray. This feature enables it to efficiently process massive datasets by distributing the computations across multiple nodes in a cluster, making it ideal for large-scale time series forecasting tasks.


from mlforecast import MLForecast
from mlforecast.target_transforms import Differences
from mlforecast.utils import PredictionIntervals
from window_ops.expanding import expanding_mean

!pip install lightgbm xgboost

# Import the necessary models from various libraries

# LGBMRegressor: A gradient boosting framework that uses tree-based learning algorithms from the LightGBM library
from lightgbm import LGBMRegressor

# XGBRegressor: A gradient boosting regressor model from the XGBoost library
from xgboost import XGBRegressor

# LinearRegression: A simple linear regression model from the scikit-learn library
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression


# Instantiate the MLForecast object
mlf = MLForecast(
    models=[LGBMRegressor(), XGBRegressor(), LinearRegression()],  # List of models for forecasting: LightGBM, XGBoost and Linear Regression
    freq='D',  # Frequency of the data - 'D' for daily frequency
    lags=list(range(1, 7)),  # Specific lags to use as regressors: 1 to 6 days
    lag_transforms = {
        1:  [expanding_mean],  # Apply expanding mean transformation to the lag of 1 day
    },
    date_features=['year', 'month', 'day', 'dayofweek', 'quarter', 'week'],  # Date features to use as regressors
)

Just call the fit models to train the select models. In this case we are generating conformal prediction intervals.

# Start the timer to calculate the time taken for fitting the models
init = time()

# Fit the MLForecast models to the data, with prediction intervals set using a window size of 28 days
mlf.fit(df, prediction_intervals=PredictionIntervals(h=horizon, n_windows=2))

# Calculate the end time after fitting the models
end = time()

# Print the time taken to fit the MLForecast models, in minutes
print(f'MLForecast Minutes: {(end - init) / 60}')

NeuralForecast
NeuralForecast is a robust collection of neural forecasting models that focuses on usability and performance. A broad collection of global models. Out of the box implementation of MLP, LSTM, RNN, TCN, DilatedRNN, NBEATS, NHITS, ESRNN, TFT, Informer, PatchTST and HINT.
A simple and intuitive interface that allows training, forecasting, and backtesting of various models in a few lines of code.
Support for GPU acceleration to improve computational speed.

Cross Validation in StatsForecast
The cross_validation method from the StatsForecast class accepts the following arguments:

df: A DataFrame representing the training data.
h (int): The forecast horizon, represented as the number of steps into the future that we wish to predict. For example, if we’re forecasting hourly data, h=24 would represent a 24-hour forecast.
step_size (int): The step size between each cross-validation window. This parameter determines how often we want to run the forecasting process.
n_windows (int): The number of windows used for cross validation. This parameter defines how many past forecasting processes we want to evaluate.

These parameters allow us to control the extent and granularity of our cross-validation process. By tuning these settings, we can balance between computational cost and the thoroughness of the cross-validation.

section: Evaluation per series and CV window
text:
Evaluation per series and CV window
In this section, we will evaluate the performance of each model for each time series and each cross validation window. Since we have many combinations, we will use dask to parallelize the evaluation. The parallelization will be done using fugue.

from typing import List, Callable

from distributed import Client
from fugue import transform
from fugue_dask import DaskExecutionEngine
from datasetsforecast.losses import mse, mae, smape

The evaluate function receives a unique combination of a time series and a window, and calculates different metrics for each model in df.

def evaluate(df: pd.DataFrame, metrics: List[Callable]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    eval_ = {}
    models = df.loc[:, ~df.columns.str.contains('unique_id|y|ds|cutoff|lo|hi')].columns
    for model in models:
        eval_[model] = {}
        for metric in metrics:
            eval_[model][metric.__name__] = metric(df['y'], df[model])
    eval_df = pd.DataFrame(eval_).rename_axis('metric').reset_index()
    eval_df.insert(0, 'cutoff', df['cutoff'].iloc[0])
    eval_df.insert(0, 'unique_id', df['unique_id'].iloc[0])
    return eval_df


str_models = cv_df.loc[:, ~cv_df.columns.str.contains('unique_id|y|ds|cutoff|lo|hi')].columns
str_models = ','.join([f"{model}:float" for model in str_models])
cv_df['cutoff'] = cv_df['cutoff'].astype(str)
cv_df['unique_id'] = cv_df['unique_id'].astype(str)

Let’s cleate a dask client.

client = Client() # without this, dask is not in distributed mode
# fugue.dask.dataframe.default.partitions determines the default partitions for a new DaskDataFrame
engine = DaskExecutionEngine({"fugue.dask.dataframe.default.partitions": 96})

The transform function takes the evaluate functions and applies it to each combination of time series (unique_id) and cross validation window (cutoff) using the dask client we created before.

evaluation_df = transform(
    cv_df.loc[:, ~cv_df.columns.str.contains('lo|hi')], 
    evaluate, 
    engine="dask",
    params={'metrics': [mse, mae, smape]}, 
    schema=f"unique_id:str,cutoff:str,metric:str, {str_models}", 
    as_local=True,
    partition={'by': ['unique_id', 'cutoff']}
)
